Bed 1.name: Japanese Maple ‘Bloodgood’ — assumed
Bed 1.light: Sun or light shade. Shelter from drying wind and harsh afternoon heat
Bed 1.water: Moist, well-drained. Fertile acid-to-neutral soil; avoid waterlogging
Bed 1.care:
Protect the fine foliage: Keep roots cool and shelter leaves from drying wind. Morning sun or dappled light usually gives good colour without scorching. A 5cm organic mulch helps, but keep it clear of the trunk.

Water slowly in dry spells: Deep, occasional watering is better than frequent surface sprinkling. Concentrate water over the root area when the upper soil begins to dry, especially while the tree is establishing or during hot windy weather.

Prune as little as possible: Remove only dead, crossing or badly placed growth. Make essential structural cuts while dormant, preferably after leaf fall and before midwinter sap movement. Do not shear the canopy into a shape.
Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Watch the red-bronze leaves unfurl and protect new growth from a late frost if a severe night is forecast.
Summer: Check soil during hot or windy spells, water deeply when needed and avoid disturbing shallow roots beneath the canopy.
Autumn: Record the colour sequence before leaf fall. Replenish mulch after the ground is moist, keeping the trunk clear.
Winter: Use the bare framework to identify dead or crossing wood, but keep pruning minimal and avoid late-winter cuts.
Bed 1.description: Best identified as Acer palmatum ‘Bloodgood’, this upright Japanese maple is the dominant canopy in Flower Bed 1. Its five- to seven-lobed leaves open deep red-purple, hold a dark wine colour through summer and brighten to scarlet in autumn. Small red spring flowers may be followed by winged fruits, but the lasting display is the dense purple foliage and graceful branching. The original label is missing, so ‘Bloodgood’ is recorded as a strong photographic best fit rather than a documented certainty.

profile.about: ‘Bloodgood’ is a widely grown purple-leaved selection of Acer palmatum. It forms an upright, bushy small tree with deeply divided leaves that remain dark red-purple for much of the growing season before becoming brighter red in autumn. That combination of sustained purple colour, broad upright habit and mature garden scale is the closest match to the Oak Lodge tree.

Bed 1.name: Japanese Aralia
Bed 1.light: Part shade. Tolerates shade but needs some light to show variegation
Bed 1.water: Fertile, well-drained. Avoid ground that is persistently parched or waterlogged
Bed 1.care:
Give it bright shade: Enough light maintains the white marbling without scorching it. Deep shade can reduce variegation; exposed sun and wind can bleach or tear the broad leaves. Its position under the Acer should be monitored as the canopy thickens.

Water while roots establish: Let the surface begin to dry, then soak the root area. An established Fatsia is fairly tolerant, but prolonged drought causes drooping and brown edges. Avoid automatic watering that leaves the crown wet.

Renew a leggy framework gradually: Cut one tired stem low in spring rather than shearing every shoot. Selective renewal encourages shoots from lower down while preserving the shrub’s architecture. Remove frost-damaged growth only once new growth shows what is alive.
Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Remove genuinely dead or frost-damaged growth and selectively shorten leggy stems once new buds are moving.
Summer: Check moisture under the Acer canopy and watch for capsid damage or scale on the large leaves and stems.
Autumn: Leave the cream flower globes for pollinators and record whether the variegation changes as light levels fall.
Winter: Shelter from severe drying wind and shake off heavy snow. Wait until spring before judging cold-damaged leaves and stems.
Bed 1.description: ‘Spider’s Web’ is a slow-growing Fatsia with large, hand-shaped evergreen leaves irregularly dusted and splashed with cream-white. The pattern is strongest on fresh growth and gives the shrub a frosted appearance beneath the Japanese maple. Mature plants develop thick stems and a rounded architectural framework, followed in autumn by spherical clusters of small cream flowers that can feed late pollinators.

Bed 1.name: Rhododendron
Bed 1.light: Part shade. Sheltered from drying wind and hot afternoon sun
Bed 1.care:
Protect its shallow roots: Mulch with leaf mould or composted bark and avoid digging nearby. Rhododendrons root close to the surface. Keep the root zone cool and evenly moist, but leave the stem base open and never bury the root flare.

Use rainwater when practical: Water deeply in dry spells, especially during bud development. Repeated hard tap water can raise pH over time. Yellow leaves with green veins may be a pH problem rather than a request for more general fertiliser.

Deadhead carefully, prune sparingly: Snap spent trusses away without damaging the buds beneath. Routine pruning is unnecessary. Remove dead wood after flowering and avoid cutting large old stems unless renovation is genuinely needed.
Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Top up an acidic organic mulch, water during dry bud development and enjoy the purplish-pink trusses in late spring.
Summer: Deadhead carefully after flowering and keep shallow roots moist in dry weather while next year’s buds form.
Autumn: Avoid late feeding or pruning. Remove fallen diseased leaves and make sure winter water can drain away.
Winter: Evergreen leaves may curl temporarily in cold weather. Water only if the ground is genuinely dry and unfrozen.
Bed 1.description: ‘Goldflimmer’ is a slow-growing evergreen rhododendron distinguished even when it is not flowering: each narrow dark-green leaf carries an irregular yellow central splash. Small trusses of funnel-shaped purplish-pink flowers arrive in late spring and early summer. It eventually forms a substantial rounded shrub, so the variegated foliage is the lasting contribution while the floral display is brief.

profile.about: ‘Goldflimmer’, also found under the synonym ‘Goldshine’, is an accepted variegated cultivar of Rhododendron. Its dark leaves with a central yellow splash distinguish it from edge-variegated shrubs. Like other rhododendrons it belongs to the heath family and needs acidic soil to take up nutrients normally.

Bed 1.name: Hosta 'Patriot'
Bed 1.light: Shade or part shade. Sheltered from hot afternoon sun and drying wind
Bed 1.water: Keep the root run cool and moist. Hosta's broad leaves lose water rapidly; check below mulch and avoid stagnant water around the crown.
Bed 1.care:
Protect Hosta shoots as they emerge: Check for slugs and snails from the first pointed spring buds. Remove hiding places near the crown and inspect after damp nights. Damaged leaves do not repair; retain sound foliage to feed the roots.

Clear foliage after natural dieback: Let autumn leaves yellow before removing collapsed growth. Divide only when crowded, in spring or autumn, keeping healthy buds on each piece. Avoid burying the crown under dense winter mulch.

Keep the cream margins sound: For this Oak Lodge specimen Patriot's exposed pale leaf edges need protection from hot sun and slug damage at the front of Bed 1.
Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Clear old foliage before the pointed shoots expand, mulch around—not over—the crown, and begin slug checks immediately.
Summer: Maintain moisture through dry spells. Remove badly damaged leaves and cut flower stems after blooming if seed is not wanted.
Autumn: Allow the leaves to yellow naturally, then clear collapsed foliage. Divide established clumps now or in early spring.
Winter: The crown is dormant below ground. Avoid standing wet and leave its position marked so it is not disturbed.
Bed 1.description: ‘Patriot’ forms a broad mound of dark green, ribbed leaves with bold, irregular cream-white margins. The pointed spring shoots expand into overlapping foliage that brightens the front-left of Bed 1, followed by pale lavender flower bells on upright stems in midsummer. The clean contrast is strongest in bright shade, provided its roots remain cool and evenly moist.

profile.about: ‘Patriot’ is a sport of Hosta ‘Francee’, selected for its much broader and brighter leaf margin. It is a medium, clump-forming hosta whose foliage supplies the main display and whose pale lavender flowers add height in midsummer.

Bed 1.name: Box Hedging
Bed 1.light: Sun to shade. Partial shade reduces scorch on dry sites
Bed 1.water: Moist, well-drained. Tolerates many soil types and pH levels
Bed 1.care:
Inspect before clipping: Look inside the hedge for webbing, caterpillars and black stem lesions. Clipping can spread contaminated material. Work only when foliage is dry, clean tools between affected sections and collect every clipping rather than leaving debris beneath the hedge.

Clip once after the main flush: August is the main shaping window; avoid creating repeated soft growth. Use sharp shears, taper the sides slightly so the base receives light, and avoid cutting in hot sun when newly exposed leaves may scorch.

Water roots, not foliage: Established box needs help mainly during prolonged dry weather. Soak the root zone and maintain airflow through the surface. Frequent overhead watering and dense wet foliage favour disease.
Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Inspect for box-tree caterpillar and remove dead leaves caught inside the hedge. Mulch lightly without touching stems.
Summer: Monitor again for caterpillars, water during sustained drought and make the main shaping clip in August on a dry, overcast day.
Autumn: Collect fallen and clipped leaves, clean tools and avoid late nitrogen that produces vulnerable soft growth.
Winter: Check snow load and wind scorch. Do not mistake cold bronzing for thirst or blight without inspecting stems and leaf lesions.
Bed 1.description: Common box is a dense, fine-textured evergreen shrub kept as a low clipped edge along the right side of Bed 1. Left unpruned, Buxus sempervirens can become a large shrub or small tree, but here its value comes from the opposite: compact geometry, small glossy leaves and a calm green structure through every season. Modern box care is as much about health surveillance as clipping because box blight and box-tree caterpillar can spread quickly.

problems.sign: Black stem streaks, dark leaf spots and rapid defoliation
problems.response: Isolate affected tools and clippings, improve airflow and hygiene, and confirm the disease before deciding whether removal is necessary.

profile.about: Buxus sempervirens is native to Britain and parts of Europe, North Africa and western Asia. Its natural form is a large evergreen shrub or small tree, with small yellowish spring flowers. Centuries of clipping created its familiar garden role as formal edging and topiary, but its current care must account for introduced caterpillars and fungal blight.
profile.provenanceNote: Species identity is secure; the hedge is recorded as common box rather than a dwarf cultivar because no cultivar label survives.

Bed 1.name: Euonymus 'Emerald 'n' Gold'
Bed 1.light: Sun or part shade. Better light usually strengthens golden colour
Bed 1.water: Water while establishing, then in drought. Evergreen Euonymus tolerates some dryness once rooted, but a newly moved root ball needs checks.
Bed 1.care:
Remove reverted Euonymus shoots: Cut all-green growth out at its origin. Those vigorous shoots can overtake the variegated plant. Retain leafy framework when shortening stems that encroach on neighbouring planting.

Inspect evergreen leaves for scale: Look for fixed bumps, sticky leaves and sooty growth. Treat the actual cause of poor foliage rather than automatically feeding. Cold-weather pink tinges on variegated leaves can be normal.

Retain the gold edge: For this Oak Lodge specimen Remove green reversions and stop Emerald 'n' Gold from overtaking the neighbouring Hosta at Bed 1's front.
Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Remove dead or reverted shoots, make any shaping cuts and add a light organic mulch without burying the stems.
Summer: Water only through real dry spells. Check stems and leaf undersides for scale, and trim growth that is obscuring neighbours.
Autumn: Cold weather may bring pink or red foliage tints. Avoid soft late growth caused by unnecessary feeding.
Winter: The evergreen framework remains visible. Brush off heavy snow and leave frost-coloured leaves unless they are genuinely dead.
Bed 1.description: ‘Emerald ’n’ Gold’ is a compact evergreen wintercreeper with small green leaves edged broadly in golden yellow. It forms a low spreading mound at the front-left of Bed 1, supplying colour throughout the year; exposed leaves often blush pink-red in cold weather. Its tiny early-summer flowers are inconspicuous, so the bright foliage and tidy groundcover habit are the real display.

Bed 1.name: Dahlia Double Dreamy® Lilac — assumed
Bed 1.position: Centre — compact dark foliage and lilac-magenta double flowers
Bed 1.light: Full sun. Warm and sheltered; support only if flower weight makes it lean
Bed 1.water: Deeply during hot flowering weather. Dahlia tubers need moisture in growth but rot in airless wet soil; leave the stem base clear.
Bed 1.care:
Deadhead the compact double Dahlias: Cut fading blooms back to a pair of leaves or a side bud. Support top-heavy shoots before wind damages them. Pinch young plants for branching, then let the formed buds develop.

Keep each tuber label through winter: Lift after frost blackens the top if the bed cannot remain well drained. Store sound tubers cool and frost-free, checking for rot. Both Double Dreamy colour identities remain assumptions; label divisions without promoting them to confirmed cultivars.

Support the central lilac display: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the dark-leaved Dahlia upright without letting its stems shade the lower Bed 1 edging.
Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Start stored tubers frost-free, divide only where each piece has a viable shoot, pinch young growth and plant out after the last frost.
Summer: Tie stems loosely, water deeply in dry spells and deadhead continuously. Watch soft tips for blackfly and young growth for slugs.
Autumn: Keep deadheading until frost blackens the top growth. Label by colour before cutting down and lifting the tubers.
Winter: Store lifted tubers cool, dry and frost-free, checking for rot. Outdoor tubers need deep mulch and excellent drainage.
Bed 1.description: Best identified as Dahlia Double Dreamy® Lilac, this compact plant combines very dark burgundy-green foliage with fully double, pompon-like flowers in lilac-magenta, their outer petals fading paler at the tips. It brings dense colour to the centre of Bed 1 from summer until frost without the height of a traditional border dahlia. The Double Dreamy match is strong from the flower form, foliage and its pairing with the yellow plant, but no original label survives.

Bed 1.name: Hosta (gold)
Bed 1.light: Part shade. Some gentle light develops the golden centre
Bed 1.water: Keep the root run cool and moist. Hosta's broad leaves lose water rapidly; check below mulch and avoid stagnant water around the crown.
Bed 1.care:
Protect Hosta shoots as they emerge: Check for slugs and snails from the first pointed spring buds. Remove hiding places near the crown and inspect after damp nights. Damaged leaves do not repair; retain sound foliage to feed the roots.

Clear foliage after natural dieback: Let autumn leaves yellow before removing collapsed growth. Divide only when crowded, in spring or autumn, keeping healthy buds on each piece. Avoid burying the crown under dense winter mulch.

Watch the relocated crown: For this Oak Lodge specimen Check the gold Hosta's root area for dryness before increasing sun exposure to intensify its yellow colour.
Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Clear the gold Hosta's old leaves before its shoots open and begin slug protection earlier than for neighbouring mature foliage.
Summer: Maintain an even root run so the pale leaves do not scorch, removing badly slugged leaves after replacements have expanded.
Autumn: Mark this crown separately as the gold Hosta while its leaves yellow, then clear them once fully collapsed.
Winter: Keep the dormant crown uncovered by Bed 1 leaf litter and avoid digging in its marked position.
Bed 1.description: ‘Gold Standard’ is a medium-to-large Hosta whose broad heart-shaped leaves change as the season develops: green centres brighten towards gold while irregular darker green margins remain. Pale lavender flower bells rise above the mound in midsummer. The plant moved from Bed 2 into Bed 1 in June 2026, so its current spread and leaf colour will reflect both the move and the amount of light it receives.

Bed 1.name: Little Heath
Bed 1.position: Front edge — 7 plants forming a low border. Added June 2026.
Bed 1.light: Sun or part shade. Sheltered from cold drying wind
Bed 1.care:
Maintain an acidic root zone: Use leaf mould, composted bark or ericaceous material as mulch. Pieris cannot use nutrients normally in alkaline soil. Keep lime-rich materials away and use rainwater where practical during dry spells.

Water the seven plants individually: A continuous border can hide one drying root ball. Check along the whole row during establishment rather than assuming one moisture reading represents every plant. Keep soil moist, never stagnant.

Prune very lightly: Remove damaged growth and faded flowers; preserve the compact natural shape. Routine shearing would spoil the variegated tips. If one plant outgrows the line, shorten individual shoots after flowering rather than clipping the entire border.
Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Watch pink buds open to white flowers, remove winter damage and top up an acidic mulch after the soil is moist.
Summer: Check all seven root balls in dry weather, use rainwater where practical and inspect leaves for lacebug stippling.
Autumn: Leave new growth to harden naturally; avoid late feeding and clear diseased fallen leaves from within the border.
Winter: Protect young plants from drying wind and avoid waterlogged soil. Wait until spring before pruning cold-marked tips.
Bed 1.description: ‘Little Heath’ is a compact Pieris with small evergreen leaves edged in silvery white and young growth flushed pink. Sparse white urn-shaped flowers open from pink buds in spring, but the fine variegated foliage is the more dependable feature. Seven plants form a repeated low border at the front of Bed 1, where their slow growth and consistent colouring create a deliberate edge rather than seven separate specimens.

Bed 1.name: Pieris ‘Forest Flame’ — label confirmed
Bed 1.position: Front-right inside the box edge — added August 2026
Bed 1.light: Sun or partial shade. Sheltered light with protection from harsh morning sun
Bed 1.water: Even root moisture. Shallow Pieris roots must not dry hard; use rainwater where available and allow excess to drain.
Bed 1.care:
Keep the root run acidic: Use acidic, humus-rich soil and a shallow leaf-mould mulch. Keep lime away and do not cultivate through the fine surface roots. Check soil pH if young leaves yellow between green veins.

Preserve next spring's flowers: Remove spent flower clusters carefully, with little routine pruning. Make any necessary shaping cuts after flowering. Protect new coloured shoots from drying winds and late frost; do not clip away developing buds later in the year.

Allow for a taller Pieris: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep Forest Flame distinct from the low Little Heath edging and allow its upright crown enough future space.
Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Protect the fresh red growth from late frost and remove faded flowers without damaging new shoots.
Summer: Maintain even moisture, mulch with leaf mould and inspect leaf undersides for lacebug.
Autumn: Refresh an acidic mulch and avoid late feeding that would produce soft frost-prone shoots.
Winter: Keep the root zone drained and leave healthy evergreen growth unpruned.
Bed 1.description: ‘Forest Flame’ is an evergreen Pieris whose young leaves open bright red, pass through pink and cream, then mature green. Branched clusters of small cream bells appear in spring. In Bed 1 it adds upright evergreen structure among the lower ‘Little Heath’ edging, but it needs acidic soil, steady moisture and protection from harsh early sun on frosted new growth.

Bed 2.name: Peony ‘Sarah Bernhardt’ — assumed
Bed 2.light: Full sun. Sheltered from wind and free from close root competition
Bed 2.water: Deep, fertile and drained. Moisture-retentive without winter waterlogging
Bed 2.care:
Keep the crown shallow: Growth buds should sit no more than about 2.5cm below the soil. Deep planting is a common reason a healthy-looking peony fails to flower. Keep mulch away from the crown so it does not gradually become buried.

Support before the flowers become heavy: Place a ring or discreet stakes around emerging shoots in spring. Early support disappears into the foliage and prevents rain-heavy flowers from pulling stems onto the path. Add it before the buds enlarge.

Leave the clump in peace: Move or divide only when flowering genuinely declines. Established peonies are deep-rooted and long-lived. If division is necessary, do it in autumn and replant each piece at the original shallow depth.
Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Clear old stems, keep the crown exposed, add support early and water deeply only if drought threatens developing buds.
Summer: Enjoy and photograph the fully open flowers for identification, deadhead as blooms fade and retain healthy foliage to feed the crown.
Autumn: Cut foliage to ground after it dies back and remove it from the bed. Divide only if the established clump has stopped performing.
Winter: The crown is dormant and needs no frost protection. Avoid piling mulch over the buds or leaving the root zone waterlogged.
Bed 2.description: The herbaceous peony in lower Bed 2 makes a substantial leafy clump with a brief early-summer flower display, then dies back in autumn. Sarah Bernhardt is the existing working cultivar assumption, not a retained-label identification. Record a fully open flower before relying on that cultivar's exact colour and form; keep the crown shallow and support heavy stems before the buds open.

Bed 2.name: Weigela ‘Prism Magic Carpet’ — label confirmed
Bed 2.light: Sun or light shade. Enough light for leaf colour without harsh scorch
Bed 2.water: Fertile and well-drained. Evenly moist; avoid very dry or waterlogged ground
Bed 2.care:
Prune immediately after flowering: Remove up to one in three of the oldest stems at the base. Weigela flowers on established side shoots. Selective renewal after bloom preserves next year’s display and keeps the shrub open without turning it into a clipped mound.

Balance colour with leaf protection: Give coloured foliage good light but watch the hottest reflected sun. Too much shade dulls golden leaves and reduces flowering; hot dry exposure can scorch them. Maintain root moisture before assuming the plant needs a shadier position.

Feed the soil modestly: Mulch in spring and avoid forcing soft, sappy growth. A light organic mulch over moist soil is usually enough. High-nitrogen feed can create lush shoots with fewer flowers and greater pest susceptibility.
Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Mulch after rain, watch the gold and bronze leaf colour develop, and wait until flowers finish before making routine cuts.
Summer: Photograph the flower and whole shrub as it matures, then remove selected old stems and shorten obstructive shoots after bloom.
Autumn: Allow growth to harden and leaves to fall naturally. Take hardwood cuttings later in the season if a backup is wanted.
Winter: Inspect the bare framework for damaged stems but reserve renovation pruning for early spring and routine renewal for after flowering.
Bed 2.description: Weigela florida ‘Prism Magic Carpet’ is the compact Weigela in the middle of Flower Bed 2, with yellow-green foliage flushed bronze on young tips. Pink trumpet-shaped flowers open on short side shoots in late spring and early summer, while the coloured leaves keep the shrub useful beyond bloom. The cultivar is confirmed by the retained Willowbrook Garden Centre label photographed in August 2026.

Bed 2.name: Silverbush
Bed 2.light: Full sun. Warm, sheltered and preferably south- or west-facing
Bed 2.water: Sharply drained. Low to moderate fertility; chalk, loam or sand
Bed 2.care:
Make drainage the priority: Keep the crown above wet soil and never water by calendar. Check deeply before watering. Grit and an open soil structure around the root zone matter more than added fertility, particularly beside a wall where drainage can vary sharply.

Water for establishment, then step back: Soak during prolonged summer drought and keep much drier in winter. A newly planted shrub needs help while roots extend, but an established silverbush should dry between waterings. Cold saturated soil is far more dangerous than a short dry spell.

Trim lightly after flowering: Shorten soft tips to preserve a compact mound. Avoid cutting hard into old leafless wood, which may not reshoot. Remove winter damage only after new spring growth shows clearly where stems are alive.
Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Wait for active growth before removing frost-damaged tips, then check drainage and enjoy the first pink-striped buds.
Summer: Deadhead or lightly trim after the main flush, watering only during prolonged drought while the root zone is genuinely dry.
Autumn: Stop feeding and reduce watering so growth hardens. Take semi-ripe cuttings as insurance if winter conditions are a concern.
Winter: Keep the evergreen mound sheltered from cold wet conditions and do not prune healthy silver growth during frost.
Bed 2.description: Silverbush forms a compact, rounded mound of narrow leaves densely coated in silver hairs, making it one of the brightest foliage plants in Flower Bed 2. Pink-striped buds open into white funnel-shaped flowers with yellow centres from late spring through summer. It comes from the Mediterranean and copes well with drought once established, but the combination of winter cold, wet soil and an exposed position is its principal weakness in Bromsgrove.

Bed 2.name: Geum ‘Totally Tangerine’ — assumed
Bed 2.position: Lower section — orange flowers. Moved from Bed 1 in July 2026.
Bed 2.light: Sun or light shade. An open position that does not bake completely dry
Bed 2.water: Moist but well-drained. Fertile border soil; avoid winter waterlogging
Bed 2.care:
Keep it moist, never stagnant: Water during prolonged dry spells, especially after the move. Most border geums dislike drying out completely but also suffer in winter wet. Check below the surface before soaking and keep the crown level with the surrounding soil.

Deadhead down to a side shoot: Remove fading stems to extend the display. Follow each spent flowering branch back to fresh buds or the basal foliage. Once the main flush ends, cutting old stems away tidies the rosette and can encourage more bloom.

Renew congested clumps: Divide every few years when the centre becomes woody or flowering weakens. Lift in spring or autumn, keep vigorous outer pieces and discard the tired centre. Replant promptly at the same depth and water through establishment.
Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Clear tired foliage, mulch lightly around the crown and divide congested clumps before flower stems extend.
Summer: Deadhead continuously, water through real drought and photograph flowers at different ages to support identification.
Autumn: Remove spent stems, divide if necessary and allow the basal rosette to remain unless foliage is diseased.
Winter: Protect the crown from waterlogging and leave healthy semi-evergreen foliage in place for shelter and structure.

Totally Tangerine is recorded as an assumed match, so the flower form and full-season behaviour still need checking. Its practical needs are a cool, moist but drained root run, removal of tired flowering stems and occasional division when the clump becomes congested.

Bed 2.name: Maiden Pink
Bed 2.light: Full sun. Open and airy, in either a sheltered or exposed aspect
Bed 2.water: Well-drained. Neutral to alkaline chalk, loam or sandy soil
Bed 2.care:
Give the crown light and air: Keep taller neighbours from collapsing over the mat. Full sun and moving air keep the evergreen foliage compact and reduce mildew. Remove fallen leaves and encroaching stems that trap winter damp over the crown.

Water only when the root zone dries: Help a young plant establish, then avoid routine watering. Dianthus tolerates short dry spells better than waterlogging. Check beneath the mat and soak only if the soil is dry; do not leave water around the crown in winter.

Shear lightly after flowering: Remove spent stems without cutting into old bare growth. Regular deadheading extends bloom. After the main flush, a light trim keeps the mat dense; divide every three to five years if the centre becomes thin.
Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Comb out dead leaves, trim any winter damage lightly and divide an ageing mat before flower stems develop.
Summer: Deadhead ruby-red flowers regularly, keep taller neighbours clear and water only if the root zone becomes genuinely dry.
Autumn: Finish the light post-flowering trim and clear debris so the evergreen mat enters winter dry and airy.
Winter: Leave healthy foliage intact, avoid standing wet and clear fallen leaves that could smother the low crown.
Bed 2.description: Maiden Pink ‘Leuchtfunk’ forms a low evergreen mat of narrow, grass-like leaves between the walls of Flower Bed 2. In summer it produces many single ruby-red flowers, each marked by a darker ring around the centre. The cultivar is also sold under the English synonym ‘Flashing Lights’. Its retained nursery label is visible in the Oak Lodge photograph, turning what was previously a generic Dianthus record into a confident cultivar identification.

Bed 2.name: Hydrangea petiolaris
Bed 2.position: Against the far wall — self-clinging climber
Bed 2.light: Partial shade or sun. Excellent for a cool wall; sun needs reliable moisture
Bed 2.water: Moist but well-drained. Humus-rich, preferably acid to neutral
Bed 2.care:
Support the plant while it establishes: Tie young stems to a temporary support until aerial roots grip. Self-clinging does not mean instantly self-supporting. Guide the first framework across sound masonry and keep it clear of gutters, roof spaces and damaged mortar.

Keep the root run cool and moist: Mulch in spring and water deeply through establishment. A wall can create a dry rain shadow. Water the root area rather than the leaves, and keep mulch clear of the stem base so moisture is conserved without encouraging rot.

Prune after flowering: Shorten outward-growing shoots and control the boundary without stripping the framework. Flowers form on the previous year’s growth. Make shaping cuts after bloom, removing only what threatens masonry, windows or neighbouring space; hard renovation can sacrifice flowers.
Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Refresh mulch after rain, tie in loose young stems and check that new aerial roots are attaching only to sound wall surfaces.
Summer: Enjoy the white lacecap heads, water during wall-side drought and prune for containment immediately after flowering.
Autumn: Record yellow foliage colour, clear diseased leaves and avoid late feeding that would create soft growth.
Winter: Inspect the bare branching framework, peeling bark and wall clearances; retie loose stems but leave routine pruning until after bloom.
Bed 2.description: Climbing hydrangea is a slow-starting but ultimately vigorous wall plant, attaching itself with aerial roots rather than twining stems. Broad green leaves make a dense summer covering and turn yellow before falling, while mature plants carry wide, flat heads of small fertile flowers surrounded by showy white florets in early summer. At Oak Lodge it is intended to clothe the far wall of Flower Bed 2, so establishment and controlled wall coverage matter more than chasing rapid growth.

Bed 2.name: Euonymus 'Emerald Gaiety'
Bed 2.light: Sun or partial shade. Good light maintains the cleanest variegation
Bed 2.water: Water while establishing, then in drought. Evergreen Euonymus tolerates some dryness once rooted, but a newly moved root ball needs checks.
Bed 2.care:
Remove reverted Euonymus shoots: Cut all-green growth out at its origin. Those vigorous shoots can overtake the variegated plant. Retain leafy framework when shortening stems that encroach on neighbouring planting.

Inspect evergreen leaves for scale: Look for fixed bumps, sticky leaves and sooty growth. Treat the actual cause of poor foliage rather than automatically feeding. Cold-weather pink tinges on variegated leaves can be normal.

Keep the relocated white edge visible: For this Oak Lodge specimen Remove solid-green shoots and trim only stems crowding the lower Bed 2 planting beside the wall.
Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Remove any solid-green Emerald Gaiety reversions at their origin and shape only stems pressing into nearby Bed 2 plants.
Summer: Inspect the white-margined leaves for scale and water deeply only through prolonged drought along the boundary.
Autumn: Let cold bring its pink tint, clearing fallen leaves caught inside the low evergreen framework.
Winter: Brush off heavy snow and retain sound white-edged shoots; postpone reshaping until spring growth confirms what is alive.
Bed 2.description: ‘Emerald Gaiety’ is a low, bushy evergreen Euonymus with rounded green leaves irregularly edged in white. Cold weather can flush those pale margins pink, giving useful colour through winter, and shoots may climb if they meet the wall. The plant moved from the former Flower Bed 3 into the lower section of Bed 2 in June 2026, where it now provides a cool-edged foliage contrast beneath taller shrubs.

Bed 2.name: Rose (inherited)
Bed 2.position: Position 8 — established by the previous owners
Bed 2.light: Sun to light shade. Best flowering usually comes with at least half a day of direct light
Bed 2.water: Deeply in sustained dry spells. Water established roses at soil level, especially beside a wall; avoid waterlogging.
Bed 2.care:
Prune an unknown rose conservatively: Remove dead, diseased and rubbing stems first. Record its height, repeat-flowering pattern and long-cane behaviour before choosing shrub, climbing or rambling pruning. Do not cut it down like a herbaceous perennial.

Keep rose foliage healthy: Feed and mulch in spring, leaving the stem base clear. Remove fallen diseased leaves and inspect new shoots for aphids. Deadhead if repeat flowers are wanted; retain selected hips where autumn fruit is part of the display.

Record this rose's own habit: For this Oak Lodge specimen Use the Bed 2 flowering photographs and new cane growth to choose pruning, independently of the yellow Bed 3 rose.
Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Mulch over moist soil, feed once growth starts and remove only dead, damaged or clearly crossing wood until the habit is understood.
Summer: Water deeply in sustained dry spells, deadhead selectively and photograph flowers, leaves, prickles and overall habit for the record.
Autumn: Leave some hips if attractive and tie in or shorten wind-rocked stems only where needed.
Winter: Avoid class-specific hard pruning until the plant's growth habit is clear; remove dead or unsafe wood in suitable weather.
Bed 2.description: This established rose in Bed 2 was inherited from the previous owners. Until its habit, flowers and repeat pattern are documented, the record deliberately stops at Rosa rather than guessing a cultivar or rose class. Give it the standard fundamentals—light, deep watering in dry spells, mulch and airflow—then use observed growth to decide the most suitable pruning approach.

Bed 3.name: Yellow Corydalis — assumed
Bed 3.position: Position 11 — against the wall, with yellow flowers
Bed 3.light: Partial or full shade. Well suited to the cooler wall-side position
Bed 3.water: During dry establishment spells. A cool, drained wall pocket suits yellow corydalis; avoid a permanently wet crown.
Bed 3.care:
Thin corydalis seedlings selectively: Keep desired seedlings and remove those crowding smaller neighbours. Pseudofumaria can seed into cracks. Pull young unwanted plants before their roots establish in difficult masonry joints.

Refresh tired soft growth: Trim exhausted flowering stems to healthy foliage. This is a low perennial, not the Kerria shrub named in the old ID. No woody-shrub pruning or annual stooling is appropriate.

Manage a small wall perennial: For this Oak Lodge specimen Thin corydalis seedlings in the Bed 3 wall gap; the old Kerria identifier is historical, not a shrub-care instruction.
Bed 3.seasonal:
Spring: Clear only damaged foliage, protect fresh shoots from slugs and leave the clump unpruned as flowering begins.
Summer: Water only if the wall-side soil becomes genuinely dry; remove selected seedheads if seedlings are spreading beyond the allocated gap.
Autumn: Thin surplus seedlings while small and leave the healthiest mound to continue flowering and overwinter.
Winter: Keep the crown free of smothering debris and remove only collapsed or diseased leaves; no woody framework pruning is required.
Bed 3.description: The plant recorded earlier as Kerria is a much smaller wall-side perennial: finely divided pale-green leaves form a soft mound, with short sprays of slender, spurred yellow flowers held above it. The Oak Lodge photographs fit yellow corydalis, Pseudofumaria lutea, rather than a woody Kerria shrub. It can flower from late spring through summer and place seedlings into cool cracks and gaps, so management is about selective thinning rather than shrub pruning.

Bed 3.name: Centaurea 'Snowy Owl'
Bed 3.light: Sun or light shade. Best flowering and sturdier stems with good light
Bed 3.water: Water when the root zone dries. Avoid drought during flowering, but let surplus moisture drain away from the clump.
Bed 3.care:
Cut cornflower back after its first flush: Remove finished stems and tired foliage near the base. Fresh leaves may make a cleaner mound and a smaller second display. Water if the soil is dry after cutting; avoid leaving mildew-covered foliage tangled in the centre.

Control the spreading clump: Divide in spring or autumn only when it becomes crowded. Replant vigorous outer sections and remove roots spreading into adjacent planting. Deadheading also limits unwanted seed.

Refresh the white-flowered clump: For this Oak Lodge specimen Cut Snowy Owl's tired first-flush foliage back before it sprawls across the lower wall-gap planting.
Bed 3.seasonal:
Spring: Clear dead stems, divide a congested clump if needed and protect emerging shoots from slugs.
Summer: Deadhead for continuity, then shear tired foliage after the first flush to encourage clean regrowth.
Autumn: Leave sound late flowers briefly for insects, then remove mildew-marked foliage before it collapses.
Winter: The crown rests below ground; avoid standing wet and keep its position marked during bed work.
Bed 3.description: ‘Snowy Owl’ is a white-flowered form of perennial cornflower, carrying finely fringed, thistle-like heads above grey-green leaves. The outer florets create a soft starburst around a paler centre from May into July. Cutting the whole clump back after its first display can replace tired, mildew-marked foliage with a fresh mound and sometimes a second, smaller flush of flowers.

Bed 3.name: Spiraea 'Double Play Big Bang'
Bed 3.light: Full sun or light shade. Sun gives the strongest foliage colour and flowering
Bed 3.water: While establishing; then in drought. Water the root area rather than wetting only the surrounding wall surface.
Bed 3.care:
Prune summer-flowering Spiraea in spring: Shorten last year's shoots before vigorous new growth starts. These Japanese Spiraeas flower on the current season's growth. Remove weak and oldest stems selectively to maintain a low, open mound.

Refresh the pink flower display: Clip faded flower clusters just above leafy shoots. A light trim may encourage another flush. Preserve enough golden foliage to rebuild the plant and avoid heavy late-autumn pruning.

Keep four crowns distinguishable: For this Oak Lodge specimen Prune the four Big Bang shrubs individually; do not include the smaller relocated Magic Carpet in the same height target.
Bed 3.seasonal:
Spring: Cut all four plants back evenly before strong growth if renewal is needed, then mulch the moist soil.
Summer: Deadhead after the main flower flush and compare vigour across the four plants before making corrective cuts.
Autumn: Leave the foliage to complete its orange-red display, then clear diseased fallen leaves.
Winter: Use the bare outlines to check that one plant is not crowding the others; take hardwood cuttings if replacements are wanted.
Bed 3.description: Double Play® Big Bang earns its name from two separate displays: young leaves open orange to pink-red before becoming luminous yellow, then broad, flat heads of bright pink flowers cover the rounded shrub in summer. The foliage warms again to orange-red in autumn. Four plants repeat that colour along the Bed 3 wall, so even growth and coordinated pruning matter more here than treating each as an isolated specimen.

Bed 3.name: Sedum ‘Rose Carpet’ — label confirmed
Bed 3.light: Full sun or partial shade. Best flower and compact growth in open light
Bed 3.water: Let the root zone dry between soakings. Mat-forming stonecrops store water in their leaves; frequent small splashes are unnecessary.
Bed 3.care:
Keep stonecrop stems out of wet debris: Maintain an open, gritty surface around the mat. Avoid rich feeding and dense organic mulch over the crown. Remove decaying stems selectively while keeping sound rooted growth.

Control the mat after flowering: Trim encroaching stems and remove unwanted rooted pieces. Replant healthy pieces only where more cover is needed. Stonecrops differ in hardiness: follow this plant's own rating rather than assuming every Sedum survives severe frost.

Protect position 1 from wet mulch: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the low Rose Carpet cushion out of the deeper organic mulch used for neighbouring shrubs.

Spring: Clear dead stems, check the crown is firm and divide only if the mat has outgrown its space.
Summer: Water newly planted roots during drought, then allow the soil to dry between soakings and enjoy the pink flower domes.
Autumn: Cut back after flowering if untidy and keep fallen leaves from trapping moisture over the crown.
Winter: Leave the dormant crown dry and airy; do not cover it with a dense wet mulch.

Bed 3.name: Weeping Cherry ‘Kiku-shidare-zakura’ — assumed
Bed 3.position: Position 10 — established weeping canopy in Bed 3
Bed 3.light: Full sun. Open light supports the best blossom display
Bed 3.water: Moist but well-drained. Moderately fertile; never persistently waterlogged
Bed 3.care:
Water the roots, not the trunk: Deep-soak only during prolonged dry weather. The established tree should not need routine shallow watering. Check beneath the canopy and soak the root zone slowly if the soil is dry well below the surface, especially during spring growth.

Prune sparingly and in summer: Make necessary cuts after flowering in a dry spell. Remove dead, damaged, crossing or obstructive growth while the tree is in leaf. Avoid autumn and winter pruning, when Prunus wounds are more vulnerable to silver leaf and bacterial canker.

Respect the graft and natural curtain: Remove suckers and lift only the branches that genuinely obstruct access. Cut shoots arising below the graft back at their origin. Shortening every pendent branch into a uniform fringe would replace the characteristic weeping habit with congested regrowth.
Bed 3.seasonal:
Spring: Enjoy and photograph the blossom before leaf expansion. Check for dead twigs, but postpone non-urgent cuts until dry summer weather.
Summer: Inspect the canopy after flowering, remove suckers and make only essential shaping or clearance cuts in dry conditions.
Autumn: Record leaf colour and clear diseased fallen foliage. Do not carry out routine pruning as the tree moves into dormancy.
Winter: Use the bare framework to spot rubbing branches, cankers and the graft union, marking work for summer rather than cutting now.
Bed 3.description: Long pendent branches give this Bed 3 cherry an umbrella-shaped framework, followed by pink spring blossom and a green summer canopy. Kiku-shidare-zakura is the recorded working assumption; neither that cultivar nor the rootstock is proven. Retain the tree's observed shape, document open flowers and make necessary pruning cuts in dry summer weather.

Bed 3.care:
Prune an unknown rose conservatively: Remove dead, diseased and rubbing stems first. Record its height, repeat-flowering pattern and long-cane behaviour before choosing shrub, climbing or rambling pruning. Do not cut it down like a herbaceous perennial.

Keep rose foliage healthy: Feed and mulch in spring, leaving the stem base clear. Remove fallen diseased leaves and inspect new shoots for aphids. Deadhead if repeat flowers are wanted; retain selected hips where autumn fruit is part of the display.

Retain the yellow-flowered framework: For this Oak Lodge specimen Tie in useful Bed 3 canes and keep the Vinca beneath them from covering the rose's stem base.

Autumn: Retain useful hips and secure any cane exposed to wall-gap winds without shortening sound growth unnecessarily.
Winter: Remove unsafe or dead wood only; wait for a confirmed rose class before applying a class-specific winter pruning regime.

Bed 3.name: Variegated Lesser Periwinkle — assumed
Bed 3.position: Position 9 — trailing beneath the inherited Rose; provisional identification from August photographs
Bed 3.light: Partial shade to shade. Tolerates sun where the root run does not dry severely
Bed 3.water: Moderate; avoid prolonged drying. Vinca tolerates some dry shade once established, but trailing plants in pots still depend on the container's moisture.
Bed 3.care:
Keep Vinca runners within bounds: Shorten trails that root into neighbouring planting. Remove unwanted rooted pieces completely. Trim after the main spring flowers, retaining leafy growth for the next display.

Remove green reversions: Cut all-green shoots back to their point of origin. Variegated forms can be overtaken by vigorous green growth. Give enough light for leaf colour without letting the shallow roots bake.

Contain the groundcover under the rose: For this Oak Lodge specimen Lift unwanted rooted runners at position 9 before they connect with neighbouring planting pockets.
Bed 3.seasonal:
Spring: Photograph the flowers face-on and side-on, then compare leaf size and variegation before refining the identity.
Summer: Water only during sustained drought and redirect runners away from smaller neighbours.
Autumn: Shorten excessive trails and remove rooted pieces only where the mat is spreading beyond its allotted position.
Winter: Leave sound evergreen growth in place and clear wet debris caught beneath the Rose.
Bed 3.description: The trailing variegated groundcover at Bed 3 position 9 is provisionally identified as lesser periwinkle, Vinca minor. Cream-edged opposite leaves and creeping stems are visible both in its dedicated photographs and beneath the inherited Rose, but no flower or label establishes a cultivar.

Bed 4.name: Apple ‘Cox’s Orange Pippin’ — assumed
Bed 4.latin: Malus domestica ‘Cox’s Orange Pippin’ · rootstock MM106 assumed
Bed 4.light: Full sun. Open light supports blossom, ripening and airflow
Bed 4.water: Deeply in dry spells during fruit swell. Mulch the root area while keeping the trunk clear; shallow frequent splashes do not reach tree roots.
Bed 4.care:
Prune according to the apple's training: Free-standing trees are normally pruned while dormant; trained forms need their own summer routine. Retain fruiting spurs and remove dead or crossing wood gradually. Do not select a pruning system from the assumed rootstock alone.

Record fruit before relying on a cultivar: Thin crowded fruitlets and pick when fruit releases readily with a gentle lift. Log flavour, skin, picking date and storage. Cox or Bramley and MM106 are working assumptions; pollination and final tree size remain unconfirmed.

Keep feeder access clear: For this Oak Lodge specimen Maintain the apple's useful framework around the bird feeders and photograph fruit before relying on the assumed Cox identity.
Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Inspect blossom after frost, mulch the moist root zone and avoid insecticide use while pollinators are working.
Summer: Thin congested fruitlets after the June drop, water through drought and carry out only suitable trained-tree pruning.
Autumn: Taste-test and record the picking window; remove damaged windfalls and store only sound fruit.
Winter: Prune a free-standing tree for an open crown, removing dead, diseased and crossing wood without over-thinning.
Bed 4.description: The Bed 4 apple provides spring blossom, summer shade and fruit, as well as the framework for the bird feeders. Cox's Orange Pippin on MM106 is an existing assumption, not a verified identification. Bed 4.name: Callistemon Inferno ('Yanferno')
Bed 4.light: Full sun. Warm, sheltered south- or west-facing conditions
Bed 4.water: Moist during active growth. Bottlebrush tolerates some dryness after rooting, but buds suffer if the root ball dries completely.
Bed 4.care:
Protect Inferno from severe frost: Use the warmest sheltered position and watch cold forecasts. This H3 bottlebrush is marginal outdoors in Bromsgrove. A fleece cover may help in brief cold, but sustained freezing can still damage the shrub.

Trim behind the bottlebrushes: Shorten flowered tips lightly after the display. Retain the leafy framework and remove dead wood once spring growth reveals it. Avoid treating this evergreen as a perennial to cut to the ground.

Plan frost shelter for Inferno: For this Oak Lodge specimen The bottlebrush is one of Bed 4's least hardy shrubs; check protection before a prolonged inland freeze.
Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Wait for clear regrowth before removing winter-damaged tips, then tip-prune young shoots for a bushier plant.
Summer: Water during drought, enjoy the bottlebrush spikes and prune only lightly immediately after flowering.
Autumn: Stop feeding, allow growth to harden and prepare fleece or temporary cover before severe frost.
Winter: Keep the root zone drained and protect the evergreen framework from hard frost and cold drying wind.
Bed 4.description: Inferno (‘Yanferno’) is a compact bottlebrush shrub with narrow, lemon-scented evergreen leaves and dense cylinders of rich red-pink stamens. The flowers can reach about 8cm long and appear through summer, sometimes continuing into autumn. Its Australian character suits the warm front-left of Bed 4, but H3 hardiness means a severe Bromsgrove winter—especially combined with wet soil—can damage or kill exposed growth.

Bed 4.name: Gaillardia ‘Arizona Sun’ — assumed
Bed 4.light: Full sun. Needs warmth and open light for sustained flowering
Bed 4.water: Allow drying between soakings. Established Gaillardia dislikes rich wet ground; drought tolerance is greater than winter-wet tolerance.
Bed 4.care:
Deadhead to keep blanket flowers coming: Remove faded heads to the next leafy shoot. Leave a few late heads only if seed is wanted. Do not expect seedlings to preserve an assumed cultivar or the same colour pattern.

Protect the crown from winter wet: Clear collapsed stems and keep heavy mulch off the centre. Lean, freely drained soil supports a sturdier clump than rich feeding. Even with good care, these hybrids can be short-lived.

Keep a dry crown near thirstier plants: For this Oak Lodge specimen Separate the Gaillardia's watering decisions from the moisture-loving Starship Lobelia in the same bed.
Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Clear dead growth, check the crown is firm and replace losses before neighbouring plants close the gap.
Summer: Deadhead down to a side shoot every week and water only when the root zone has dried.
Autumn: Leave a few final heads to ripen seed, then clear soggy stems away from the crown.
Winter: Prioritise air and drainage; do not cover the crown with a dense wet mulch.
Bed 4.description: Gaillardia × grandiflora carries daisy-like flowers banded in ember shades of red, orange and yellow above a compact leafy clump. With regular deadheading it can flower from June until October, making it one of Bed 4’s longest displays. The plant is often short-lived in cold wet soil, so keeping the crown drained and allowing some late seedheads is more useful than treating it like an indefinitely permanent shrub.

Bed 4.name: Abelia 'Kaleidoscope'
Bed 4.light: Full sun. Shelter and sun strengthen colour and flowering
Bed 4.water: Deeply during dry spells. Young Abelias need establishment moisture; established roots tolerate short dry spells.
Bed 4.care:
Keep the variegated framework: Remove solid-green reversions at their origin. Give the shrub good light for leaf colour. Cut a reverted shoot back to where it starts rather than repeatedly clipping its tip.

Thin Abelia in spring: Wait until winter damage can be distinguished from living growth. Remove dead tips and selected old or crowded stems. Avoid repeated summer shearing, which removes the shoots carrying the late flowers.

Retain the warm foliage contrast: For this Oak Lodge specimen Give the established Kaleidoscope light around the apple planting and remove reversions without shearing all its flower shoots.
Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Remove dead tips after new growth shows, mulch lightly and make only selective shaping cuts.
Summer: Water during establishment, leave fragrant flowers for insects and avoid shearing the coloured tips.
Autumn: Allow the foliage to complete its orange-red change and stop feeding so shoots harden before frost.
Winter: Expect partial leaf loss in cold weather; wait until spring before deciding which stems are dead.
Bed 4.description: ‘Kaleidoscope’ is a compact Abelia grown as much for changing foliage as for flowers. Green leaves edged in yellow brighten through summer, then deepen through orange and red in autumn; pink-tinged white, lightly fragrant trumpets appear from July into September. It stays semi-evergreen in shelter but may shed more leaves after a cold Bromsgrove spell, which is normal seasonal behaviour rather than automatic evidence of failure.

Bed 4.name: Abelia 'Radiance'
Bed 4.light: Sun to partial shade. Good light supports cream-edged foliage; shelter reduces winter leaf loss.
Bed 4.water: Deeply during dry spells. Young Abelias need establishment moisture; established roots tolerate short dry spells.
Bed 4.care:
Keep the variegated framework: Remove solid-green reversions at their origin. Give the shrub good light for leaf colour. Cut a reverted shoot back to where it starts rather than repeatedly clipping its tip.

Thin Abelia in spring: Wait until winter damage can be distinguished from living growth. Remove dead tips and selected old or crowded stems. Avoid repeated summer shearing, which removes the shoots carrying the late flowers.

Keep the pale Abelia separate: For this Oak Lodge specimen Distinguish Radiance's cream-edged shoots from nearby Kaleidoscope when inspecting reversions and recording growth.
Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: After the last hard frost, remove only dead tips and any completely green reverted shoots; add a thin mulch while keeping it clear of the stems.
Summer: Let the white-and-green framework fill out, watering deeply only in prolonged heat; lightly shorten wayward shoots after the first flower flush.
Autumn: Leave late flowers for insects and stop feeding so the cream-margined growth hardens before cold weather.
Winter: Keep fallen leaves from banking against the crown and wait until spring before judging frost-darkened shoot tips or reshaping the shrub.
Bed 4.description: Radiance adds a compact mound of cream-edged evergreen to semi-evergreen foliage around the Bed 4 apple. Pale tubular flowers extend its interest into late summer, while cold weather may cause some normal leaf loss. Keep its light variegation distinct from nearby Kaleidoscope, remove all-green reversions and prune selectively in spring rather than repeatedly shearing the flowering shoots.

Bed 4.name: Lobelia 'Starship Scarlet Bronze Leaf'
Bed 4.position: Former Achillea position — planted out in August 2026
Bed 4.light: Sun or partial shade. Shelter tall spikes from wind
Bed 4.water: Consistently moist in growth. This upright perennial Lobelia needs a moister root run than drought-tolerant neighbours in Bed 4.
Bed 4.care:
Keep Starship's crown hydrated: Mulch the soil around the clump after spring growth starts. Water thoroughly when the soil begins to dry. This scarlet perennial does not share the short seasonal life or trailing habit of bedding Lobelia.

Manage the upright flowering stems: Remove faded spikes and clear dead stems after dieback. Protect the crown in severe cold without sealing it beneath soggy debris. Divide a congested clump in spring when new growth is visible.

Water the new bed root run: For this Oak Lodge specimen Starship now grows in Bed 4, so check soil around its moved crown rather than following its former pot location.
Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Protect emerging shoots from slugs, mulch lightly and divide only if the clump becomes congested.
Summer: Keep evenly moist while it establishes and support only if wind threatens the stems.
Autumn: Cut down after foliage and stems finish, leaving a short marker over the dormant crown.
Winter: Keep the crown free of soggy debris and add a protective mulch without burying it deeply.
Bed 4.description: Starship Scarlet Bronze Leaf is not a trailing bedding Lobelia: it is a tall perennial with dark bronze foliage and upright scarlet flower spikes from July into September. In August it left its blue pot and was planted into Bed 4 where Achillea Summer Berries had grown. The richer root run gives its moisture-loving crown more resilience, while the vivid tubular flowers stand 60–90cm high for pollinators.

Bed 5.name: Chinese Wisteria ‘Prolific’ — assumed
Bed 5.light: Full sun. A sunny wall gives the best flower-bud formation
Bed 5.water: During drought, especially while buds develop. Check the dry boundary root zone; established Wisteria needs moisture but little nitrogen.
Bed 5.care:
Shorten Wisteria shoots twice yearly: In July–August cut unwanted whippy shoots to five or six leaves. In January–February shorten those same shoots to two or three buds. Keep shoots needed to extend the permanent framework.

Maintain a strong permanent support: Tie selected structural stems to sound wires or supports. Keep twining growth out of gutters and away from vulnerable fittings. Feed only for a demonstrated need; excessive nitrogen favours foliage over flowers.

Keep the boundary framework accessible: For this Oak Lodge specimen Train selected Wisteria extensions while shortening side shoots so they do not engulf the pots beneath.
Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Tie in the permanent framework and enjoy the racemes; remove frost-killed tips only after growth is clear.
Summer: In July or August shorten long whippy side shoots to five or six leaves and keep growth away from roofs and gutters.
Autumn: Inspect anchors after leaf fall and plan structural changes while the framework is visible.
Winter: In January or February shorten the same side shoots again to two or three buds to form flowering spurs.
Bed 5.description: This vigorous woody climber carries hanging lilac spring flower clusters along the Bed 5 boundary, then produces long leafy shoots through summer. Chinese Wisteria Prolific is the recorded assumption and remains unconfirmed. Its main care is a strong trained framework and twice-yearly shortening of side shoots so the canopy does not engulf the planting and pots below.

profile.about: Wisteria are long-lived woody climbers from eastern Asia and North America. Bed 5.name: Rose ‘Golden Showers’ — assumed
Bed 5.light: Full sun. At least four hours of direct light with moving air
Bed 5.water: Deeply during sustained drought. Roses beside walls need checks below the rain shadow, especially when supporting repeat flowers.
Bed 5.care:
Train main canes before shortening laterals: Tie flexible structural growth across the support, with room for thickening. On established climbing roses, shorten flowered side shoots in late winter and renew old canes gradually. Keep healthy main canes; do not prune the whole plant to ground level.

Sustain the repeat rose display: Feed and mulch in spring, then deadhead to healthy leaves. Use a rose feed at its label rate and clear diseased fallen leaves. Keep selected hips only where their autumn display matters more than further flowers.

Keep the supported rose distinct: For this Oak Lodge specimen Train the rose clear of the Wisteria and retain Golden Showers as an assumption until the flower record proves it.
Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Feed and mulch after rain, tie new structural shoots horizontally where possible and inspect early leaves for black spot.
Summer: Deadhead repeat-flowering stems, water deeply during drought and tie in strong new canes before wind damages them.
Autumn: Stop deadheading only if hips are wanted; collect diseased fallen leaves and shorten wind-rocked growth.
Winter: Prune according to the observed rose class, retaining a balanced framework and replacing old unproductive canes gradually.
Bed 5.description: The supported Bed 5 rose adds summer flowers among the boundary framework. Golden Showers is a working identification rather than a proven cultivar, so flower photographs and repeat-flowering observations remain useful. Keep its main canes clear of the Wisteria and train them deliberately, preserving the distinction between woody framework and shorter flowering side shoots.

Bed 5.name: Yucca ‘Color Guard’ — assumed
Bed 5.light: Full sun. Open light strengthens the yellow central stripe
Bed 5.water: Little after establishment. Yucca tolerates drought but needs sharp drainage around its rigid rosette.
Bed 5.care:
Preserve the sword-leaved rosette: Cut fully dead lower leaves close to their base. Keep the pointed tips away from paths and wear gloves when handling. Do not shear the leaves across the middle or treat the plant as flexible Phormium fans.

Remove the spent flower stalk: Cut the old flowering stem near its base after the display. Retain healthy foliage and leave offsets unless overcrowded. Clear wet leaves from the centre in winter rather than adding moisture-holding mulch.

Keep sharp leaves away from access: For this Oak Lodge specimen Maintain clearance around the lower-left Yucca without cutting across its rigid sword leaves.
Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Pull away dead leaves with gloves, clear debris from the crown and top-dress with grit rather than rich mulch.
Summer: Leave established roots on the dry side, remove a spent flower stalk at its base and check spikes for aphids.
Autumn: Stop feeding, keep fallen leaves out of the rosette and preserve open drainage around the crown.
Winter: Do not wrap the rosette in moisture-trapping material; leave sound leaves intact and remove cold damage only when spring growth resumes.
Bed 5.description: The lower-left Bed 5 plant forms a rigid basal rosette rather than the flexible fan expected from Phormium. Its evergreen leaves have green margins and a broad pale-yellow central stripe, making Yucca filamentosa ‘Color Guard’ the strongest current match. Mature plants can send a 1–2m stem of creamy white bells above the roughly 75cm foliage clump in midsummer, but the identity remains marked as assumed until a label or flower provides stronger evidence.

Bed 5.name: Alstroemeria ‘Indian Summer’ — label confirmed
Bed 5.light: Sun or light shade. Warm and sheltered from wind
Bed 5.water: Even moisture in the deep pot. Fleshy roots need moisture in growth and drainage through winter; never leave the pot standing in water.
Bed 5.care:
Remove spent Alstroemeria stems carefully: On a well-rooted plant, pull finished flower stems gently from the base. If the young crown lifts or resists, cut instead. Support taller shoots and feed during flowering without damaging the fleshy root system.

Shelter the perennial crown: Insulate or move the container during severe cold. Keep the dormant root system only lightly moist. Disturb established roots sparingly; split an overcrowded clump in spring rather than dividing every year.

Protect the central perennial roots: For this Oak Lodge specimen Avoid pulling hard on Alstroemeria stems while its roots share the big pot with seasonal trailers.
Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Top-dress or repot before growth becomes tall, then begin watering as shoots extend.
Summer: Water and feed through flowering; pull finished stems from the base instead of leaving hollow stubs.

Bed 5.name: Petunia 'Bee's Knees'
Bed 5.light: Full sun. Sheltered warmth gives the strongest display
Bed 5.water: Evenly moist while flowering. Water the compost thoroughly and drain; hanging trails do not show how dry the central root ball has become.
Bed 5.care:
Remove Petunia flowers with their seed bases: Pinch spent blooms back to a leaf joint. Do not pull off only the coloured trumpet and leave the seed capsule. Shorten a few leggy trails at a time to keep flowers elsewhere on the plant.

Feed the seasonal container display: Use a flowering-plant feed during active growth at the label rate. Apply to moist compost. Protect deliberately overwintered plants from frost; outdoor flowering normally finishes as temperatures fall.

Give Bee's Knees room to trail: For this Oak Lodge specimen Shorten bare yellow-Petunia stems before they tangle through the Alstroemeria and the two Nemesias.
Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Plant out after frost, pinch young tips if sparse and protect the new pot from cold wind.
Summer: Feed weekly once flowering strongly, deadhead with the seed capsule and trim any bare trailing stems.
Autumn: Keep flowering while nights remain mild, then compost after frost or take cuttings before cold.
Winter: The outdoor plant is seasonal; retain only healthy cuttings under bright frost-free cover.
Bed 5.description: ‘Bee’s Knees’ supplies unusually clear, non-fading yellow trumpet flowers around the edge of the Bed 5 big pot. Its branching stems soften the rim while the Alstroemeria rises through the centre. Like other petunias it performs by continuous replacement rather than one flush: sun, steady feeding, removal of seed capsules and an occasional trim of bare stems keep flowers coming until frost.

Bed 5.name: Vinca minor 'Illumination'
Bed 5.position: Big pot — trailing over the rim
Bed 5.light: Sun to shade. Part shade protects foliage while retaining gold colour
Bed 5.water: Moderate; avoid prolonged drying. Vinca tolerates some dry shade once established, but trailing plants in pots still depend on the container's moisture.
Bed 5.care:
Keep Vinca runners within bounds: Shorten trails that root into neighbouring planting. Remove unwanted rooted pieces completely. Trim after the main spring flowers, retaining leafy growth for the next display.

Remove green reversions: Cut all-green shoots back to their point of origin. Variegated forms can be overtaken by vigorous green growth. Give enough light for leaf colour without letting the shallow roots bake.

Contain the original gold-centred Vinca: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep this established big-pot specimen separate in the record from the additional Vinca on the Bed 2/3 wall.
Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Trim winter-damaged runners, top-dress the pot and enjoy violet-blue flowers among fresh gold leaves.
Summer: Guide or shorten stems that tangle with seasonal plants and water when the shared pot begins to dry.
Autumn: Remove rooted escapes outside the pot and decide which runners should remain for winter structure.
Winter: The evergreen foliage remains; raise the pot on feet and water only when compost is genuinely dry.
Bed 5.description: ‘Illumination’ is the permanent trailing element in the Bed 5 big pot. Its evergreen leaves have broad golden centres framed by narrow green margins, producing bright cascades even when the summer bedding has finished; small violet-blue flowers appear mainly in spring. Stems root when they contact soil, so the plant can be divided or allowed to spill, but should not be permitted to escape into places where its creeping habit would be difficult to control.

Bed 5.name: Nemesia ‘Wisley Vanilla’ — label confirmed
Bed 5.position: Big pot — compact flowering filler added July 2026
Bed 5.light: Sun or light shade. Shelter from drying wind and intense reflected heat
Bed 5.water: Even moisture without saturation. Fine Nemesia roots suffer if the root ball dries hard; some shade helps during intense heat.
Bed 5.care:
Trim Nemesia after a tired flower flush: Shorten spent shoots to healthy leafy growth. Keep the crown intact and maintain moisture for the new shoots. A pause in hot weather may recover as conditions cool; more feed alone will not restore heat-stressed bloom.

Plan frost protection separately from trimming: Treat these plants as tender unless protected over winter. Take healthy non-flowering cuttings if the cultivar is worth keeping. Avoid cold wet soil around the crown, whether in a pot or the front border.

Retain the Wisley Vanilla label: For this Oak Lodge specimen Trim the white scented Nemesia independently of the moved Aroma Heart of Gold sharing the Bed 5 pot.
Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Plant after frost, pinch tips once and allow the small root ball to establish before heavy flowering.
Summer: Keep evenly moist and trim the whole first tired flush to restore a compact flowering mound.
Autumn: Enjoy renewed cool-weather flowers and take cuttings before frost only if this plant is worth retaining.
Winter: Compost the outdoor plant after frost or keep rooted cuttings bright and frost-free.
Bed 5.description: The retained label identifies this Bed 5 pot plant as Nemesia Wisley Vanilla. Its small pale flowers provide close-range scent and a light contrast to the darker Aroma Heart of Gold sharing the container. A trim after a tired flush, even moisture and shelter from severe heat help it flower again; winter survival should not be assumed without protection.

Bed 5.name: Lythrum 'Robin'
Bed 5.light: Full sun or part shade. Flowers best with good light
Bed 5.water: Keep continuously moist. Lythrum is moisture-loving; this pot must not follow the dry-soil routine used for succulents.
Bed 5.care:
Maintain Robin's moisture reserve: Use moisture-retentive compost and check often in hot weather. Thoroughly rewet the whole root ball before the flower spikes flag. The small container dries faster than the damp ground this species naturally favours.

Cut old stems after dieback: Remove spent spikes if seed is not wanted. Leave sound late stems for structure if useful, then cut them near ground level before spring regrowth. Divide when the pot becomes root-bound.

Check the separate medium pot first: For this Oak Lodge specimen Robin's moisture demand is higher than most Bed 5 pot plants; inspect its root ball during every hot dry spell.
Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Top-dress, divide only if root-bound and restart generous watering as shoots extend.
Summer: Never allow the pot to bake dry; deadhead some spikes for neatness while leaving others for insects.
Autumn: Cut down after foliage yellows or leave sound seedheads briefly, preventing unwanted seed if necessary.
Winter: The crown is dormant; keep the pot from freezing solid or sitting in sour stagnant water.
Bed 5.description: ‘Robin’ is a compact purple loosestrife that sends dense magenta-pink flower spikes above narrow leaves in summer. Bees and other insects work along each spike as the small starry flowers open, making this standalone medium pot one of the strongest pollinator stations in the container group. Unlike most neighbouring pots it dislikes drying out and is fully hardy, although its exposed root ball still needs frost and drainage awareness.

Bed 5.name: Begonia ‘Carmen’ — label confirmed
Bed 5.light: Bright partial shade. Gentle morning sun; shelter from harsh midday heat
Bed 5.water: Let the surface begin drying. Keep the fleshy Begonia crown out of stagnant water; water the compost rather than the flowers.
Bed 5.care:
Protect the double blooms: Remove fading flowers and soft stems before grey mould spreads. Give bright sheltered light with protection from scorching midday sun. Do not handle the brittle stems as roughly as woody shrubs.

Confirm the Begonia group before winter storage: Keep it frost-free while the tuber or root type remains unresolved. Different begonias need different dormant or actively growing winter routines. A Carmen label alone is insufficient reason to dry the whole root system as a tuber.

Shelter the little pot's flowers: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep Carmen's brittle red-flowered stems out of strong wind and avoid soaking its fleshy centre.
Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Restart stored tubers or young plants warm and bright, then place outdoors only after frost.
Summer: Water the compost rather than the crown, feed while flowering and remove decaying petals promptly.
Autumn: Reduce water as growth slows and bring the pot under cover before cold nights.
Winter: Keep dormant tubers dry and frost-free, or maintain a leafy plant bright and just moist if its group requires it.
Bed 5.description: ‘Carmen’ fills the small Bed 5 pot with double red flowers above fleshy, asymmetrical leaves. It gives saturated colour in bright shade or gentle morning sun, where petunias would flower poorly, but the succulent stems and crown rot quickly if cold wet compost is treated as a request for more water. Several begonias have been sold under the name ‘Carmen’, so the retained garden name is useful but the exact cultivar group remains unresolved.

Bed 5.name: Nemesia 'Aroma Heart of Gold'
Bed 5.latin: Nemesia Aroma Heart of Gold (Aroma Series)
Bed 5.position: Bed 5 big pot — moved from Bed 1 in August 2026
Bed 5.light: Sun or light shade. Best in a warm, sheltered position
Bed 5.water: Moist, well-drained. Fertile loam or sandy soil; acid to neutral
Bed 5.care:
Water by touch, not by routine: Check the top 2–3cm of soil and water when it feels dry. Its roots are fairly shallow, so a hot or windy spell can slow flowering quickly. Water thoroughly at soil level, then allow the surface to dry slightly rather than keeping the bed constantly wet.

Keep the flowers coming: Pinch young tips and trim spent flowering shoots after the first flush. Pinching encourages a fuller plant. Once the first main display fades, remove the tired flowering growth rather than only picking individual blooms; fresh shoots should produce the next flush.

Feed only while it is working: Use a balanced liquid feed during active flowering if growth or colour begins to fade. A plant growing in fertile bed soil needs less feeding than one in a container. Avoid heavy feeding that produces soft leafy growth at the expense of flowers.

Decide how to overwinter it: Treat the Bed 1 plant as vulnerable to a Bromsgrove winter. H3 means it may survive only a mild, sheltered winter. The reliable option is to take softwood cuttings from non-flowering shoots in late summer and keep them frost-free; otherwise regard the outdoor plant as seasonal.
Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: If cuttings were overwintered, pinch them once they are growing strongly. Harden plants off gradually and put them outside only after frost risk has passed.
Summer: Keep the root run evenly moist in dry weather. Pinch for shape, feed if flowering weakens, then trim the first tired flowering shoots to prompt another flush.
Autumn: Enjoy the late flowers while weather stays mild. Take non-flowering softwood cuttings before cold nights if this cultivar is to be kept for next year.
Winter: Do not rely on Aroma Heart of Gold surviving outdoors in the Bed 5 big pot; keep any rooted cuttings bright, frost-free and lightly moist.

profile.about: Nemesia is a southern African genus whose species may be annuals, perennials or small sub-shrubs. Bed 5.name: Cabbage Tree
Bed 5.position: Lower centre of Bed 5 — architectural burgundy fountain
Bed 5.light: Full sun. Warm and sheltered from cold wind
Bed 5.water: Water young roots in dry weather. Established Cordyline tolerates drought; avoid a saturated stem base in winter.
Bed 5.care:
Keep the growing crown intact: Remove fully dead lower leaves without cutting across live blades. The central spear makes the next leaves. A trunked Cordyline is not a grass to shear or divide routinely; allow its natural skirt or remove dead leaves individually.

Protect Red Star in cold weather: Shield the crown from prolonged frost and wet. The coloured form is less dependable in severe cold than green Cordyline. Wait for recovery in spring before cutting damaged stems; new shoots may appear below an injured crown.

Use the Bed 5 location: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the Red Star Cordyline's trunk base drained in Bed 5; its old stone-prefixed ID does not place it in the gravel bed.
Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Remove winter-damaged leaves once growth restarts and cut below genuine crown rot only when live tissue is clear.
Summer: Water young roots during drought and remove only fully dead lower leaves; do not trim healthy leaf tips into shapes.
Autumn: Clear debris from the crown and prepare fleece or a loose leaf tie before exceptional cold.
Winter: Protect the growing point from hard frost and trapped rain, leaving damage assessment until spring.
Bed 5.description: Cordyline australis ‘Red Star’ begins as a dense fountain of burgundy sword leaves and gradually develops a trunk, becoming a palm-like vertical landmark in the lower section of Bed 5. Mature Cordylines can send large scented cream flower panicles above the crown in warm years. The dark cultivar is less reliably hardy than plain green cabbage trees, so cold wet around the crown and trunk is the central risk.
