Stone Bed.name: Houseleek ‘Rubin’ — assumed
Stone Bed.position: Left-centre — rosettes in gravel
Stone Bed.light: Full sun. Open light keeps rosettes compact and strongly coloured
Stone Bed.water: Very little once rooted. Houseleeks need sun and fast drainage; wet winter rosettes are a greater risk than a dry surface.
Stone Bed.care:
Keep each houseleek rosette open: Lift fallen leaves and invading stonecrop from the colony. Do not cover the fleshy growing points with compost or rich mulch. Avoid routine feeding, which opens up the compact rosettes.

Replace only the rosette that flowered: A flowering rosette dies after seed production; nearby offsets continue. Remove the dead rosette without disturbing the whole colony. Set healthy offsets into gritty soil when more plants are wanted.

Retain the older red colony: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the assumed Rubin rosettes distinct from the newer labelled houseleeks when taking offsets or recording colour.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Remove dead flowering gaps, re-seat healthy offsets in fresh grit and clear leaf litter from rosette centres.
Summer: Water only newly placed offsets; enjoy flower stalks, then remove the dead parent rosette after bloom.
Autumn: Stop feeding and clear fallen leaves before wet weather settles into the mat.
Winter: Leave dry cold rosettes alone and protect the bed from debris or runoff that holds water around them.
Stone Bed.description: Houseleeks build a low mosaic of fleshy pointed rosettes among the Stone Bed gravel. Each mature rosette flowers only once, lifting a starry summer cluster before that rosette dies, but surrounding offsets close the gap and continue the colony. Their name Sempervivum means ‘always living’; in a British gravel bed the real threat is not drought but shade, rich soil and winter water trapped inside the rosettes.

profile.about: Sempervivum are mountain succulents from Europe and Asia, adapted to exposed rock through water-storing leaves and clonal offsets. Seasonal colour is fluid, so identifying cultivars from a summer photograph is unreliable. The colony is maintained by its younger offsets rather than by keeping every parent rosette alive indefinitely.

Stone Bed.name: Echeveria ‘Perle von Nürnberg’ — assumed
Stone Bed.position: Centre-left — grey rosette beside the houseleeks
Stone Bed.light: Full sun or very bright light. Acclimatise the powder-coated leaves gradually to intense sun
Stone Bed.water: Soak, then let compost dry. Reduce watering sharply in a cool bright winter home; never let water collect around the crown.
Stone Bed.care:
Lift tender Echeveria before frost: Overwinter in bright, frost-free conditions. Do not apply the hardy Sempervivum routine to these rosettes. A sheltered patch of gravel cannot prevent freezing during a cold Bromsgrove winter.

Preserve the leaf surface: Handle leaves as little as possible and water the soil. Powdery bloom or fine hairs help protect the foliage. Remove dead basal leaves gently and check sheltered rosette bases for mealybugs.

Lift the powdery rosette before frost: For this Oak Lodge specimen Handle the assumed Perle von Nürnberg by its pot or roots so the protective leaf bloom remains intact.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Restart watering gradually under cover, remove only fully dry lower leaves and return outdoors after frost risk has passed.
Summer: Water deeply only after the soil dries, keep water out of the crown and avoid rubbing away the protective powdery bloom.
Autumn: Lift before cold nights, pot into gritty compost and inspect closely for vine weevil or mealybugs before bringing under cover.
Winter: Keep frost-free in bright light and almost dry; do not leave the rosette outdoors with the hardy Sempervivums.
Stone Bed.description: This newly planted Echeveria forms a large symmetrical rosette of broad, fleshy leaves covered in a powdery grey-purple bloom, with a fine pink edge catching the light. The photographs most closely fit ‘Perle von Nürnberg’, but several related hybrids can look nearly identical without a retained label or flowers, so the cultivar remains an explicit working assumption. It suits the Stone Bed’s sun and sharp drainage through summer, but unlike the hardy houseleeks beside it, it will not survive a Bromsgrove winter outdoors.

Stone Bed.name: Common Houseleek — assumed
Stone Bed.position: Established green rosettes with red tips among the gravel.
Stone Bed.light: Full sun. The open Stone Bed provides strong light and airflow
Stone Bed.water: Very little once rooted. Houseleeks need sun and fast drainage; wet winter rosettes are a greater risk than a dry surface.
Stone Bed.care:
Keep each houseleek rosette open: Lift fallen leaves and invading stonecrop from the colony. Do not cover the fleshy growing points with compost or rich mulch. Avoid routine feeding, which opens up the compact rosettes.

Replace only the rosette that flowered: A flowering rosette dies after seed production; nearby offsets continue. Remove the dead rosette without disturbing the whole colony. Set healthy offsets into gritty soil when more plants are wanted.

Keep the red-tipped rosettes visible: For this Oak Lodge specimen Remove encroaching fine stonecrop before it masks the assumed common houseleek colony.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Remove dead rosettes, re-seat lifted offsets and top up grit beneath leaves without covering the central growing point.
Summer: After a rosette flowers, let insects use the blooms, then remove that dying rosette while preserving its offsets.
Autumn: Separate overcrowded chicks if they are holding moisture and clear every fallen leaf from the colony.
Winter: Keep rosette hearts free of debris and protect from water running off adjacent plants into the colony.
Stone Bed.description: The established green rosettes with pointed red tips best fit common houseleek, Sempervivum tectorum. That species is a useful working identity, but the many similar hybrids mean the record remains explicitly assumed.

Stone Bed.name: Ajuga ‘Fancy Finch’ — label confirmed
Stone Bed.position: Cooler edge of the Stone Bed. Added July 2026.
Stone Bed.light: Partial shade. Protect gold leaves from scorching midday sun
Stone Bed.water: Keep their root pockets moist. Ajuga needs humus and moisture beneath the gravel, unlike neighbouring Sempervivum.
Stone Bed.care:
Direct Ajuga's runners: Lift or trim rooted runners before they cover small alpines. Keep each carpet open to air. Replant vigorous pieces where coverage is wanted rather than repeatedly feeding a crowded, declining centre.

Remove finished spring spikes: Snip flower stalks down to the leaf mat. Retain sound evergreen foliage and clear rotting leaves from the crown. Shade during the hottest part of the day reduces scorching in the lighter-leaved forms.

Protect the gold leaves from dry heat: For this Oak Lodge specimen Maintain the cooler moist pocket beneath Fancy Finch and stop it spreading over the smaller succulent rosettes.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Remove tatty leaves before blue flower spikes rise and pin selected cream-splashed runners into the intended patch.
Summer: Cut spent spikes, water during real drought and remove any plain-green reversion before it outruns the variegated plant.
Autumn: Thin dense runners away from succulent crowns and clear leaves that would smother the low rosettes.
Winter: Retain sound evergreen rosettes but remove any black central growth during mild dry weather.

Stone Bed.name: Hydrangea ‘Snowflake’ — label confirmed
Stone Bed.position: Back of the bed — moisture-retentive planting pocket. Added July 2026.
Stone Bed.light: Sun or partial shade. Afternoon shade reduces heat and drought stress
Stone Bed.water: Moist below the gravel. Check this shrub's deeper root pocket separately from the dry succulent planting.
Stone Bed.care:
Keep oakleaf Hydrangea's old wood: Prune only lightly after flowering when necessary. Snowflake forms the next flower buds on existing stems. Avoid the hard spring cut used for panicle hydrangeas; remove dead stems once growth makes them clear.

Make room for the broad leaves: Maintain a humus-rich pocket and space around its crown. Mulch its root area without covering the stem base or neighbouring alpine rosettes. Afternoon shade can reduce leaf scorch in hot weather.

Water its own deeper pocket: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep organic mulch around Snowflake's roots while preserving the dry gravel around adjacent alpines.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Remove only dead wood once buds are obvious, mulch the root area and preserve old stems that carry this year's flowers.
Summer: Deep-water during dry spells and support very heavy double flower panicles without pruning healthy canes.
Autumn: Enjoy the burgundy foliage, leave sound flower heads for structure and clear wet debris from the crown.
Winter: Retain the papery panicles if stable, checking after storms for split or rubbing wood rather than hard-pruning.

Stone Bed.name: Chick Charms Houseleek Mix — label confirmed
Stone Bed.position: Mixed rosette group in open gravel. Added July 2026.
Stone Bed.light: Full sun. The open Stone Bed provides strong light and airflow
Stone Bed.water: Very little once rooted. Houseleeks need sun and fast drainage; wet winter rosettes are a greater risk than a dry surface.
Stone Bed.care:
Keep each houseleek rosette open: Lift fallen leaves and invading stonecrop from the colony. Do not cover the fleshy growing points with compost or rich mulch. Avoid routine feeding, which opens up the compact rosettes.

Replace only the rosette that flowered: A flowering rosette dies after seed production; nearby offsets continue. Remove the dead rosette without disturbing the whole colony. Set healthy offsets into gritty soil when more plants are wanted.

Keep the series as a mix: For this Oak Lodge specimen Propagate labelled offsets as Chick Charms mix unless a retained tag identifies an individual cultivar.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Map the differently coloured rosettes, remove dead centres and give crowded chicks their own gritty pockets.
Summer: Remove each spent flowering rosette after bloom while keeping its offsets labelled as part of the mix.
Autumn: Reduce crowding where the mixed rosettes overlap and clear windblown leaves before they lodge in the centres.
Winter: Keep every rosette heart uncovered and photograph winter colour rather than mistaking normal colour change for damage.
Stone Bed.description: The retained tag confirms a Chick Charms houseleek group but does not name the individual cultivars in the pot. The journal therefore records the commercial series as a mix and avoids inventing component names from seasonal colour alone.

Stone Bed.name: Achillea ‘King Alfred’ — label confirmed
Stone Bed.position: Sunny front edge. Added July 2026.
Stone Bed.light: Full sun. The open Stone Bed provides strong light and airflow
Stone Bed.water: Little once rooted. This alpine yarrow needs lean, sharply drained ground; avoid frequent watering around its mat.
Stone Bed.care:
Keep King Alfred low and open: Trim faded flower stalks without cutting away the whole leaf cushion. Do not feed or stake it as though it were tall border yarrow. Sun and lean soil preserve its compact grey-green habit.

Lift wet debris from the mat: Keep winter leaves and rich mulch away from the small crown. Separate a healthy rooted edge only when renewal is needed. A mat deteriorating in wet shade needs better conditions, not more fertiliser.

Preserve the miniature cushion: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep taller leaves away from King Alfred's low pale-yellow flowers and avoid applying border-yarrow feeding.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Cut old stems to basal shoots, divide a congested crown if needed and keep mulch away from the centre.
Summer: Deadhead the yellow flower plates to side buds or leave selected heads for insects, supporting only stems that actually lean.
Autumn: Stop feeding and leave a few sound seed heads while removing collapsed growth that would trap moisture.
Winter: Keep the crown open and dry; save structural stems until late winter if they remain upright.
Stone Bed.description: Achillea ‘King Alfred’ is a miniature yarrow rather than a tall border Achillea, making a low aromatic grey-green mat with small pale-yellow flower heads in late spring and early summer.

Stone Bed.name: Golden Stonecrop ‘Aureum’ — label confirmed
Stone Bed.position: Front gravel — bright golden mat. Added July 2026.
Stone Bed.light: Full sun. The open Stone Bed provides strong light and airflow
Stone Bed.water: Let the root zone dry between soakings. Mat-forming stonecrops store water in their leaves; frequent small splashes are unnecessary.
Stone Bed.care:
Keep stonecrop stems out of wet debris: Maintain an open, gritty surface around the mat. Avoid rich feeding and dense organic mulch over the crown. Remove decaying stems selectively while keeping sound rooted growth.

Control the mat after flowering: Trim encroaching stems and remove unwanted rooted pieces. Replant healthy pieces only where more cover is needed. Stonecrops differ in hardiness: follow this plant's own rating rather than assuming every Sedum survives severe frost.

Stop gold stonecrop covering rosettes: For this Oak Lodge specimen Remove Aureum stems that root into the houseleek colonies while keeping its own bright patch intact.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Trim black tips and spread sound golden pieces over open gritty soil to renew the carpet.
Summer: Prevent faster green neighbours shading the colour and snip flower remains without scalping the mat.
Autumn: Remove fallen leaves immediately because the fine golden growth rots quickly beneath a damp cover.
Winter: Maximise light, avoid watering and keep roof or path runoff from saturating its shallow rooting layer.
Stone Bed.description: Sedum acre ‘Aureum’ is a tiny vigorous stonecrop whose bead-like leaves glow yellow-gold in strong sun. It can spread quickly, so its main care need is keeping it from covering slower houseleeks and alpines.

Stone Bed.name: Cobweb Houseleek — label confirmed
Stone Bed.position: Open gravel — white-webbed rosettes. Added July 2026.
Stone Bed.light: Full sun. The open Stone Bed provides strong light and airflow
Stone Bed.water: Very little once rooted. Houseleeks need sun and fast drainage; wet winter rosettes are a greater risk than a dry surface.
Stone Bed.care:
Keep each houseleek rosette open: Lift fallen leaves and invading stonecrop from the colony. Do not cover the fleshy growing points with compost or rich mulch. Avoid routine feeding, which opens up the compact rosettes.

Replace only the rosette that flowered: A flowering rosette dies after seed production; nearby offsets continue. Remove the dead rosette without disturbing the whole colony. Set healthy offsets into gritty soil when more plants are wanted.

Leave the natural cobweb hairs: For this Oak Lodge specimen Do not wash away the fine white webbing from the houseleek tips or mistake it for spider-mite damage.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Pick debris from the natural cobweb fibres with tweezers and re-seat small offsets without covering their centres.
Summer: Water below the rosettes during exceptional drought and remove a flowering parent only after its chicks are secure.
Autumn: Thin overlapping rosettes so the webbed centres dry quickly after rain and clear every fallen leaf.
Winter: Give this woolly colony maximum ventilation and overhead shelter if prolonged rain keeps its centres wet.
Stone Bed.description: Cobweb Houseleek produces tight rosettes linked across their tips by fine white hairs, an adaptation that gives the colony its unmistakable webbed appearance. Pink star flowers rise in summer from mature rosettes that then die and are replaced by offsets.

Stone Bed.name: Houseleek ‘Purple Quartz’ — label confirmed
Stone Bed.position: Open gravel — large purple-flushed rosettes. Added July 2026.
Stone Bed.light: Full sun. The open Stone Bed provides strong light and airflow
Stone Bed.water: Very little once rooted. Houseleeks need sun and fast drainage; wet winter rosettes are a greater risk than a dry surface.
Stone Bed.care:
Keep each houseleek rosette open: Lift fallen leaves and invading stonecrop from the colony. Do not cover the fleshy growing points with compost or rich mulch. Avoid routine feeding, which opens up the compact rosettes.

Replace only the rosette that flowered: A flowering rosette dies after seed production; nearby offsets continue. Remove the dead rosette without disturbing the whole colony. Set healthy offsets into gritty soil when more plants are wanted.

Allow space for the larger rosettes: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the Big Sam Purple Quartz colony from being crowded by faster stonecrop mats.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Remove winter-damaged outer leaves and space offsets so the named rosette keeps a clear purple form.
Summer: Let any flowering rosette complete its cycle, then label and retain the best-coloured chicks before removing the parent.
Autumn: Clear leaf litter to preserve colour and airflow, moving crowded offsets to separate gritty pockets.
Winter: Photograph cold-season colour, keep the heart dry and do not water merely because the outer leaves tighten.

Stone Bed.name: Sedum ‘Angelina’ — label confirmed
Stone Bed.position: Trailing through the sunny front gravel. Added July 2026.
Stone Bed.light: Full sun. The open Stone Bed provides strong light and airflow
Stone Bed.water: Let the root zone dry between soakings. Mat-forming stonecrops store water in their leaves; frequent small splashes are unnecessary.
Stone Bed.care:
Keep stonecrop stems out of wet debris: Maintain an open, gritty surface around the mat. Avoid rich feeding and dense organic mulch over the crown. Remove decaying stems selectively while keeping sound rooted growth.

Control the mat after flowering: Trim encroaching stems and remove unwanted rooted pieces. Replant healthy pieces only where more cover is needed. Stonecrops differ in hardiness: follow this plant's own rating rather than assuming every Sedum survives severe frost.

Contain the golden trails: For this Oak Lodge specimen Trim Angelina before it bridges separate alpine planting pockets and roots into slower-growing neighbours.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Shorten winter-battered stems and push vigorous cuttings into intended gaps before they run into small rosettes.
Summer: Trim spent yellow flower heads and edge the spreading mat away from slower alpines.
Autumn: Enjoy the orange-red colour change while lifting any sections that are trapping leaves or moisture beneath them.
Winter: Keep runoff away and use healthy loose tips as insurance if central stems succumb to prolonged wet.
Stone Bed.description: Sedum ‘Angelina’ trails through the gravel with bright golden needle-like leaves that take on orange tones in cold weather. It is hardy and vigorous, so selective trimming will protect the smaller rosette plants beside it.

Stone Bed.name: Echeveria ‘Devotion’ — label confirmed
Stone Bed.position: Sunny gravel — velvety upright rosettes. Added July 2026.
Stone Bed.light: Full sun. The open Stone Bed provides strong light and airflow
Stone Bed.water: Soak, then let compost dry. Reduce watering sharply in a cool bright winter home; never let water collect around the crown.
Stone Bed.care:
Lift tender Echeveria before frost: Overwinter in bright, frost-free conditions. Do not apply the hardy Sempervivum routine to these rosettes. A sheltered patch of gravel cannot prevent freezing during a cold Bromsgrove winter.

Preserve the leaf surface: Handle leaves as little as possible and water the soil. Powdery bloom or fine hairs help protect the foliage. Remove dead basal leaves gently and check sheltered rosette bases for mealybugs.

Keep the velvety foliage frost-free: For this Oak Lodge specimen Lift Devotion with its roots intact and keep its hairy leaves dry in bright protected winter conditions.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Remove dried lower leaves, check for mealybug in the leaf joints and acclimatise gradually to stronger outdoor light.
Summer: Keep rain out of the fuzzy rosette, water the gritty mix only after drying and preserve airflow around the leaves.
Autumn: Move under cover before cold wet nights, inspecting every leaf joint so pests are not carried indoors.
Winter: Keep bright, frost-free and almost dry; never allow the soft-leaved rosette to touch a cold window or stand in water.
Stone Bed.description: Echeveria pulvinata Devotion (‘Bcec12001’) carries pointed velvety green leaves that develop burgundy tips and margins. It is H2 and must come out of the Stone Bed before frost, just like ‘Perle von Nürnberg’.

Stone Bed.care:
Move Rubrum before hard cold: Plan a bright frost-free winter home for the root ball. This burgundy fountain grass is not reliably hardy in Bromsgrove. Leaving ornamental grasses standing for winter does not make this tender one safe outdoors.

Cut back when spring growth restarts: Remove old leaves without cutting through new shoots. Keep the overwintered clump ventilated and only slightly moist until growth resumes. Harden it off after frost risk before returning it to the gravel bed.

Arrange movable winter protection: For this Oak Lodge specimen Plan how to lift or pot the broad Rubrum clump before freezing weather makes moving it difficult.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Keep the overwintered plant frost-free until nights warm, then cut dead blades above visible shoots and harden it off gradually.
Summer: Feed and water while the burgundy fountain is growing strongly, tying only if exposure flattens the whole clump.
Autumn: Save or photograph seed heads, stop feeding and move the plant under cover before the first damaging frost.
Winter: Maintain a bright frost-free crown with minimal water, removing dead blades that could harbour mould.

Stone Bed.care:
Direct Ajuga's runners: Lift or trim rooted runners before they cover small alpines. Keep each carpet open to air. Replant vigorous pieces where coverage is wanted rather than repeatedly feeding a crowded, declining centre.

Remove finished spring spikes: Snip flower stalks down to the leaf mat. Retain sound evergreen foliage and clear rotting leaves from the crown. Shade during the hottest part of the day reduces scorching in the lighter-leaved forms.

Retain its moist dark-leaved patch: For this Oak Lodge specimen Check the soil under Midnight Mystery rather than copying the neighbouring drought-tolerant stonecrop routine.

Spring: Comb out black leaves, peg selected dark runners into bare gravel gaps and remove any unwanted escapees.
Summer: Cut flower spikes after bees finish and keep the spreading rosettes from climbing into succulent crowns.
Autumn: Thin the darkest rooted offsets for replanting and clear all windblown leaves from the low mat.
Winter: Retain healthy evergreen rosettes but improve airflow if the central leaves stay wet or begin to blacken.

Stone Bed.name: New Zealand Flax (dark)
Stone Bed.position: Centre — dark burgundy spikes
Stone Bed.light: Full sun. Sun gives the deepest leaf colour
Stone Bed.water: Moderate; allow drainage. Water Phormium through active growth, then reduce in cold weather without keeping its crown wet.
Stone Bed.care:
Cut damaged blades at the base: Remove whole dead or badly split leaves individually. Do not cut across every leaf or pull hard on partly living fans. Use clean tools near the base without damaging the central growing points.

Retain the evergreen fans through winter: Protect exposed roots and avoid cold, saturated compost. Wait until spring to judge superficial frost injury. Divide only a congested healthy clump in spring; this is not a plant needing routine annual division.

Maintain the dark fan's clearance: For this Oak Lodge specimen Cut individual damaged Platt's Black blades at the base without shading or slicing adjacent alpine plants.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Pull out damaged leaves one by one at the base and mulch around, never into, the crown.
Summer: Water only through sustained drought and cut a finished flower stalk cleanly at the base.
Autumn: Clear debris from the leaf fans and stop feeding before cold weather.
Winter: Tie or wrap the crown for exceptional frost, then delay damage assessment until spring growth resumes.
Stone Bed.description: ‘Platt’s Black’ forms a fountain of narrow, arching leaves in very dark purple-brown, reading almost black against the pale Stone Bed gravel. The foliage is the year-round display; an established clump may eventually produce tall flower stems, but these are secondary to its silhouette. It remains more compact and arching than large green Phormiums, while still needing shelter from severe frost and a crown that never sits wet in winter.

Stone Bed.name: Agapanthus
Stone Bed.position: Position 9 — Stone Bed
Stone Bed.light: Full sun. Strong light is important for reliable flowering
Stone Bed.water: Water during active growth. Provide moisture for developing flowers while keeping the crown well drained in winter.
Stone Bed.care:
Record its winter foliage: Note whether the leaves die back or remain evergreen. Evergreen and deciduous Agapanthus differ in cold tolerance. Until the form is identified, provide conservative frost protection instead of assigning a precise hardiness rating.

Feed for flowers; divide sparingly: Use a suitable flowering feed in growth and remove spent stalks. Good sun is essential. Split only when congested or flowering declines; repeated disturbance can delay the display. Record flower colour and height when it blooms.

Measure position 9 in flower: For this Oak Lodge specimen Record flower colour, stalk height and winter leaf retention before assigning this Agapanthus a cultivar or hardiness.
Stone Bed.seasonal:
Spring: Clear dead foliage, protect emerging shoots from severe late frost and apply a balanced feed only if growth is weak.
Summer: Water during establishment and prolonged dry weather, then photograph the whole plant, foliage and flowers for identification.
Autumn: Deadhead at the base or retain sound seedheads deliberately; stop feeding as growth slows.
Winter: Keep the crown drained and use a dry mulch during severe weather until its hardiness and evergreen or deciduous habit are known.
Stone Bed.description: This Agapanthus occupies position 9 in the Stone Bed. August photographs now document its strap-shaped foliage and gravel-bed setting, while flower colour, mature height and whether it is evergreen or deciduous remain unresolved. Agapanthus generally performs best in full sun with moisture-retentive but well-drained soil.

Patio.name: Honeysuckle ‘Serotina’ — assumed
Patio.light: Sun with cool roots. Top growth flowers in light; root zone benefits from shade
Patio.water: Keep the shaded root run moist. Honeysuckle may flower in sun while its roots need shelter from wall-side drought.
Patio.care:
Train the new honeysuckle stems: Tie shoots into the support before they become a tangled mass. Keep growth away from gutters and neighbouring crowns. Mulch the root area without burying the stem base.

Time pruning to observed flowering: Use light cuts after the main display and record the flowering season. Serotina is an assumed late-flowering form. Avoid hard winter cuts until the plant's habit is clear; retain selected berrying growth if wanted.

Keep the right Patio support clear: For this Oak Lodge specimen Guide the honeysuckle on its own support and inspect the sheltered root area for drought beneath the house wall.
Patio.seasonal:
Spring: Mulch the cool root zone, tie new framework stems and thin only obviously dead tangles.
Summer: Enjoy evening scent, water through wall-side drought and prune lightly after flowering if access is blocked.
Autumn: Leave berries for birds where safe, retie loose stems and clear diseased fallen leaves.
Winter: Inspect supports and remove congested old wood gradually rather than stripping the entire framework.
Patio.description: The honeysuckle climbs its support at the far right of the Patio, providing fragrant tubular summer flowers above a shaded root run. Serotina is the current assumed cultivar, not a retained-label certainty. Guide the new shoots before they tangle, record the flowering window and keep the wall-side roots from drying during warm weather.

Patio.name: Clematis montana ‘Rubens’ — assumed
Patio.position: Left side of house wall — mature woody stems
Patio.light: Sun or partial shade. Keep roots cool while flowering growth reaches light
Patio.water: Moist roots beneath the wall. The large montana canopy needs a deep root run that does not dry hard in summer.
Patio.care:
Prune montana just after flowering: Shorten encroaching shoots after the late-spring display. It flowers on old wood. The hard February cut used for viticella would remove this year's flowers; only renovate severely when necessary and expect a reduced display.

Check the weight on its supports: Keep mature stems off gutters and weak masonry. Guide young shoots into sound wires before they tangle. Keep roots cool with mulch while leaving the crown clear of wet debris.

Retain the left-wall spring display: For this Oak Lodge specimen Make containment cuts after the montana flowers, while checking that its mature weight remains safely supported.
Patio.seasonal:
Spring: Tie loose stems before flowering, then make any major containment pruning immediately after the May display.
Summer: Guide fresh replacement shoots across sound wires and water deeply during prolonged drought.
Autumn: Retie the season’s framework and keep vigorous stems clear of gutters, windows and roof edges.
Winter: Do not routine-prune this group; inspect bare supports and remove only dead, damaged or dangerous stems.
Patio.description: Clematis montana covers the left house wall with mature woody stems and a sheet of pale pink flowers in May. It flowers on shoots made the previous year, so routine winter pruning would remove the coming display; containment cuts belong immediately after flowering. Its scale is an asset only while wires, masonry and routes remain sound—an established montana can extend 8–12m and become extremely heavy.

Tree.name: Pear ‘Conference’ — assumed
Tree.latin: Pyrus communis ‘Conference’ · rootstock Quince A assumed
Tree.light: Full sun. Warm shelter helps blossom and fruit ripen
Tree.water: Deeply while fruit develops in drought. The mature tree needs moisture below the surface, with mulch clear of the trunk.
Tree.care:
Preserve pear fruiting spurs: Prune the free-standing framework in winter, removing overcrowded wood gradually. If any branches are deliberately trained as an espalier or cordon, use the appropriate summer pruning method there instead. Avoid taking off a large share of the canopy at once.

Pick pears before they soften on the tree: Test for an easy release, then ripen a small batch indoors. Record the harvest window and ripening behaviour. Conference and Quince A remain assumed; do not promise a specific pollination group or storage period.

Record the upper-terrace harvest: For this Oak Lodge specimen Test a few pears for indoor ripening before picking the whole crop; keep Conference and Quince A qualified.
Tree.seasonal:
Spring: Protect blossom from severe forecast frost where practical and mulch after rain without touching the trunk.
Summer: Water deeply through fruit swell, thin only overloaded clusters and prune trained forms in late summer if applicable.
Autumn: Lift and twist fruit while still firm, ripen indoors and record flavour, colour and storage life.
Winter: Prune a free-standing tree for sound open structure, removing dead, diseased and crossing branches conservatively.
Tree.description: The mature upper-terrace pear supplies white spring blossom, a broad summer canopy and a crop that should be tested for picking while still firm. Conference on Quince A is the existing working assumption; fruit and graft evidence have not confirmed it. Record harvest and indoor-ripening behaviour rather than promising a particular storage period or pollination group.

Big Pot 1.name: Fuchsia
Big Pot 1.light: Sun or partial shade. Shelter from cold wind and fierce reflected heat
Big Pot 1.water: Even moisture while flowering. Check the mixed pot below the surface; drain thoroughly after watering and reduce during dormancy.
Big Pot 1.care:
Wait for Fuchsia's spring buds: Cut winter-killed stems back to live growth after severe frost has passed. Mrs Popple can regenerate from its base. Retain living framework where possible and pinch young shoots early if a bushier plant is needed.

Support the long flowering season: Feed the container during active growth and remove spent flowers and berries. Use the feed label rate on moist compost. Hardy-in-the-ground does not mean freeze-proof in a glazed pot; shelter or insulate its roots in hard weather.

Leave space around the lower pot's crown: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep trailing plants from matting over Mrs Popple's woody base in the decking-corner container.
Big Pot 1.seasonal:
Spring: Cut old top growth back after strong basal buds show, top-dress and restart watering gradually.
Summer: Keep the pot evenly moist, feed while flowering and deadhead only if berries are not wanted.
Autumn: Let growth harden, reduce feeding and decide whether the pot needs wrapping or moving into shelter.
Winter: Protect the root ball from freezing solid and keep compost only lightly moist while the crown rests.
Big Pot 1.description: ‘Mrs Popple’ is a vigorous upright Fuchsia with large single flowers: scarlet tubes and sepals flare around violet-purple petals from midsummer until frost. In a border it can form a metre-wide shrub; in Big Pot 1 its roots and final size are restricted, so consistent moisture and feeding matter. H4 hardiness applies most safely in the ground—an exposed glazed pot needs insulation or shelter in a severe winter.

Big Pot 1.name: Verbena
Big Pot 1.light: Full sun. Warm and open after frost
Big Pot 1.water: Moderate, with reliable drainage. Flowering Verbena needs moisture in growth, but a persistently wet crown encourages decline.
Big Pot 1.care:
Trim finished Verbena flower clusters: Cut back to leafy branching growth before trails become bare. Give full light and air around the stems. Water the roots during drought; stressed plants are more prone to a powdery coating on the leaves.

Match winter care to the selection: Keep tender bedding forms frost-free if retaining them. Margaret's Memory has greater hardiness than tender pot Verbena, but still needs free winter drainage. Do not assume all plants sold as Verbena have the same lifespan.

Refresh the front-left pink trails: For this Oak Lodge specimen Trim a few Showboat Light Pink stems at a time so the lower pot keeps flowers during regrowth.
Big Pot 1.seasonal:
Spring: Plant after frost, pinch the first extension shoots and let the roots fill before strong feeding.
Summer: Deadhead whole clusters, trim bare trails to leaves and feed lightly for continued flowering.
Autumn: Take cuttings before frost only if the cultivar is worth retaining; otherwise enjoy it until cold.
Winter: The outdoor display is seasonal; keep any cuttings bright, ventilated and frost-free.
Big Pot 1.description: ‘Showboat Light Pink’ trails soft pink flower clusters from the front-left of Big Pot 1, bridging the upright Fuchsia and lower cascades. Each rounded head is made from many small five-lobed flowers that bees and butterflies can work in succession. Heat and sun drive flowering, but a dry pot quickly triggers mildew and bare stems; regular trimming is what keeps the plant branching rather than merely extending.

Big Pot 1.name: Calibrachoa
Big Pot 1.light: Full sun. Warm and sheltered for maximum flower count
Big Pot 1.water: Moist but airy compost. Fine roots react quickly to both drought and saturation; inspect the root ball before watering.
Big Pot 1.care:
Feed Calibrachoa while it grows: Use a suitable container feed at the stated dilution. Young leaves yellowing between green veins can indicate poor iron uptake in alkaline compost. Check pH and drainage before adding more general fertiliser.

Refresh trails without routine heavy deadheading: Lightly shorten bare shoots to encourage branching. Many spent flowers fall naturally. Clear rotten blooms, give strong light and keep any overwintered stock bright and frost-free.

Inspect the miniature pink trumpets: For this Oak Lodge specimen Check the fine Cabaret roots and young leaf colour before adding water or feed to the whole lower pot.
Big Pot 1.seasonal:
Spring: Plant after frost, pinch sparse tips and begin feeding only once roots are active.
Summer: Check moisture daily in heat, feed weekly at label strength and trim any bare lengths back to leaves.
Autumn: Reduce feed as nights cool and take cuttings before frost only for planned overwintering.
Winter: Compost the outdoor plant or keep young cuttings frost-free; old waterlogged plants rarely overwinter well.
Big Pot 1.description: ‘Cabaret Special Pink Star’ produces hundreds of small petunia-like trumpets, each patterned with a bright pink star, on fine stems that spill over Big Pot 1. Big Pot 1.name: Lobelia
Big Pot 1.light: Sun or partial shade. Light shade helps through the hottest weather
Big Pot 1.water: Do not let the fine roots dry hard. Trailing bedding Lobelia can fail quickly at a hot pot rim even while larger companions look well.
Big Pot 1.care:
Refresh a tired Lobelia cascade: Trim spent or straggling growth lightly after its first flush. Maintain moisture and use a modest container feed as new shoots emerge. A fully dead, dried crown will not recover merely through heavier feeding.

Treat bedding Lobelia as frost-tender: Plant outside after frost and clear collapsed growth at season's end. These fine trailing plants are not the upright Starship perennial in Bed 4. Avoid promising a dormant hardy crown for next spring.

Check the shaded lower-pot rim: For this Oak Lodge specimen Rewet the fine blue-and-white Lobelia roots before the cascade browns beneath the taller container flowers.
Big Pot 1.seasonal:
Spring: Plant after frost, pinch lightly for branching and never bury the small crown.
Summer: Check moisture daily, trim a tired mat by one third and feed lightly to trigger a fresh cascade.
Autumn: Continue watering while flowering, then compost after frost; seed will not reliably reproduce the cultivar.
Winter: No outdoor crown persists; replace the seasonal plant next spring.
Big Pot 1.description: Waterfall Deep Blue Ice makes a fine cascade of tiny dark green leaves and deep blue flowers marked by a large white central splash. At only about 15cm high it disappears beneath the other planting while spilling 30cm over Big Pot 1’s edge. The small root system gives almost no drought reserve: one hot dry afternoon can brown the centre, while a midsummer trim can restore fresh branching if the roots remain healthy.

Big Pot 1.light: Full sun. Sheltered from drying wind
Big Pot 1.water: Evenly moist while flowering. Water the compost thoroughly and drain; hanging trails do not show how dry the central root ball has become.
Big Pot 1.care:
Remove Petunia flowers with their seed bases: Pinch spent blooms back to a leaf joint. Do not pull off only the coloured trumpet and leave the seed capsule. Shorten a few leggy trails at a time to keep flowers elsewhere on the plant.

Feed the seasonal container display: Use a flowering-plant feed during active growth at the label rate. Apply to moist compost. Protect deliberately overwintered plants from frost; outdoor flowering normally finishes as temperatures fall.

Keep Midnight Sky's name unresolved: For this Oak Lodge specimen Retain the recorded Midnight Sky name and a fresh label; white speckling alone does not prove NightSky's breeder identity.
Big Pot 1.seasonal:
Spring: Plant outdoors after frost and pinch once if the young plant has few branches.
Summer: Deadhead below the seed capsule, feed weekly and cut bare trails back to leafy side shoots.
Autumn: Enjoy the final pattern changes in cool weather, then take cuttings or compost before frost.
Winter: Keep only young cuttings bright and frost-free; the outdoor pot plant is seasonal.
Big Pot 1.description: The Petunia recorded as Midnight Sky trails from the front-right of Big Pot 1 with dark purple flowers and variable white markings. Midnight Sky and NightSky are different commercial selections, so the speckled flowers do not justify assigning the NightSky breeder code Kleph15313. Retain the recorded name while checking a label, and use ordinary tender Petunia care: good light, regular feeding and selective deadheading.

Big Pot 2.name: Verbena
Big Pot 2.light: Full sun. Warm, open and sheltered
Big Pot 2.water: Moderate, with reliable drainage. Flowering Verbena needs moisture in growth, but a persistently wet crown encourages decline.
Big Pot 2.care:
Trim finished Verbena flower clusters: Cut back to leafy branching growth before trails become bare. Give full light and air around the stems. Water the roots during drought; stressed plants are more prone to a powdery coating on the leaves.

Match winter care to the selection: Keep tender bedding forms frost-free if retaining them. Margaret's Memory has greater hardiness than tender pot Verbena, but still needs free winter drainage. Do not assume all plants sold as Verbena have the same lifespan.

Keep the bicolour front edge branching: For this Oak Lodge specimen Trim Venturi Pink Bicolour where its trails become bare, preserving flowering shoots elsewhere in the upper pot.
Big Pot 2.seasonal:
Spring: Plant after frost and pinch early extensions once to establish a branching framework.
Summer: Deadhead whole clusters, shorten bare trails and feed lightly while buds continue.
Autumn: Take healthy cuttings before frost only if the exact bicolour is wanted again.
Winter: Treat as seasonal or keep cuttings frost-free in bright ventilation.
Big Pot 2.description: ‘Venturi Pink Bicolour’ forms rounded clusters in pink and white on spreading stems at the front of Big Pot 2. The bicolour pattern reads as a lighter bridge between the violet Fuchsia petals and the purple-white Petunia beside it. Regular removal of whole faded clusters and a trim before the centre becomes bare keep the plant branching and flowering until frost.

Big Pot 2.light: Full sun. Shelter from drying wind and hard rain
Big Pot 2.water: Evenly moist while flowering. Water the compost thoroughly and drain; hanging trails do not show how dry the central root ball has become.
Big Pot 2.care:
Remove Petunia flowers with their seed bases: Pinch spent blooms back to a leaf joint. Do not pull off only the coloured trumpet and leave the seed capsule. Shorten a few leggy trails at a time to keep flowers elsewhere on the plant.

Feed the seasonal container display: Use a flowering-plant feed during active growth at the label rate. Apply to moist compost. Protect deliberately overwintered plants from frost; outdoor flowering normally finishes as temperatures fall.

Big Pot 2.seasonal:
Spring: Plant after frost and pinch once if the young framework is sparse.
Summer: Feed weekly, deadhead below each seed capsule and shorten selected long stems before they become bare.
Autumn: Enjoy the final flowers until cold, then compost or take cuttings before frost.
Winter: The outdoor plant is seasonal; retain only healthy frost-free cuttings.
Big Pot 2.description: Sky Purple White Sky carries broad trumpet flowers patterned in purple and white rather than the speckled galaxy of Big Pot 1’s NightSky. The strong two-tone blooms fill Big Pot 2’s front edge from May into October. As stems lengthen, cutting selected bare trails back to leafy side shoots preserves the pot’s rounded shape far better than allowing every shoot to reach maximum length.

Big Pot 2.name: Nepeta ‘Walker’s Low’ — assumed
Big Pot 2.light: Full sun. Open light keeps growth compact and flower-rich
Big Pot 2.water: Let the upper root zone dry. Catmint tolerates dryness better than the neighbouring Fuchsia and Lobelia; avoid a permanently wet crown.
Big Pot 2.care:
Shear catmint after the first flowers: Cut spent stems back to fresh basal or low leafy growth. A drink after cutting helps a second flush if the pot is dry. Do not leave lanky stems tangled through the other container plants.

Give the grey foliage light and air: Keep taller companions from covering the catmint's centre. Avoid extra nitrogen, which encourages weak sprawling growth. Walker's Low is an assumed identity; do not rely on seed to reproduce it.

Balance the upper pot's mixed needs: For this Oak Lodge specimen Let Nepeta's crown dry slightly while checking the more thirsty Lobelia and Fuchsia roots separately.
Big Pot 2.seasonal:
Spring: Clear Big Pot 2's dead Nepeta stems and divide only if its root plug is congested among the mixed planting.
Summer: Shear this rim plant after its first flush so fresh aromatic growth can trail without tangling the Fuchsia.
Autumn: Remove collapsed stems that hold moisture against the pot edge while leaving a short labelled crown.
Winter: Keep Big Pot 2 freely drained and do not water the dormant Nepeta just because evergreen companions need checking.
Big Pot 2.description: This second catmint clump supplies hardy grey-green foliage and lavender-blue spikes through the centre of Big Pot 2. It connects the seasonal pink and purple flowers while remaining useful to bees. Because both big pots contain Nepeta, their response to sun, moisture and post-flowering cutting can be compared directly.

profile.about: Nepeta is a mint-family genus of aromatic perennials. Big Pot 2.name: Fuchsia
Big Pot 2.light: Sun or partial shade. Shelter from cold wind and fierce reflected heat
Big Pot 2.water: Even moisture while flowering. Check the mixed pot below the surface; drain thoroughly after watering and reduce during dormancy.
Big Pot 2.care:
Wait for Fuchsia's spring buds: Cut winter-killed stems back to live growth after severe frost has passed. Mrs Popple can regenerate from its base. Retain living framework where possible and pinch young shoots early if a bushier plant is needed.

Support the long flowering season: Feed the container during active growth and remove spent flowers and berries. Use the feed label rate on moist compost. Hardy-in-the-ground does not mean freeze-proof in a glazed pot; shelter or insulate its roots in hard weather.

Protect the upper pot's exposed roots: For this Oak Lodge specimen Insulate or shelter Mrs Popple's glazed container in prolonged cold even if the lower-pot Fuchsia appears sheltered.
Big Pot 2.seasonal:
Spring: Wait for basal buds in Big Pot 2, cut dead stems above them and top-dress without disturbing neighbouring roots.
Summer: Water this more exposed upper pot consistently, feed while the Fuchsia flowers and turn foliage outward from crowded companions.
Autumn: Stop feeding Big Pot 2 early enough for stems to firm, and decide on frost protection before cold nights arrive.
Winter: Insulate the upper pot's root ball from freezing wind and keep it only lightly moist while the Fuchsia crown rests.
Big Pot 2.description: A second ‘Mrs Popple’ anchors the rear of Big Pot 2 with the same scarlet-and-violet single flowers and upright woody framework. Its hardiness is greater than the surrounding bedding, but its roots are still exposed by container culture. Keeping both Fuchsias lets Oak Lodge compare microclimate and retain the better-performing crown after winter.

Little Pot 1.light: Partial shade to sun. Sheltered pot position
Little Pot 1.water: Even moisture, never stagnant. A hellebore in a small pot needs checks even when cool weather reduces demand.
Little Pot 1.care:
Reveal the winter flowers selectively: Remove damaged or spotted leaves rather than all healthy evergreen growth. Cut affected leaves at the base with clean tools. Keep the emerging buds clear of decaying petals and dense debris.

Give Bennotta lasting root room: Use a deep, drained container and top-dress in spring. Shelter the pot from drying wind and summer heat. Hellebores resent unnecessary disturbance; repot for crowding rather than routinely splitting the crown.

Keep Little Pot 1's winter crown clear: For this Oak Lodge specimen Remove collapsed hellebore leaves and petals without treating this new winter planting as the removed summer bedding.
Little Pot 1.seasonal:
Spring: Cut away old or spotted leaves at the base as flower stems rise, then top-dress the pot and photograph the bloom colour for cultivar confirmation.
Summer: Allow clean foliage to feed the crown, water through prolonged drought and move to dappled shade if the small pot heats sharply.
Autumn: Remove badly marked leaves, refresh the top layer of compost and keep the drainage hole clear ahead of the winter flowering cycle.
Winter: Turn the outward-facing flowers into view, clear fallen petals and leaves promptly, and water sparingly on frost-free mornings when the compost is dry.
Little Pot 1.description: Ice N' Roses Bennotta is the new winter-flowering centrepiece in Little Pot 1, replacing the summer Geranium and Petunia display. Its dark evergreen foliage and deep pink-red flowers bring colour through the quiet months, provided the small pot drains freely.

Little Pot 2.light: Full sun. Open light gives the strongest stems and most flowers
Little Pot 2.water: Moderate; dry slightly between checks. The small pot needs summer water but not a cold wet crown through winter.
Little Pot 2.care:
Deadhead the golden daisies: Cut finished stems to leafy side growth before seed builds up. If flowering becomes sparse, trim the tired display back and support the fresh regrowth with modest feed and water.

Renew only when the clump tires: Watch for a bare centre or a crowded root ball. Divide or repot in spring when new growth is evident. Keep Early Sunrise visibly assumed; seed-raised plants may not match the original.

Use the upper stair-wall pot: For this Oak Lodge specimen Coreopsis now grows in Little Pot 2; inspect that small root ball rather than the Echinacea's former shared history.
Little Pot 2.seasonal:
Spring: Clear dead growth, top-dress lightly and wait for healthy shoots before increasing water.
Summer: Deadhead to a leafy joint, then shear a tired plant by up to half for a compact second flush.
Autumn: Stop feeding, leave some sound foliage and check that drainage holes remain open.
Winter: Raise the pot on feet and keep the dormant crown drained; add shelter until its hardiness is confirmed.
Little Pot 2.description: The Coreopsis moved into Little Pot 2 on the upper stair wall carries golden daisy flowers above a compact leafy clump. Early Sunrise is the existing assumed match; the original garden name Gold does not prove a cultivar. Deadheading and a light trim of exhausted stems sustain the display, while the small pot needs summer moisture and an airy crown through winter.

profile.about: Coreopsis is a North American genus in the daisy family, ranging from short-lived annuals to reliably hardy clump-forming perennials. Cercis Pot.position: Single standard-form specimen in a large pot
Cercis Pot.light: Full sun. Warm light develops the strongest foliage colour
Cercis Pot.water: Deeply while establishing. Keep the young redbud root ball moist but aerated; shelter reduces leaf scorch and wind damage.
Cercis Pot.care:
Let the redbud build its framework: Remove only dead, damaged or crossing branches as needed. Avoid repeated heading-back of healthy branches. Check ties before they constrict the trunk, and protect the root collar from a bank of mulch.

Give the coloured leaves good light: Use sun with shelter from drying wind. Water below the canopy during dry establishment weather. Fresh foliage can scorch if roots dry while leaves are exposed; extra fertiliser does not solve that imbalance.

Plan for the specimen pot to fill: For this Oak Lodge specimen Check Carolina Sweetheart's root space and support ties; a tree-sized canopy cannot remain indefinitely in exhausted potting mix.
Cercis Pot.seasonal:
Spring: Top-dress after growth starts, check that ties allow trunk expansion and watch for pink-purple flowers on older bare wood.
Summer: Water deeply through dry spells, rotate only if the crown becomes strongly one-sided and avoid high-nitrogen feeding.
Autumn: Let growth harden naturally, remove the saucer if it traps rain and check whether the roots have filled the pot.
Winter: Raise the pot on feet, wrap or shelter the root ball during severe frost and keep compost just moist rather than saturated.
Cercis Pot.description: Carolina Sweetheart (‘Nccc1’) is a slow-growing eastern redbud selected for foliage that changes repeatedly through the season. New heart-shaped leaves open maroon-red, then mature through green with white margins and irregular pink, cream and red sectors. The young standard now occupies the Lobelia Pot’s former corner. Although the tree itself is H5, container roots are more exposed than roots in open ground, so steady moisture, winter insulation and a realistic plan for a larger root run matter more than routine pruning.

profile.about: Cercis canadensis is a North American member of the pea family whose pink-purple flowers can emerge directly from older branches before the leaves. Its mature leaf colour is deliberately irregular, so green, cream, pink and maroon sectors are normal rather than a nutrient disorder.

Front Pot.care:

Keep the rosette warm and drained: Avoid heavy feeding and water held against the crown. Treat as seasonal bedding or overwinter in bright frost-free conditions. Protect before freezing weather rather than relying on winter mulch.

Front Pot.description: ‘Sunny Side Up’ forms a low silver-green rosette beneath large cream-white daisies marked by a dark ring around their golden centres. The flowers open only in strong light, closing at night and often staying folded on dull days, so the Front Pot changes visibly with the weather. It tolerates heat and brief dryness far better than its trailing companions but cannot survive a Bromsgrove frost.

Front Pot.name: Calibrachoa Can-Can Sunrise — assumed
Front Pot.light: Full sun. Shelter from hard rain and drying wind
Front Pot.water: Moist but airy compost. Fine roots react quickly to both drought and saturation; inspect the root ball before watering.
Front Pot.care:
Feed Calibrachoa while it grows: Use a suitable container feed at the stated dilution. Young leaves yellowing between green veins can indicate poor iron uptake in alkaline compost. Check pH and drainage before adding more general fertiliser.

Refresh trails without routine heavy deadheading: Lightly shorten bare shoots to encourage branching. Many spent flowers fall naturally. Clear rotten blooms, give strong light and keep any overwintered stock bright and frost-free.

Check the fine roots beside the Gazanias: For this Oak Lodge specimen The assumed Can-Can Sunrise needs steadier moisture than the daisies, but cannot tolerate permanently saturated compost.
Front Pot.seasonal:
Spring: Plant after frost, tease circling roots gently and begin feeding after active growth resumes.
Summer: Check daily in heat, feed weekly at label strength and trim individual bare trails back to leaves.
Autumn: Reduce feed as nights cool and enjoy flowers until frost ends the display.
Winter: Compost the outdoor plant or keep young cuttings frost-free only if its colour proves worth retaining.
Front Pot.description: Calibrachoa sends fine branching stems over the Front Pot rim, carrying hundreds of small petunia-like trumpets between the two larger Gazanias. It is the pot’s continuous colour engine, flowering from late spring until frost when moisture, acidity and feed remain balanced. Unlike the drought-tolerant Gazanias, its compact root system reacts quickly to both a dried-out root ball and cold saturation.

Front Pot.name: Bacopa ‘Snowflake’ — assumed
Front Pot.position: Trailing — delicate white flowers at the edges
Front Pot.light: Sun or partial shade. Flowers well with good light and shelter
Front Pot.water: Steady moisture through flowering. Bacopa is more drought-sensitive than the Gazanias; check its own root area in the mixed pot.
Front Pot.care:
Prevent a drought break in flowering: Rewet the root ball before the fine stems wilt badly. Severe drying can interrupt flowers for some time even after watering resumes. Keep drainage open rather than compensating with constant saturation.

Shorten bare trails selectively: Trim to healthy leafy growth and feed lightly during active growth. Most little flowers fall without individual deadheading. Preserve bright frost-free stock only if overwintering deliberately; Snowflake remains an assumed identity.

Front Pot.description: White Bacopa threads delicate five-lobed flowers through the Front Pot edge, softening the heavy Gazania daisies with a much finer scale. Its small rounded leaves stay dense only when the root ball remains evenly moist; one severe drying can stop flowering and leave bare sections that recover slowly. The white-flowered plant resembles cultivars such as ‘Snowflake’, but Oak Lodge has no label proving that name.

Wall Pot 1.name: Phormium 'Flamingo'
Wall Pot 1.position: Former Candy House Calibrachoa pot on the steps — planted September 2026
Wall Pot 1.light: Sun or partial shade. Shelter the container from wind that catches its tall leaves.
Wall Pot 1.water: Moderate; allow drainage. Water Phormium through active growth, then reduce in cold weather without keeping its crown wet.
Wall Pot 1.care:
Cut damaged blades at the base: Remove whole dead or badly split leaves individually. Do not cut across every leaf or pull hard on partly living fans. Use clean tools near the base without damaging the central growing points.

Retain the evergreen fans through winter: Protect exposed roots and avoid cold, saturated compost. Wait until spring to judge superficial frost injury. Divide only a congested healthy clump in spring; this is not a plant needing routine annual division.

Check the wall pot's stability: For this Oak Lodge specimen Flamingo's strap leaves catch wind; secure the container and plan more root room as the clump expands.
Wall Pot 1.seasonal:
Spring: Pull out only fully dead blades from the base, inspect the fan for winter damage and replace the top few centimetres of exhausted potting mix.
Summer: Water the wall pot deeply during hot spells and rotate it if one-sided light is distorting the pink-striped fan; avoid high-nitrogen feed.
Autumn: Stop feeding, remove leaves that have split beyond recovery and secure the pot before autumn gales catch the strap-like foliage.
Winter: Keep the crown on the dry side, shield the container during prolonged hard frost and do not cut superficially scorched leaves until spring.
Wall Pot 1.description: Flamingo replaced the seasonal Calibrachoa in the Steps wall pot. Arching sword-shaped leaves striped pink and olive-green provide the lasting display; flowers are occasional on mature plants, not a year-round feature. The clump can approach a metre in height and spread, so its small container needs secure placement, drainage and a plan for increasing root room.

Wall Pot 2.name: Echinacea Mooodz Glory — label confirmed
Wall Pot 2.position: Single compact specimen filling the former Coreopsis pot
Wall Pot 2.light: Full sun. Partial shade is tolerated but sun supports stronger flowering
Wall Pot 2.water: Moderate in active growth. A pot dries faster than a border, but winter drainage remains essential for the coneflower crown.
Wall Pot 2.care:
Manage flowers and seed cones separately: Deadhead early flowers for continuity, leaving selected later cones if wanted. Cut a finished stem to a healthy leaf or side bud. Sound autumn cones can remain for structure rather than stripping the plant bare.

Protect emerging basal growth: Clear collapsed leaves before spring shoots open and check for slugs. Do not keep the dormant pot wet. Divide or repot only when the established root system becomes crowded, retaining strong growing points.

Protect the white coneflower's crown: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep Mooodz Glory's own pot drained through winter and mark where new basal shoots should emerge.
Wall Pot 2.seasonal:
Spring: Clear dead stems carefully as new shoots emerge, top-dress lightly and avoid disturbing the crown unnecessarily.
Summer: Water after the upper compost begins to dry and cut fading stems to a leafy joint for further flowers.
Autumn: Leave selected firm cones for structure, stop feeding and keep fallen petals and leaves away from the crown.
Winter: Raise the pot on feet, protect it from prolonged rain and leave the dormant crown undisturbed.
Wall Pot 2.description: Echinacea Mooodz Glory (‘Hilmooglor’) fills the former Coreopsis pot with sturdy dark-green foliage and white, slightly drooping ray florets around prominent golden-green cones. The compact selection flowers from summer into autumn and is hardy to H5, but the crown still needs sharp winter drainage in a small glazed pot. Deadheading can extend the display; retaining a few sound cones later gives structure and potential food for birds.

profile.about: Echinacea are North American daisy-family perennials with a raised cone of disc florets surrounded by rays. Mooodz Glory is the trade name for ‘Hilmooglor’, selected for compact growth and white flowers. The RHS notes that Echinacea dislike disturbance and perform best in deep, drained soil, which makes careful long-term container culture more important than frequent repotting.

Hanging Basket 3.name: Fuchsia (cultivar to confirm)
Hanging Basket 3.position: Retained in the refreshed Hanging Basket 3 on the Decking
Hanging Basket 3.light: Sun or partial shade. Protect from the fiercest afternoon heat and drying wind
Hanging Basket 3.water: Moist while actively growing. Container Fuchsia dries rapidly in warm wind; reduce water in cool dormant conditions.
Hanging Basket 3.care:
Keep Fuchsia flowering on fresh shoots: Remove finished flowers and berries, and pinch young growth before flowering. Feed during active growth using the container-feed rate. Avoid repeatedly cutting off shoots already carrying a display of buds.

Do not borrow Mrs Popple's hardiness: Use frost-free shelter while these cultivars remain unresolved. Inspect living buds in spring before removing old wood. A trailing habit or a Fuchsia flower does not establish reliable outdoor winter survival.

Keep Basket 3's large flowers supported: For this Oak Lodge specimen Arrange the arching Fuchsia stems clear of the new Cyclamen and fern rather than clipping the whole basket together.
Hanging Basket 3.seasonal:
Spring: Plant out after frost, pinch young tips for branching and protect from cold wind.
Summer: Check moisture daily in heat, feed weekly and remove developing berries with the spent flowers.
Autumn: Take labelled cuttings or move a healthy plant under cover before the first frost if it is to be retained.
Winter: Keep selected stock frost-free with reduced water; otherwise renew the seasonal basket next year.
Hanging Basket 3.description: The basket Fuchsia provides the largest flowers in the hanging display, carrying pendant bicolour blooms along arching stems from June until cold weather. Each flower hangs beneath its ovary with reflexed sepals around a softer inner corolla, a structure well suited to bees. The trailing habit is secure, but colour and cultivar are not recorded, so pruning, final spread and any claim of exceptional hardiness remain deliberately general.

Hanging Basket 3.name: Fern (cultivar to confirm)
Hanging Basket 3.position: Retained in the refreshed Hanging Basket 3 on the Decking
Hanging Basket 3.light: Bright shade to partial shade. Filtered light protects soft fronds while its exact shade preference remains unresolved.
Hanging Basket 3.water: Keep evenly moist, not saturated. Until the fern is identified, check its own root ball rather than letting the basket dry completely.
Hanging Basket 3.care:
Protect the retained fronds: Keep it in bright shade and remove only dead foliage. Do not deadhead, shear or feed this foliage plant to encourage flowers. Ferns reproduce by spores; brown spore patches can be normal rather than disease.

Resolve winter hardiness before frost: Use sheltered, frost-free holding conditions while its identity is unknown. Photograph the whole frond, its underside and the crown. An unidentified basket fern must not automatically inherit the hardiness of the garden Dryopteris.

Keep a frond for identification: For this Oak Lodge specimen Photograph the retained Basket 3 fern's underside before removing old fronds; its winter requirements are still unresolved.
Hanging Basket 3.seasonal:
Spring: Remove only brown fronds at their base and photograph new croziers, scale texture and mature fronds to narrow the identification.
Summer: Shield the fronds from hot midday sun, maintain even moisture around the compact root ball and mist only when airflow can dry the foliage.
Autumn: Keep chrysanthemum and Lysimachia stems from pressing into the fern crown and record whether the fronds remain evergreen as temperatures fall.
Winter: Because the species is unconfirmed, protect Basket 3 from hard frost; keep the crown just moist and retain diagnostic fronds until identification is secure.
Hanging Basket 3.description: The retained fern brings divided green fronds to Hanging Basket 3, contrasting with the new autumn flowers and trailing Lysimachia. Ferns do not flower: their display is foliage, and brown spore patches on frond undersides can be normal. Its species and hardiness remain unresolved, so preserve identification photographs and use cautious frost protection rather than assuming a hardy woodland fern.

Hanging Basket 3.position: Flowering addition to the refreshed Hanging Basket 3 on the Decking

Hanging Basket 3.care:
Keep the autumn flower heads clean: Remove whole faded heads and damaged leaves promptly. Give open light and airflow. Do not pinch a plant already in bud for its autumn display; that removes the flowers being grown.

Treat winter survival as unresolved: Shelter the root ball from hard frost and persistent wet if keeping it. Florist and garden Chrysanthemums differ in hardiness. Retain healthy basal growth and confirm the type before relying on an outdoor return.

Protect the autumn buds: For this Oak Lodge specimen Do not pinch the newly planted Basket 3 Chrysanthemum as though preparing a summer nursery plant.
Hanging Basket 3.seasonal:
Spring: If the plant survives, cut old stems to sound basal growth, refresh the surface and record new leaf shape for identification.
Summer: Pinch only while stems are vegetative, support developing shoots and inspect young tips for aphids before flower buds tighten.
Autumn: This is the main flowering period: deadhead to a side shoot, keep petals dry when watering and photograph the blooms for cultivar comparison.
Winter: After flowering, shelter the uncertain Chrysanthemum from prolonged frost and keep the crown barely moist until its hardiness is known.

Hanging Basket 3.name: Cyclamen (cultivar to confirm)
Hanging Basket 3.position: Autumn addition to the refreshed Hanging Basket 3 on the Decking
Hanging Basket 3.light: Bright, sheltered partial shade. Cool bright shelter preserves flowers; avoid heat and freezing exposure.
Hanging Basket 3.water: Lightly moist during leaf growth. Water around the root ball, keeping the tuber and flower-stalk centre out of standing wet.
Hanging Basket 3.care:
Remove finished Cyclamen stalks: Gently twist spent flowers away at the base without leaving rotting stubs. Keep the plant cool and bright. Remove yellow leaves individually and keep crowded basket companions from covering the growing point.

Do not assume hardy Cyclamen care: Shelter from frost until the species is known. Autumn bedding may be tender C. persicum rather than hardy C. hederifolium. Reduce water if it becomes naturally dormant; do not force a leafless resting tuber into soggy growth.

Keep the tuber undivided: For this Oak Lodge specimen Do not apply the old perennial-template division advice to Basket 3's Cyclamen; protect it until its species is known.
Hanging Basket 3.seasonal:
Spring: Record whether leaves and flowers persist before assuming a hardy cycle; remove spent stems with a clean twist rather than leaving stubs.
Summer: If foliage naturally disappears, keep the tuber shaded and almost dry; if it remains active, continue cautious edge watering.
Autumn: As growth resumes, keep the top of the tuber clear, remove yellow leaves and photograph flower and leaf pattern for species identification.
Winter: Shelter Basket 3 during severe frost until the Cyclamen is identified, and keep rain from pooling in the crown or around the tuber.
Hanging Basket 3.description: Swept-back flowers and patterned leaves make the Cyclamen a low autumn focus in Hanging Basket 3. Its species is unknown, which matters: common bedding C. persicum and hardy garden cyclamens have different winter limits. Keep the tuber undivided, clear decaying flower stalks from its centre and shelter it from frost until the identity is resolved.

Baskets.name: Calluna Trio Mix (2 plants)
photos: images/September Hanging Baskets & Pots/Hanging Basket 1 & 2 - Heather.jpeg
Baskets.group: Shared planting · red Basket 1 & green Basket 2
Baskets.position: One plant in each of red Basket 1 and green Basket 2 — Patio Kitchen & Lounge
Baskets.light: Sun to light shade. Keep the heather clear of taller companions; deep shade weakens its compact growth.
Baskets.water: Keep the shallow roots from drying. Calluna needs acidic, drained soil; small plugs in baskets can dry before the surrounding compost.
Baskets.care:
Clip Calluna within green growth: In spring, remove last year's flowered tips lightly. Leave leafy shoots below every cut. Cutting into a bare woody centre is unlikely to regenerate a dense plant.

Retain an open, acidic planting pocket: Give the heather sun and keep larger neighbours from covering it. Use rainwater where practical. Avoid lime and rich manure; lightly maintain the soil rather than forcing soft growth with heavy feeding.

Check both heather root plugs: For this Oak Lodge specimen One Calluna plant is recorded in each matching basket; inspect both rather than assuming a three-plant commercial mix count.
Baskets.seasonal:
Spring: After flowering, lightly clip each Calluna mound below its spent flower spikes but never into bare old wood; top-dress around the plugs.
Summer: Check the two Calluna root plugs, one in each matching basket, and use rainwater to rewet them thoroughly before they dry hard.
Autumn: Keep both basket heathers open to light and remove dead sprigs while the mixed selection supplies late-season colour.
Winter: Keep drainage holes open and shelter the hanging root balls from drying easterly wind; do not feed while growth is resting.
Baskets.description: Two Calluna plants from the recorded Trio Mix now provide low evergreen structure across the matching baskets, one in Basket 1 and one in Basket 2. The commercial mix name does not mean three plants are present in each basket. Keep the shallow root plugs moist in acidic compost and lightly clip flowered tips in spring without cutting into bare wood.

Baskets.name: Viola 'Rocky Purple Picotee' (2 plants)
Baskets.group: Shared planting · red Basket 1 & green Basket 2
Baskets.position: One plant in each of red Basket 1 and green Basket 2 — Patio Kitchen & Lounge
Baskets.light: Sun to partial shade. Give the low purple flowers light without baking the exposed root plugs.
Baskets.water: Moist, with free drainage. Small Viola and pansy roots dry quickly; cool, saturated compost can rot their crowns.
Baskets.care:
Remove flowers and seed capsules: Pinch each spent stem back to a leaf joint. Clear rain-damaged blooms promptly to limit grey mould. A light feed during growth helps sustain flowers in a container.

Let cool weather set the pace: Expect pauses during hard frost or summer heat. Trim stretched stems to leafy growth if the crown is sound. Give light shade in hot weather and avoid burying small crowns under fallen leaves.

Deadhead each matching basket: For this Oak Lodge specimen One Rocky Purple Picotee grows in Basket 1 and one in Basket 2; keep both low crowns clear.
Baskets.seasonal:
Spring: Pinch out seed pods and leggy stems to a leafy joint, then feed lightly to support a fresh cool-season flush.
Summer: Expect flowering to ease in heat; keep the two plants shaded at the hottest part of the day and trim rather than forcing soft growth.
Autumn: Deadhead both plants several times a week and check that their crowns have not been buried by settling basket compost.
Winter: Remove storm-damaged flowers promptly, keep the liner drained and water on mild mornings rather than immediately before a freeze.
Baskets.description: One Rocky Purple Picotee Viola was used in each matching Basket 1 and Basket 2, continuing the purple-and-pale flower theme across the pair.

Baskets.group: Shared planting · red Basket 1 & green Basket 2
Baskets.position: One plant in each of red Basket 1 and green Basket 2 — Patio Kitchen & Lounge
Baskets.light: Sun to partial shade. Bright cool conditions support flowers; shade from hot midday sun if needed.
Baskets.water: Moist, with free drainage. Small Viola and pansy roots dry quickly; cool, saturated compost can rot their crowns.
Baskets.care:
Remove flowers and seed capsules: Pinch each spent stem back to a leaf joint. Clear rain-damaged blooms promptly to limit grey mould. A light feed during growth helps sustain flowers in a container.

Let cool weather set the pace: Expect pauses during hard frost or summer heat. Trim stretched stems to leafy growth if the crown is sound. Give light shade in hot weather and avoid burying small crowns under fallen leaves.

Preserve the warm-coloured pair: For this Oak Lodge specimen Remove spent Fire pansy flowers in both matching baskets, including their developing seed capsules.
Baskets.seasonal:
Spring: Cut each pair of plants back to compact leafy growth if they have stretched, then resume deadheading as new buds open.
Summer: Give afternoon shade during heat, remove every seed capsule and replace plants only if the crowns fail rather than merely pausing in flower.
Autumn: Keep the fiery blooms coming by deadheading to the next leaf and applying a dilute high-potash feed after watering.
Winter: Pick off rain-spoiled petals, keep air moving through the basket and avoid leaving wet flowers to freeze overnight.

Front Bed 1.name: Hydrangea Endless Summer ‘The Original’ — assumed
Front Bed 1.position: Top of the bed, nearest the front door
Front Bed 1.light: Morning sun and afternoon shade. Shelter new growth from late frost and drying wind
Front Bed 1.water: Keep the root zone moist. Big mophead leaves wilt readily in heat; check soil before adding water to an already wet bed.
Front Bed 1.care:
Keep the mophead's flower buds: In spring, remove old heads to the first strong pair of buds. Retain healthy stems and thin a few old ones only if crowded. Endless Summer is assumed, so do not depend on repeat flowering to compensate for severe pruning.

Mulch the broad root area: Use organic mulch over moist soil, clear of the stems. Morning light and afternoon shelter reduce scorch. Soil chemistry can influence flower colour, but adding products without checking pH can damage roots.

Preserve the upper anchor's buds: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep strong old stems through winter rather than cutting this mophead like the Bloody Marie panicle Hydrangea.
Front Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Remove each old flower head to the first strong pair of buds and take one or two oldest stems at the base if congested.
Summer: Water deeply in dry weather and photograph mature flower colour, head shape and fertile florets for identification.
Autumn: Leave fading heads in place and refresh mulch only after the ground is moist.
Winter: Retain the old heads over the buds and avoid pruning during hard frost.
Front Bed 1.description: This Hydrangea macrophylla makes the broad-leaved upper anchor of Front Bed 1, carrying rounded mophead clusters from July into September. The flower colour can shift with cultivar and soil chemistry, while the same large leaves that create its lush effect also lose water rapidly in heat. Old flower heads are useful winter protection for the buds below, so spring—not autumn—is the moment for its light annual prune.

profile.about: Hydrangea macrophylla includes mophead and lacecap cultivars originating from East Asia. Most flower on shoots arising from the previous year’s stems, which is why hard spring pruning sacrifices bloom. Front Bed 1.name: Lavender ‘Hidcote’ — assumed
Front Bed 1.position: Bottom of the bed, below the brick pillar
Front Bed 1.light: Full sun. Open light and airflow preserve compact growth
Front Bed 1.water: Sparingly once established. English lavender needs a dry, airy crown and little extra water in normal weather.
Front Bed 1.care:
Trim lavender while leaves remain: Shorten spent flower shoots after the summer display. Keep green foliage below the cuts; old bare wood may not regrow. Give full sun and avoid hard autumn renovation.

Keep fertility and moisture modest: Do not heap rich mulch against the woody base. Drainage and ventilation matter more than feeding. Take cuttings from healthy non-flowering shoots before an old plant becomes too woody to reshape.

Keep the mound below the pillar sunny: For this Oak Lodge specimen Prevent taller Front Bed 1 foliage from shading the Lavender and avoid mulching its woody centre.
Front Bed 1.seasonal:
Spring: Remove winter damage and lightly reshape only where green leaves remain below every cut.
Summer: Enjoy peak bee activity, then trim flower stalks and about 2–3cm of leafy growth after bloom.
Autumn: Stop feeding and keep fallen leaves from holding moisture around the base.
Winter: Leave the mound open to light and air; never cover the crown with wet mulch.
Front Bed 1.description: English lavender forms a compact silver-grey mound below the brick pillar, releasing aromatic oil whenever its narrow leaves are brushed. Purple flower spikes rise above the foliage from June into August and provide concentrated nectar for bees. Its longevity depends less on feeding than on full sun, fast drainage and an annual trim that stays within leafy growth rather than cutting into bare old stems.

Front Bed 2.description: Coprosma ‘Inferno’ is the upright, glossy-leaved anchor at the back-left of Front Bed 2. Its green leaves carry yellow-orange margins through spring and summer, then deepen into red, pink and purple-brown as temperatures fall. That winter colour comes with limited cold tolerance: the shrub is rated H3, so the exposed front bed should be treated as a trial site and protected from severe frost and drying wind.

profile.about: Coprosma are New Zealand looking-glass plants named for their exceptionally glossy leaves. ‘Inferno’ is an accepted female cultivar with upright growth and a strong seasonal colour shift; its flowers are insignificant and berries are unlikely without a compatible male plant. In Bromsgrove the key horticultural question is winter survival, not flowering.
