Front Bed 2.name: Coprosma 'Pina Colada'
Front Bed 2.light: Full sun. Warm shelter gives best colour and winter survival
Front Bed 2.water: Moderate; avoid saturation. Glossy evergreen foliage needs moisture in dry spells, with much less demand in cold weather.
Front Bed 2.care:
Plan for a cold-sensitive evergreen: Shelter from drying wind and protect during severe frost. These Coprosmas are marginal in a cold inland garden. Fleece helps with brief cold; a container under cover is more dependable during prolonged freezing.

Reshape after winter damage is clear: Trim lightly in spring once fresh growth starts. Remove dead tips rather than cutting deeply into uncertain wood in autumn. Maintain light around the foliage and avoid late feeding that forces soft shoots.

Check the gold-leaved back-right roots: For this Oak Lodge specimen Watch Pina Colada's pale foliage for scorch and dry roots before trying to restore colour with fertiliser.
Front Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Wait for new growth before removing frost damage and lightly trim only obvious imbalance.
Summer: Water deeply while establishing but allow the soil surface to breathe between waterings.
Autumn: Enjoy the strongest orange colour and prepare temporary protection for severe cold.
Winter: Use fleece during hard frost, keep cold wind off the foliage and do not trap moisture around the crown.
Front Bed 2.description: Coprosma repens ‘Pina Colada’ forms the bright back-right counterpart to ‘Inferno’, with thick wavy leaves that move from lime and golden yellow into orange-red as weather cools. Its compact glossy foliage gives year-round colour without relying on flowers. Like all H3 Coprosmas, however, it is only conditionally permanent here: sharp drainage, a sheltered aspect and protection during severe Bromsgrove frost decide whether it returns cleanly in spring.

profile.about: Coprosma repens is a New Zealand evergreen shrub with leathery mirror-bright leaves. ‘Pina Colada’ is selected for golden-lime foliage suffused with orange-red, particularly in cool weather. It is normally more at home in mild coastal gardens or containers, making its Front Bed 2 performance a useful microclimate record.

Front Bed 2.name: Coprosma ‘City Knights’ — label confirmed
Front Bed 2.position: Back-right edge — glossy burgundy foliage with red flashes
Front Bed 2.light: Sun or partial shade. Bright shelter supports the deepest red colour
Front Bed 2.water: Moderate; avoid saturation. Glossy evergreen foliage needs moisture in dry spells, with much less demand in cold weather.
Front Bed 2.care:
Plan for a cold-sensitive evergreen: Shelter from drying wind and protect during severe frost. These Coprosmas are marginal in a cold inland garden. Fleece helps with brief cold; a container under cover is more dependable during prolonged freezing.

Reshape after winter damage is clear: Trim lightly in spring once fresh growth starts. Remove dead tips rather than cutting deeply into uncertain wood in autumn. Maintain light around the foliage and avoid late feeding that forces soft shoots.

Check competition beside the hedge: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the newly planted City Knights root ball moist while the established hedge draws water from the surrounding ground.
Front Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Wait for live buds before removing winter-marked tips, then mulch lightly without burying the stem base.
Summer: Water deeply while establishing, check beneath the mulch and avoid rich feed that produces soft green growth.
Autumn: Stop feeding, let cooler weather deepen the colour and prepare temporary frost protection.
Winter: Use fleece during severe frost and cold wind, removing it in milder weather so the shrub does not remain damp.
Front Bed 2.description: Coprosma ‘City Knights’ adds the darkest foliage to Front Bed 2, with small mirror-bright leaves combining deep burgundy, red, near-black and occasional green flashes. It now sits against the hedge beside the two July Coprosmas, turning the back of the compact bed into a three-part foliage group. The label confirms the cultivar, while its long-term size and precise hardiness are less completely documented than ‘Inferno’ and ‘Pina Colada’; it should therefore share their cautious H3 winter routine until Oak Lodge experience proves otherwise.

Front Bed 2.name: Hebe ‘Kiwi’ — label confirmed
Front Bed 2.light: Sun or partial shade. Warm shelter with good airflow
Front Bed 2.water: During establishment and drought. Hebe roots require drainage; repeated soaking in cold weather encourages dieback.
Front Bed 2.care:
Trim Hebe lightly after flowering: Shorten spent shoots while leaving green leaves below each cut. Avoid cutting back into old bare wood. Remove winter-damaged shoots only when spring growth reveals living tissue.

Keep wind and wet away from the crown: Maintain shelter and free-draining soil. Watch variegated plants for all-green reversions and remove those at their origin. Do not feed late enough to produce frost-vulnerable autumn growth.

Retain the compact front-left outline: For this Oak Lodge specimen Trim Kiwi lightly after its purple spikes finish without cutting the small evergreen framework into bare wood.
Front Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Remove winter damage only after new growth shows, then apply a light organic mulch.
Summer: Deadhead faded spikes and trim only the green shoot tips needed to hold the compact shape.
Autumn: Stop feeding and keep fallen leaves from sealing the crown.
Winter: Protect from cold drying wind and ensure water drains away from the root collar.
Front Bed 2.description: Hebe ‘Kiwi’, sold in the Horopito range, makes a compact evergreen mound at the front-left of the bed. Glossy leaves and darker new growth provide structure before short purple flower spikes appear in summer and draw pollinating insects to the front path. Its precise commercial naming is less well documented than the two Coprosmas, so the retained label is recorded without inventing a breeder epithet.

Front Bed 2.name: Polemonium ‘Golden Feathers’ — label confirmed
Front Bed 2.position: Front-right — replacing Begonia Cocktail 'Gin' in July 2026
Front Bed 2.light: Sun or partial shade. Afternoon shade is useful in hot weather
Front Bed 2.water: Maintain cool, moist soil. Gold-edged Jacob's ladder scorches in hot dry ground; keep moisture available without stagnant roots.
Front Bed 2.care:
Remove finished flower stems: Cut the old stems back to the fern-like leaf mound. Retain healthy variegated foliage and remove solid-green reversions. Do not shear away the whole mound merely because flowering ends.

Renew a tired clump in cool weather: Divide in spring or autumn if its centre becomes congested. Replant healthy portions at their previous depth. Light shade and a moisture-retentive mulch help the pale leaf margins remain sound.

Protect the gold leaf margins: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep Golden Feathers' front-right root pocket moist and shade it from the hottest reflected afternoon sun.
Front Bed 2.seasonal:
Spring: Clear dead foliage, mulch the moist root zone and enjoy the main flower display.
Summer: Deadhead after flowering and cut tired foliage back if needed to encourage a fresh compact clump.
Autumn: Let the herbaceous top die back and mark the crown so it is not disturbed.
Winter: The dormant crown is fully hardy; avoid leaving it sealed beneath wet compacted mulch.
Front Bed 2.description: Polemonium ‘Golden Feathers’ replaces Begonia Cocktail ‘Gin’ at the front-right of Front Bed 2. Its fern-like leaves are divided into dark-green leaflets edged bright gold, followed by lilac-mauve bell flowers in spring and early summer. It is fully hardy, but the fine foliage performs best where the soil stays evenly moist and harsh afternoon sun cannot scorch the margins.

Front Bed 3.name: Cercis 'Eternal Flame'
Front Bed 3.position: Bedroom 3 end of Front Bed 3 — red circle in the September plan
Front Bed 3.light: Full sun. Good light supports the red, orange and yellow foliage sequence.
Front Bed 3.water: Deeply while establishing. Keep the young redbud root ball moist but aerated; shelter reduces leaf scorch and wind damage.
Front Bed 3.care:
Let the redbud build its framework: Remove only dead, damaged or crossing branches as needed. Avoid repeated heading-back of healthy branches. Check ties before they constrict the trunk, and protect the root collar from a bank of mulch.

Give the coloured leaves good light: Use sun with shelter from drying wind. Water below the canopy during dry establishment weather. Fresh foliage can scorch if roots dry while leaves are exposed; extra fertiliser does not solve that imbalance.

Allow a small tree's eventual spread: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the September redbud's root area clear while planning for a crown up to about four metres across.
Front Bed 3.seasonal:
Spring: Watch the bare stems for flower and leaf break, keep mulch clear of the trunk and remove only damaged wood because Cercis dislikes unnecessary pruning.
Summer: Water this establishing tree deeply during dry weeks, keep grass and weeds away from the root zone and avoid high-nitrogen feeding.
Autumn: Record the orange, red and purple colour progression, clear leaves from the trunk flare and stake ties before autumn gales.
Winter: Check the stake without tightening it against the bark and leave sound branches untouched; prune only dead wood in a suitable dry spell.
Front Bed 3.description: Eternal Flame is a deciduous redbud whose heart-shaped foliage combines fresh red leaves with older orange and yellow tones through the growing season. Mature branches can carry dark pink flowers in mid-spring before the leaves. The new Front Bed 3 tree needs sun, establishment moisture and space for an eventual crown about 2.5–4m high and wide.

Front Bed 3.name: Climbing Rose 'Super Fairy'
Front Bed 3.position: On the wall by the Bedroom 3 window
Front Bed 3.light: Full sun. South- or west-facing wall is ideal
Front Bed 3.water: Deeply when the wall-side soil dries. The long flowering canes depend on a well-mulched, moist but drained root area.
Front Bed 3.care:
Manage Super Fairy as a repeat rambler: Tie in flexible new canes and renew congested old wood selectively. Do not automatically apply a once-flowering rambler's complete post-bloom cut. Keep the framework that supports later flushes and clear growth from the window.

Remove finished flower clusters: Deadhead complete faded sprays when further flowering is wanted. Feed and mulch in spring. Check that ties allow the long canes to thicken and that dense leaf cover is not trapping persistent damp against the wall.

Keep Super Fairy off the window: For this Oak Lodge specimen Tie flexible flowering canes around the Bedroom 3 opening while retaining shoots for the repeat display.
Front Bed 3.seasonal:
Spring: Feed, mulch and fan new structural stems towards empty support.
Summer: Deadhead whole faded clusters, water the rain-shadowed roots and tie extensions before wind rubs them.
Autumn: Stop feeding, retain sound late flowers and check that long canes cannot strike the window or masonry.
Winter: Retain the main framework, remove dead or crossing canes and shorten flowering laterals according to rambling-rose guidance.
Front Bed 3.description: Super Fairy (‘Helsufair’) sends long arching stems across the wall by the Bedroom 3 window and flowers in generous clusters rather than isolated large blooms. The small fully double flowers open pale pink and repeat from summer into autumn, giving a softer, longer display than a once-flowering rambler. Its eventual 2.5–4m scale means the support should be treated as permanent infrastructure, with new stems placed deliberately before they harden.

profile.about: Super Fairy is the trade name for Rosa ‘Helsufair’, an AGM repeat-flowering rose classified by the RHS within the rambler group. Front Bed 3.name: Variegated Dogwood
Front Bed 3.position: Below the Bedroom 1 window — moved from Back Bed 2 in July 2026
Front Bed 3.light: Sun or partial shade. Good light strengthens variegation and stem colour
Front Bed 3.water: Moist while the moved shrub establishes. Check the transplanted root area during dry weather; mature dogwood tolerates wetter ground than many neighbouring shrubs.
Front Bed 3.care:
Renew colourful dogwood stems in spring: Once established, remove a proportion of the oldest dull stems low down. New stems provide the strongest red winter colour. Allow this relocated shrub to root well before a severe renovation cut.

Remove green reversions cleanly: Trace all-green branches to their origin before cutting. Retain the variegated canopy and give the broad shrub space. A light surface mulch conserves moisture without burying the stool.

Let the relocated dogwood root first: For this Oak Lodge specimen Avoid stooling the whole moved shrub before it establishes beneath the Bedroom 1 window.
Front Bed 3.seasonal:
Spring: For the first spring after moving, remove only dead wood; later take roughly one-third of the oldest stems at ground level.
Summer: Water deeply through dry spells while the new root system spreads and remove only intrusive suckers.
Autumn: Enjoy foliage colour and mark the oldest dull stems before leaves obscure the framework again.
Winter: Display the red stems and avoid cutting until late winter or early spring.
Front Bed 3.description: Cornus alba ‘Elegantissima’ combines cream-edged grey-green leaves with vivid red young stems, so its strongest season begins after the foliage falls. Moved from Back Bed 2 to the front wall bed in July 2026, it now needs establishment water before any ambitious stooling. Once rooted, removing a proportion of old dull stems each spring will keep the winter framework colourful without forcing a recently moved plant to rebuild everything at once.

Front Bed 3.name: Red Hot Poker ‘Royal Standard’ — assumed
Front Bed 3.position: Front of the wall bed — moved from Back Bed 1 in July 2026
Front Bed 3.light: Full sun. Open light is essential for strong flowering
Front Bed 3.water: Moist in summer, drained in winter. Kniphofia needs water for flowering but resents a cold saturated crown.
Front Bed 3.care:
Cut spent poker stalks at their base: Retain healthy strap-shaped leaves after flowering. Remove damaged old leaves in spring, taking care around emerging shoots. Do not cut the whole foliage fountain down every autumn.

Let the moved clump re-establish: Divide only when necessary in spring. Keep the centre free of wet debris and provide sun. Royal Standard remains an assumption, so photograph complete flower spikes before making cultivar-specific predictions.

Give the moved poker open sun: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the clump at the front of the wall bed from being shaded by the relocated dogwood.
Front Bed 3.seasonal:
Spring: Clear dead leaves carefully, feed lightly and divide only after the relocated clump is strongly established.
Summer: Water during drought in the first season and remove each finished spike at its base.
Autumn: Stop feeding and leave healthy leaves to replenish the crown.
Winter: Keep the crown clear of wet debris and avoid tying foliage into a moisture-trapping bundle.
Front Bed 3.description: This Kniphofia lifts dense orange-red poker spikes above a fountain of narrow strap leaves at the front of the wall bed. Individual tubular flowers open progressively along each spike, creating a long nectar source for bees. The move from Back Bed 1 gives it a sunnier open position, but cultivar-level care remains impossible until mature height, the yellow-to-red colour transition and flowering time are recorded.

profile.about: Kniphofia are African rhizomatous perennials with torch-like racemes of pendent tubular flowers. Garden breeding has produced cultivars from under 50cm to more than 2m, with different colour changes as florets age. Those traits, rather than the common orange-red colour alone, are needed to identify the Oak Lodge plant.

Front Bed 3.name: Leucothoe 'Little Flames'
Front Bed 3.position: Below the wall trellis — compact evergreen added July 2026
Front Bed 3.light: Sun or partial shade. Some shade protects moisture and leaf quality
Front Bed 3.water: Even moisture around shallow roots. Leucothoe dislikes both drying out and airless wet soil; rainwater suits its acidic root run.
Front Bed 3.care:
Preserve Little Flames' arching shoots: Remove damaged or misplaced stems after flowering. Avoid shearing the evergreen foliage into a hard outline. Allow the coloured young growth to develop above older leaves.

Mulch gently in acid soil: Use leaf mould or another lime-free organic mulch. Do not bury the crown or hoe through surface roots. Shelter from strong drying wind and intense sun if the leaves scorch.

Protect the low acidic root pocket: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep Little Flames beneath the trellis clear of alkaline rubble and dense competing roots.
Front Bed 3.seasonal:
Spring: Top-dress with leaf mould or composted bark and remove only damaged growth after flowering.
Summer: Use rainwater in drought and keep wall plants from taking moisture from its shallow roots.
Autumn: Allow cool weather to deepen foliage colour and refresh an airy acidic mulch if needed.
Winter: Leave the compact framework unpruned and clear heavy wet leaf litter from the crown.
Front Bed 3.description: Leucothoe ‘Little Flames’ is a low evergreen beneath the wall trellis, named for the vivid red young stems and leaves that rise like small flames above the older green foliage. White urn-shaped flowers hang in spring, but the coloured new growth is its main contribution. It prefers acidic humus-rich soil and steady moisture, making rainwater and a leaf-mould mulch more useful than routine general fertiliser.

Front Bed 4.water: During long dry spells. An established Photinia has a broad root system; soak its root area rather than sprinkling the trunk.
Front Bed 4.care:
Prune for red replacement growth: Make selective cuts in spring or early summer. Shortening shoots encourages another red flush but can reduce flowering. Avoid a heavy late-season trim that exposes tender new leaves to frost.

Open congested growth: Remove crowded branches and clear badly spotted fallen leaves. Improve airflow before treating leaf spots. Preserve the established canopy while preventing it from shading all the smaller Front Bed 4 plants.

Balance canopy and lower planting: For this Oak Lodge specimen Thin selected Photinia branches if they shade the new plants rather than repeatedly clipping the entire canopy.
Front Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Photograph the new flush and flowers, then make only light shaping cuts after the first colour display.
Summer: Water only through sustained drought and keep the new underplanting from competing directly at the stem bases.
Autumn: Leave sound growth to mature and clear diseased fallen foliage from beneath the canopy.
Winter: Avoid stimulating soft growth and inspect the branch framework for crossing stems or wall contact.
Front Bed 4.description: The established Photinia supplies a multi-stem evergreen canopy on Front Bed 4's return-wall side. Red Robin is the recorded assumption, consistent with red young growth but unproven without stronger identification evidence. Selective pruning can balance the colourful new foliage with the need for light beneath the canopy, rather than repeatedly shearing away its natural framework.

Front Bed 4.description: The Pilgrim (‘Auswalker’) is an English shrub rose being trained against the left side of the Front Bed 4 wall. Front Bed 4.description: The Generous Gardener (‘Ausdrawn’) occupies the right wall support with long climbing growth and glossy foliage. Front Bed 4.name: Physocarpus Cluster 1 (2 × Little Devil + 1 × Lady in Red)
Front Bed 4.position: Cluster 1 — two Little Devils with one Lady in Red moved from Cluster 3 in August 2026
Front Bed 4.light: Sun or partial shade. Brighter light produces stronger foliage colour
Front Bed 4.water: Water each crown while establishing. Three shrubs share each group; check around every root ball instead of assuming one wet spot serves them all.
Front Bed 4.care:
Keep three separate ninebark crowns: Thin crossing branches rather than clipping the group into one hedge. Remove selected oldest stems after flowering when renewal is needed. Regular hard cutting produces foliage at the expense of the flowers.

Watch the centre for mildew: Maintain light and airflow between Little Devil and Lady in Red. Do not force soft dense growth with heavy feed. Water the ground in drought and remove badly affected foliage when practical.

Retain two Little Devils and one Lady: For this Oak Lodge specimen Check the added Lady in Red's roots separately from the two established Little Devils in Cluster 1.
Front Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Mulch all three root zones and remove only dead or badly crossing stems while the group establishes.
Summer: Enjoy flowers, water each root ball through prolonged drought and make any light thinning immediately after bloom.
Autumn: Allow foliage to colour and fall naturally; keep all three bases free of dense debris.
Winter: View all three frameworks and remove a small number of oldest stems only once a shrub becomes congested.
Front Bed 4.description: Physocarpus Cluster 1 now combines its two retained Little Devil ninebarks with the Lady in Red moved from the removed Cluster 3. The compact burgundy Little Devils form the lower pair while Lady in Red adds a taller red-to-bronze layer and pink summer flowers. All three crowns should remain readable rather than being clipped into one mass.

Autumn: Stop feeding, clear heavy leaf litter and let the evergreen framework harden before frost.
Winter: Protect from drying wind and check soil before responding to temporary cold-weather leaf droop.

Front Bed 4.name: Nemesia ‘Lady Penelope’ — assumed
Front Bed 4.position: Location 7 — moved from the former Nemesia Pot in August 2026
Front Bed 4.light: Sun or light shade. Shelter from drying wind and intense afternoon heat
Front Bed 4.water: Even moisture without saturation. Fine Nemesia roots suffer if the root ball dries hard; some shade helps during intense heat.
Front Bed 4.care:
Trim Nemesia after a tired flower flush: Shorten spent shoots to healthy leafy growth. Keep the crown intact and maintain moisture for the new shoots. A pause in hot weather may recover as conditions cool; more feed alone will not restore heat-stressed bloom.

Plan frost protection separately from trimming: Treat these plants as tender unless protected over winter. Take healthy non-flowering cuttings if the cultivar is worth keeping. Avoid cold wet soil around the crown, whether in a pot or the front border.

Use the front-bed root conditions: For this Oak Lodge specimen Check Lady Penelope at Front Bed 4 location 7; the old pot-based watering instructions no longer describe its setting.
Front Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Harden off only after frost, pinch tips once and establish the root ball before heavy flowering.
Summer: Keep its dropper aimed at the moved root ball, feed lightly and trim a tired flush by about a third for fresh shoots.
Autumn: Enjoy the cool-weather repeat flowers and take cuttings before frost only if the plant is to be retained.
Winter: Keep rooted cuttings bright and frost-free or treat the outdoor plant as seasonal.
Front Bed 4.description: The pink-and-white Nemesia that was first recorded in Bed 1, then briefly occupied the blue pot, now grows at Front Bed 4 location 7 in place of Magic Carpet. Its rose-pink upper petals, white lower lip, pink side markings and yellow eye closely match ‘Lady Penelope’. Because no label survives and similar Nemesia hybrids overlap, the cultivar remains visibly qualified as an assumption rather than being presented as confirmed.

The new position should reduce ivy pressure but still needs steady establishment moisture.

Front Bed 4.light: Light dappled shade. Shelter from cold drying wind and harsh early sun
Front Bed 4.water: Keep the shallow root mat moist. Use rainwater where practical; flower-bud development suffers after prolonged summer drought.
Front Bed 4.care:
Keep acidic roots close to the surface: Mulch with leaf mould without covering the root collar. Avoid lime, deep hoeing and digging through the fine roots. Check soil pH and drainage before feeding a yellowing shrub.

Protect next year's flower buds: Shape sparingly just after flowering. If deadheading, remove the old truss without snapping the new shoots below it. Later pruning removes buds already forming for spring.

Front Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Top-dress with ericaceous material, renew an airy acidic mulch and remove spent trusses carefully without damaging new buds.
Summer: Use rainwater where practical and water deeply through dry spells, especially from late June while next year’s flower buds form.
Autumn: Keep fallen leaves from sealing the root zone and avoid late feeding that encourages soft growth.
Winter: Protect the evergreen foliage from drying wind and do not interpret temporary cold-weather leaf droop as drought without checking the soil.
Front Bed 4.description: Rhododendron ‘Libretto’ is a broad, compact evergreen hybrid planted in the sheltered brick corner of Front Bed 4. Large dark-purple funnel-shaped flowers carry an olive-yellow to green flare in late May and early June. It can reach around 1.5–1.75m after ten years, so the new shrub needs room to keep its naturally rounded framework without crowding the Physocarpus clusters.

profile.about: ‘Libretto’ was bred by Hans Hachmann in Germany from ‘Lee’s Best Purple’ and ‘Purple Splendour’. Front Bed 4.name: Festuca 'Elijah Blue' (3 plants)
Front Bed 4.position: Three blue-grey tufts along the front-left edge
Front Bed 4.light: Full sun. Strong light maintains the bluest foliage
Front Bed 4.water: Little extra water once rooted. Blue fescue keeps its best compact colour in lean, sunny, freely drained ground.
Front Bed 4.care:
Comb the blue tufts in spring: Remove dead blades gently and snip old flower stems. Avoid cutting through every living leaf as if mowing a lawn. Rich feeding and damp shade encourage loose green growth rather than a dense blue mound.

Renew a hollow centre by division: Lift a tired tuft in spring and retain healthy outer pieces. Space the replacements so air reaches each crown. Mark the three plants separately; a gap in one should not prompt disturbance of the other two.

Check each of the three blue tufts: For this Oak Lodge specimen Renew only a Festuca whose centre is failing and keep damp leaf litter out of the other crowns.
Front Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Comb dead leaves out by hand, trim only damaged tips and divide any clump with a dead centre.
Summer: Leave or remove the fine flower stems according to the desired texture; water only during establishment drought.
Autumn: Stop feeding and clear wet fallen leaves from between the tufts.
Winter: Retain the blue foliage and avoid cutting the whole evergreen clump to ground level.
Front Bed 4.description: Three Festuca glauca ‘Elijah Blue’ form compact cushions of intensely ice-blue, hair-fine leaves along the front-left edge. Narrow blue-green flower plumes rise in early summer and mature straw-gold, but the foliage is the main year-round feature. Rich or wet soil turns a dense blue tuft into a loose green one, while older clumps naturally open at the centre and are best renewed by division rather than hidden by shearing.

Front Bed 4.name: Pieris 'Polar Passion'
Front Bed 4.position: Moved from Front Bed 5 into the former Flaming Silver position in August 2026
Front Bed 4.light: Partial shade. Shelter from cold wind and strong early sun
Front Bed 4.water: Even root moisture. Shallow Pieris roots must not dry hard; use rainwater where available and allow excess to drain.
Front Bed 4.care:
Keep the root run acidic: Use acidic, humus-rich soil and a shallow leaf-mould mulch. Keep lime away and do not cultivate through the fine surface roots. Check soil pH if young leaves yellow between green veins.

Preserve next spring's flowers: Remove spent flower clusters carefully, with little routine pruning. Make any necessary shaping cuts after flowering. Protect new coloured shoots from drying winds and late frost; do not clip away developing buds later in the year.

Follow Polar Passion to Front Bed 4: For this Oak Lodge specimen Check its moved root ball in Flaming Silver's former position rather than its old Front Bed 5 location.
Front Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Mulch with ericaceous material, remove spent flowers gently and protect new growth from late frost.
Summer: Use rainwater in drought and avoid lime-rich feed or amendments.
Autumn: Allow flower buds to develop untouched and clear smothering fallen leaves.
Winter: Protect from cold drying wind and do not prune away the spring flower buds.
Front Bed 4.description: Pieris japonica Polar Passion (‘Ppobas’) is the labelled evergreen with cream-edged leaves, colourful young growth and hanging spring flower clusters. It needs acidic, humus-rich soil and steady moisture without waterlogging; harsh early sun can scorch growth already chilled by frost. Its slow rounded habit makes it a permanent middle layer rather than a plant to clip routinely.

Front Bed 4.name: Dahlia Dalina Maxi ‘Tampico’ — label confirmed
Front Bed 4.light: Full sun. Shelter flower stems from strong wind
Front Bed 4.water: Deeply during active flowering. Keep the tuber zone moist but aerated, with mulch clear of the main stems.
Front Bed 4.care:
Support and deadhead Tampico: Cut each fading bloom to the next strong pair of leaves. Support stems before heavy decorative flowers lean. Pinching is useful on young growth, but not a reason to remove the current late-season display.

Keep the tubers safe from frost and wet: After frost blackens foliage, choose lifting or suitable in-ground protection. In cold wet ground, lift and store sound labelled tubers cool and frost-free. Start them into growth in spring and plant out after frost risk.

Retain Tampico's own tuber label: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the red-and-white front-bed Dahlia separate from both dark-leaved Double Dreamy plants when lifting.
Front Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Start protected tubers or young plants under cover, planting outside only after frost risk has passed.
Summer: Water deeply in dry weather, deadhead to a lower side bud and add support if stems lean.
Autumn: Keep deadheading until frost, then label and lift the tuber for frost-free storage or apply a deep dry mulch in a mild sheltered spot.
Winter: Keep lifted tubers barely dry, frost-free and checked for rot or shrivelling.
Front Bed 4.description: Dahlia Dalina Maxi Tampico (‘Datretten’) brings red-and-white decorative flowers to the open front of Front Bed 4 from late summer until frost. Like other dahlias it grows from a tender tuber, needs fertile freely drained soil and continues flowering when spent heads are removed. The new plant should be checked for slug damage while it settles and protected from Bromsgrove winter cold.

Front Bed 4.name: Verbena ‘Margaret’s Memory’ — label confirmed
Front Bed 4.position: Sunny front edge beside Dahlia 'Tampico' — added August 2026
Front Bed 4.light: Full sun or partial shade. Best flowering in open light
Front Bed 4.water: Moderate, with reliable drainage. Flowering Verbena needs moisture in growth, but a persistently wet crown encourages decline.
Front Bed 4.care:
Trim finished Verbena flower clusters: Cut back to leafy branching growth before trails become bare. Give full light and air around the stems. Water the roots during drought; stressed plants are more prone to a powdery coating on the leaves.

Match winter care to the selection: Keep tender bedding forms frost-free if retaining them. Margaret's Memory has greater hardiness than tender pot Verbena, but still needs free winter drainage. Do not assume all plants sold as Verbena have the same lifespan.

Keep the sunny edge drained: For this Oak Lodge specimen Protect Margaret's Memory's low crown from winter wet beside Tampico rather than automatically replacing it as tender pot Verbena.
Front Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Remove winter-damaged growth only after fresh shoots show and protect new leaves from slugs.
Summer: Deadhead or lightly cut back a tired flush, watering while the new planting establishes.
Autumn: Take stem-tip cuttings as insurance and stop feeding as temperatures fall.
Winter: Keep wet leaves away from the crown and leave sound semi-evergreen growth in place.
Front Bed 4.description: Glandularia ‘Margaret’s Memory’, still widely sold as Verbena, makes a low spreading mound of finely divided dark-green foliage beneath lilac-pink flowers with a darker eye. It can flower from spring into late autumn and is unusually hardy for this style of Verbena, though free drainage and a sheltered crown remain important through winter.

Front Bed 4.name: Calluna Trio Mix (2 plants)
Front Bed 4.position: Former Delosperma pocket near the established canopy — two plants remain after one moved to a hanging basket in September 2026
Front Bed 4.light: Full sun. An open sunny position supports dense growth and flowering
Front Bed 4.water: Keep the shallow roots from drying. Calluna needs acidic, drained soil; small plugs in baskets can dry before the surrounding compost.
Front Bed 4.care:
Clip Calluna within green growth: In spring, remove last year's flowered tips lightly. Leave leafy shoots below every cut. Cutting into a bare woody centre is unlikely to regenerate a dense plant.

Retain an open, acidic planting pocket: Give the heather sun and keep larger neighbours from covering it. Use rainwater where practical. Avoid lime and rich manure; lightly maintain the soil rather than forcing soft growth with heavy feeding.

Maintain the two remaining plants: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the Front Bed 4 heathers open to sun after one plant from this group moved into a basket.
Front Bed 4.seasonal:

Cut yarrow after the first flower plates: Remove faded stems to low leafy growth. A second display is possible if the plant has enough moisture. Leave some late heads only where seed and winter structure are wanted.

Summer: Deadhead to side shoots for repeat flowers, or leave selected heads where their structure is wanted.

Front Bed 4.description: Achillea sends up broad, level flower plates made from dozens of tiny florets above aromatic, finely divided foliage. The Oak Lodge planting contains red, pink or yellow tones rather than one documented cultivar, flowering from June into September. Those flat heads create landing platforms for bees, hoverflies and other beneficial insects, while overly rich soil or shade produces the one thing yarrow does badly: lush stems that collapse.

Front Bed 4.name: Azalea japonica 'Lotte'
Front Bed 4.position: Location 16 — new position beside the existing Front Bed 4 planting, added August 2026
Front Bed 4.light: Partial or dappled shade. Shelter from strong wind and frost pockets
Front Bed 4.water: Keep the shallow root mat moist. Use rainwater where practical; flower-bud development suffers after prolonged summer drought.
Front Bed 4.care:
Keep acidic roots close to the surface: Mulch with leaf mould without covering the root collar. Avoid lime, deep hoeing and digging through the fine roots. Check soil pH and drainage before feeding a yellowing shrub.

Protect next year's flower buds: Shape sparingly just after flowering. If deadheading, remove the old truss without snapping the new shoots below it. Later pruning removes buds already forming for spring.

Keep location 16's root mat cool: For this Oak Lodge specimen Mulch around Lotte lightly without burying its new crown beneath surrounding shrub leaves.
Front Bed 4.seasonal:
Spring: Renew an airy leaf-mould mulch around Lotte, use rainwater when needed and snap off spent flowers without disturbing the new shoots below.
Summer: Keep the shallow roots cool in dry weather and avoid pruning after the next flower buds begin to form.
Autumn: Stop feeding Lotte, clear heavy leaves from its centre and leave the evergreen shoots to harden naturally.
Winter: Shield this Azalea from drying wind and check the root zone before reacting to temporary frost droop with more water.
Front Bed 4.description: Azalea japonica ‘Lotte’ creates the new location 16 in Front Bed 4. The International Rhododendron Register records ‘Lotte’ as a compact Satsuki evergreen azalea with glossy foliage and deep-pink flowers. It shares the shallow, acid-loving root behaviour of the other Rhododendrons in the bed, so its dedicated dropper should maintain even moisture without burying the crown or leaving the soil stagnant.

Front Bed 5.name: Mexican Orange Blossom
Front Bed 5.position: Mid boundary bed — lime-yellow foliage
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or partial shade. Sun strengthens yellow foliage; shelter limits scorch
Front Bed 5.water: Water new roots, then in drought. Choisya needs drainage through winter and shelter from drying cold winds.
Front Bed 5.care:
Shape Sundance after its spring flowers: Shorten only the shoots needed to keep the shrub in bounds. Retain a leafy framework and remove winter damage once new growth shows. A light trim may encourage later flowering; repeated shearing loses its natural mound.

Protect the golden leaves from scorch: Keep establishment moisture steady in hot weather. Some shelter from intense reflected sun helps pale foliage. Check soil and exposure before interpreting browned margins as a nutrient shortage.

Preserve the golden mid-bed mound: For this Oak Lodge specimen Shape Sundance after flowering without removing all the evergreen shelter it gives the lower boundary planting.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Feed only if growth is weak, mulch and wait until after flowering for any shaping.
Summer: Water a young shrub in drought and remove only badly placed extensions.
Autumn: Enjoy repeat flowers, then stop pruning so new growth can harden before frost.
Winter: Leave the evergreen framework intact and protect fresh shoots from severe cold wind if forecast.
Front Bed 5.description: Choisya ternata ‘Sundance’ forms a rounded mass of glossy three-part leaves in vivid yellow to lime green, brightest where the boundary bed receives sun. Clusters of starry white flowers release an orange-blossom fragrance in spring and may return in autumn. The shrub is drought resistant once established but H4 rather than invulnerable, so a sheltered site and restraint with late pruning help its yellow shoots mature before winter.

Front Bed 5.name: Shrub Rose (cultivar to confirm)
Front Bed 5.position: Boundary end of the bed — established shrub rose
Front Bed 5.light: Full sun. Light shade is tolerated but sun improves flowering and ripening hips
Front Bed 5.water: Deeply in sustained dry spells. Water established roses at soil level, especially beside a wall; avoid waterlogging.
Front Bed 5.care:
Prune an unknown rose conservatively: Remove dead, diseased and rubbing stems first. Record its height, repeat-flowering pattern and long-cane behaviour before choosing shrub, climbing or rambling pruning. Do not cut it down like a herbaceous perennial.

Keep rose foliage healthy: Feed and mulch in spring, leaving the stem base clear. Remove fallen diseased leaves and inspect new shoots for aphids. Deadhead if repeat flowers are wanted; retain selected hips where autumn fruit is part of the display.

Treat the boundary rose as observed: For this Oak Lodge specimen Retain the established shrub framework and hips; the old climber ID does not prove a rambling growth class.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Feed and mulch after rain, then wait for the flowering pattern before making more than a light structural prune.
Summer: Deadhead selected blooms if repeat flowering is wanted, but leave some spent flowers to develop hips and photograph the full bloom.
Autumn: Retain sound hips for colour and birds, and clear leaves badly affected by black spot.
Winter: Remove dead, damaged and crossing stems, thinning rather than shortening every shoot until the rose class is known.
Front Bed 5.description: The established rose at the boundary end is a freestanding shrub, not the wall climber previously recorded here. Its compound leaves, thorny stems and red-orange fruits securely identify Rosa; those fruits are rose hips, formed when pollinated flowers mature. Flower form, colour and repeat pattern have not yet been recorded clearly enough to assign a cultivar or rose class, so the profile deliberately keeps pruning conservative.

profile.about: Rose hips are the seed-bearing fruits of roses. They enlarge after the petals fall and commonly turn orange, red or dark purple as they ripen, supplying autumn colour and food for birds. Shrub roses include many species and hybrids with different flowering and pruning habits, so fruit alone cannot recover a cultivar.
profile.provenanceNote: Photographs securely show a shrub rose and rose hips. The earlier Kiftsgate assumption is withdrawn because the plant’s habit and current evidence do not support that very large rambler.

Front Bed 5.name: Bay Tree
Front Bed 5.position: Established standard in the boundary bed
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or partial shade. Warm shelter reduces leaf scorch
Front Bed 5.water: Water deeply in prolonged drought. The standard's evergreen crown loses moisture year-round; avoid a wet, buried trunk base.
Front Bed 5.care:
Maintain the bay standard: Trim the head in spring or summer and remove basal suckers. Keep the clear stem and check any support tie for constriction. Make small regular shaping cuts instead of exposing the whole framework at once.

Inspect folded leaves and sticky growth: Check for bay sucker and scale before treating. Remove affected leaves or small colonies where practical. Cold or waterlogged roots can also yellow foliage; diagnosis should come before feeding.

Maintain the standard's clear stem: For this Oak Lodge specimen Remove basal suckers and inspect the bay's head separately from the nearby shrub previously mistaken for another bay.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Remove frost-damaged tips only after new growth shows the living boundary.
Summer: Trim lightly with secateurs, remove basal suckers and water deeply only in sustained drought.
Autumn: Stop feeding and make sure mulch does not touch the trunk.
Winter: Protect the exposed head in severe cold or drying wind and avoid pruning during frost.
Front Bed 5.description: The established standard is bay, Laurus nobilis: leathery aromatic evergreen leaves held on a clipped head above a clear stem. It brings permanent height to Front Bed 5 and can supply culinary leaves when the plant is healthy and has not been sprayed. Bay tolerates clipping but responds best to selective late-spring or summer cuts, with the root zone kept drained and the crown protected from the harshest wind.

Front Bed 5.name: Japanese Skimmia
Front Bed 5.latin: Skimmia japonica (cultivar and sex to confirm)
Front Bed 5.position: Established evergreen shrub beneath the boundary planting
Front Bed 5.light: Partial shade to shade. Avoid hot afternoon sun and reflected heat
Front Bed 5.water: Avoid a dry root ball. Shade and reliable drainage matter; yellowing alone does not mean iron deficiency.
Front Bed 5.care:
Shade the Skimmia's roots: Keep moisture steady without standing water. Skimmias do not require ericaceous compost. Check exposure, dryness and drainage before trying to correct yellow leaves with iron or acidifying products.

Preserve flowers and possible berries: Prune only wayward or damaged shoots, usually in spring. Heavy clipping removes flower buds. Female forms generally need a nearby male to set fruit; two female plants do not supply that pollen.

Record sex from flowers, not leaves: For this Oak Lodge specimen Document the boundary Skimmia's flowers and fruit before using it as a pollination partner for the potted females.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Photograph flowers closely, mulch moist soil and prune only dead or awkward stems.
Summer: Keep the root zone cool and evenly moist during drought, especially where afternoon sun reaches the plant.
Autumn: Record any berries on the boundary Skimmia and clear heavy fallen leaves; investigate dryness or harsh exposure if its foliage yellows.
Winter: Leave the evergreen framework intact and clear heavy leaf litter from the crown.
Front Bed 5.description: This second evergreen was previously filed as another bay, but its broad clustered leaves and compact shrub habit identify Japanese skimmia instead. Skimmia japonica prefers cool partial shade and moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil. The cultivar and sex remain open: spring flowers and any autumn berries will show whether it is male, female or a self-fertile form and may narrow the name.

Front Bed 5.name: Hardy Fuchsia (cultivar to confirm)
Front Bed 5.position: Established flowering shrub in the boundary bed
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or partial shade. Shelter from cold drying wind
Front Bed 5.water: Moist while growing and flowering. Mulch the border root run and water during sustained dryness without saturating the crown.
Front Bed 5.care:
Leave the old framework through winter: Wait for spring buds before cutting back dead stems. A hardy Fuchsia may regrow from low down after frost. Do not discard a dormant crown solely because its upper branches look dead.

Allow a loose flowering shrub: Thin crowded shoots and remove spent flowers if needed. The border plant can become much larger than basket Fuchsia. Keep neighbouring stems from tangling through it and avoid hard trimming during its summer display.

Keep the border crown over winter: For this Oak Lodge specimen Wait for spring regrowth before deciding how much of this established Fuchsia's framework has died back.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Wait for live buds, then cut dead or frost-damaged stems back to healthy growth and mulch.
Summer: Water in dry spells, deadhead if fruit is not wanted and avoid high-nitrogen feeding.
Autumn: Allow late flowers to continue, then stop feeding and leave stems as winter protection.
Winter: Keep the crown mulched but airy and do not cut the framework down before the worst frost.
Front Bed 5.description: The established fuchsia has the small leaves, woody framework and pendant flowers of the hardy Fuchsia magellanica group. It flowers on the current season’s growth from summer into autumn and may keep some top growth in mild winters, while hard frost can cut it back to the protected base. The exact hybrid or cultivar cannot be recovered safely from these photographs alone.

Front Bed 5.name: Clematis (cultivar to confirm)
Front Bed 5.position: Twining through support at the boundary side
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or partial shade. Keep the root run cool and shaded
Front Bed 5.water: Moist roots through summer. Clematis viticella needs a deep, drained root run; wall-side soil can remain dry after rain.
Front Bed 5.care:
Use Group 3 pruning for viticella: In late winter, cut old stems to strong low buds, about 30cm above ground. It flowers on the new season's shoots. This is deliberately different from the spring-flowering montana on the Patio.

Guide the new climbing shoots: Provide slender supports that leaf stalks can grip. Spread shoots before they tangle into a single knot. Mulch around the roots, keeping the crown clear and moisture available as the canopy expands.

Cut the summer climber in late winter: For this Oak Lodge specimen Mark this viticella as Group 3 so its pruning is not confused with the Patio's spring montana.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Tie new shoots to support and mulch after cutting back and feeding.
Summer: Water in prolonged drought and guide stems away from the bay and fruit-tree crowns.
Autumn: Leave sound seed heads if wanted and clear diseased foliage after leaf fall.
Winter: In February, cut all stems to strong buds about 30–45cm above ground while the viticella fit remains supported.
Front Bed 5.description: This established climber is best recorded within the Clematis viticella group from its fine twining growth and summer-flowering habit. Viticella clematis flower on new shoots and are normally cut back hard in late winter, making them easier to renew through a busy mixed boundary than spring-flowering old-wood types. The species-group fit is useful for care, but flower photographs are still needed before a cultivar is named.

Front Bed 5.name: Hydrangea Bloody Marie — label confirmed
Front Bed 5.position: Former Honeysuckle position at the open drive-side edge — added August 2026
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or partial shade. Sun is suitable where the soil stays reliably moist
Front Bed 5.water: Keep soil moist in growth. Panicle Hydrangea needs more moisture than the dry-loving Euphorbia and Gaura nearby.
Front Bed 5.care:
Prune the panicle Hydrangea in spring: Shorten last year's shoots to healthy buds on a sound framework. H. paniculata flowers on new growth. Remove weak and crossing stems; avoid borrowing the old-wood pruning rule used for the Stone Bed's oakleaf Hydrangea.

Support colour with good conditions: Mulch, water in drought and leave room for the flower heads. The cream-to-pink ageing of panicles is not the acid/alkaline blue-pink response of mopheads. Do not add bluing products to change this cultivar's colour.

Keep the drive-side root run moist: For this Oak Lodge specimen Check Bloody Marie's new planting pocket where the Honeysuckle stood, especially as the panicles expand.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Mulch after rain and prune last year’s shoots to a healthy framework before active growth begins.
Summer: Water the full root area through dry spells and support any stem pulled down by heavy flower panicles.
Autumn: Leave sound flowerheads for structure if wanted and stop nitrogen-rich feeding.
Winter: Check wind rock and retain the woody framework until the early-spring pruning window.
Front Bed 5.description: Hydrangea paniculata Bloody Marie is the new drive-side shrub in the former Honeysuckle position. Its large cone-shaped panicles open cream, pass through soft pink and deepen toward red from July to September. Unlike a mophead hydrangea it flowers on the current season’s shoots, so any shaping belongs in late winter or early spring rather than after buds have expanded.

Front Bed 5.description: Euphorbia × martinii ‘Ascot Petite’ forms a compact evergreen mound in Polar Passion’s former position. The architectural display suits a dry, sunny pocket, but the milky sap is a strong skin and eye irritant, so all cutting and handling needs gloves and eye care.

Front Bed 5.name: Flaming Silver
Front Bed 5.position: Moved from Front Bed 4 into the sheltered middle of Front Bed 5 in August 2026
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or partial shade. Shelter red young growth from harsh frost
Front Bed 5.water: Even root moisture. Shallow Pieris roots must not dry hard; use rainwater where available and allow excess to drain.
Front Bed 5.care:
Keep the root run acidic: Use acidic, humus-rich soil and a shallow leaf-mould mulch. Keep lime away and do not cultivate through the fine surface roots. Check soil pH if young leaves yellow between green veins.

Preserve next spring's flowers: Remove spent flower clusters carefully, with little routine pruning. Make any necessary shaping cuts after flowering. Protect new coloured shoots from drying winds and late frost; do not clip away developing buds later in the year.

Check the moved silver-edged Pieris: For this Oak Lodge specimen Maintain acidic mulch and moisture around Flaming Silver in its sheltered Front Bed 5 position.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Use rainwater where practical, top-dress with ericaceous material and prune only damaged shoots after flowering.
Summer: Maintain even moisture through drought without leaving the root ball saturated.
Autumn: Let growth ripen and keep alkaline builders’ rubble or lime-rich mulch away from the roots.
Winter: Protect an early red flush from severe frost and clear water-trapping debris around the stem base.
Front Bed 5.description: Pieris japonica ‘Flaming Silver’ combines three foliage stages in one compact shrub: new growth opens bright red, matures green and retains a bold silvery-white margin. Branching clusters of creamy bell flowers appear in spring. This display depends on acidic soil and healthy fine roots; lime-rich rubble near the wall or repeated tap-water alkalinity can cause chlorosis long before the plant is visibly dry.

Front Bed 5.name: Astrantia trio
Front Bed 5.position: Three-plant group moved from Front Bed 4 to the wall-side pocket in Front Bed 5 in August 2026
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or light shade. Light shade helps where soil dries quickly
Front Bed 5.water: Consistently moist in growth. Astrantia needs more summer moisture than drought-loving border plants; avoid dry shade.
Front Bed 5.care:
Cut spent masterwort stems for a fresh flush: Remove tired flowers and marked foliage to the basal growth. Water the clump if the soil is dry after cutting. Leave selected seedheads only if self-sowing is wanted; seedlings will not reliably reproduce the named trio.

Retain the three named crowns: Divide in spring or autumn only when crowded. Keep Buckland, Claret and Star of Love labelled separately within the group. Do not merge their colours into a fictitious single cultivar.

Water the relocated wall-side group: For this Oak Lodge specimen Check all three Astrantia crowns for dryness rather than assuming the wall pocket stays cool and moist.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Mulch the moist root zone, mark each cultivar and support only if stems lean into neighbours.
Summer: Deadhead the first flush to encourage more flowers, leaving selected heads only after the final display.
Autumn: Cut down collapsed stems and divide only a cultivar that has become congested.
Winter: Keep labels in place while the deciduous crowns are invisible and avoid disturbing dormant roots.
Front Bed 5.description: Buckland, Claret and Star of Love form a three-cultivar Astrantia group in the wall-side pocket of Front Bed 5, following their August move from Front Bed 4. Papery bracts surround pin-cushion flowerheads in contrasting pink and claret shades above lobed leaves. Keep the three crowns labelled and their soil moist; they do not suit the dry treatment used for the former nearby Festuca setting.

Front Bed 5.name: Pittosporum 'Tom Thumb'
Front Bed 5.position: Compact dark-leaved evergreen in the July planting
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or partial shade. Warm shelter gives the best foliage and winter survival
Front Bed 5.water: Moderate until established. A mature drained clump tolerates dry spells; avoid wet roots during cold weather.
Front Bed 5.care:
Retain Tom Thumb's natural mound: Trim lightly in late spring if a shoot spoils the outline. Green young leaves normally darken to purple, so do not remove every green tip as a reversion. Avoid routine hard pruning into old wood.

Shelter the evergreen foliage: Protect from cold drying wind and prolonged hard frost. Keep the root collar exposed to air. Wait until spring growth starts before judging which frost-marked tips have actually died.

Let the fresh green leaves darken: For this Oak Lodge specimen Tom Thumb's lime new growth is normal; retain it unless a branch stays persistently unlike the purple mound.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Wait for new growth before removing frost damage, then mulch moist ground lightly.
Summer: Water while establishing and trim only shoots that genuinely spoil the rounded habit.
Autumn: Stop feeding so young growth hardens and clear wet leaf litter from the crown.
Winter: Shield from severe cold wind while keeping the root zone open and drained.
Front Bed 5.description: Pittosporum tenuifolium ‘Tom Thumb’ forms a dense rounded mound whose lime-green young leaves darken to rich purple. It is naturally compact and slow enough to need little routine pruning. The main risk is exposed winter cold: sharp drainage and shelter from drying wind matter more than feeding, while frost-damaged tips should be left until spring growth shows where living wood begins.

Front Bed 5.name: Gaura 'Gaudi Red'
Front Bed 5.position: Sunny open pocket in the July planting
Front Bed 5.light: Full sun. Warm shelter extends the flowering season
Front Bed 5.water: Moderate until rooted, then sparingly. Gaura tolerates summer dryness but can rot in persistently wet winter soil.
Front Bed 5.care:
Refresh Gaura's airy flowers lightly: Shorten exhausted stems to encourage a compact new flush. Avoid heavy nitrogen feed, which makes weak growth. Give the moving flower stems space instead of repeatedly clipping them into a dense mound.

Leave protective growth through winter: Cut old stems back in spring when new growth becomes visible. Keep the crown above wet debris and consider cuttings as insurance. Frequent division is less useful than sound drainage for this often short-lived perennial.

Keep the open pocket lean: For this Oak Lodge specimen Protect Gaudi Red from wet mulch and rich feeding so its compact airy stems remain firm.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Cut the old stems back only after the worst frosts and protect emerging crown growth from slugs.
Summer: Deadhead or lightly shear tired stems to encourage a fresh flush, watering only while establishing.
Autumn: Leave some sound stems for protection and stop feeding as growth slows.
Winter: Keep the crown open to air and divert runoff; do not cover it with wet mulch.
Front Bed 5.description: Gaura Gaudi Red (‘Florgaured’), now botanically placed in Oenothera, makes a compact airy clump of burgundy-green leaves and slender stems carrying deep pink-red flowers from summer into autumn. The moving flowers give lightness among evergreen shrubs, but the crown is short-lived where winter soil stays wet. Full sun, lean feeding and sharp drainage are more valuable than rich compost.

Front Bed 5.name: Heather 'Tib'
Front Bed 5.position: Front edge — pink-flowered heather added July 2026
Front Bed 5.light: Full sun. Open light keeps growth dense
Front Bed 5.water: Keep the shallow roots from drying. Calluna needs acidic, drained soil; small plugs in baskets can dry before the surrounding compost.
Front Bed 5.care:
Clip Calluna within green growth: In spring, remove last year's flowered tips lightly. Leave leafy shoots below every cut. Cutting into a bare woody centre is unlikely to regenerate a dense plant.

Retain an open, acidic planting pocket: Give the heather sun and keep larger neighbours from covering it. Use rainwater where practical. Avoid lime and rich manure; lightly maintain the soil rather than forcing soft growth with heavy feeding.

Keep Tib's double pink spikes labelled: For this Oak Lodge specimen Trim its own spent tips lightly in spring and avoid merging this dark-green mound with the golden heathers.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Clip off last year’s flowered tips without cutting below green leaves.
Summer: Use rainwater during establishment drought and let the double pink spikes develop fully.
Autumn: Leave late flowers for insects and clear smothering leaf litter from the mound.
Winter: Retain the evergreen structure and avoid pruning in hard frost.
Front Bed 5.description: Calluna vulgaris ‘Tib’ forms a compact dark-green mound carrying short spikes of double deep-pink flowers from summer into early autumn. The coloured calyces hold the display well, while the tiny scale-like leaves keep structure through winter. It is exceptionally hardy but not tolerant of alkaline soil, and the old flowered tips must be clipped lightly each year before the centre becomes woody and open.

Front Bed 5.name: Bell Heather ‘Providence’ — label confirmed
Front Bed 5.position: Front edge — matching plants to the left and right of the central planting
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or partial shade. Shelter from cold drying wind
Front Bed 5.water: Even moisture in acid soil. Daboecia needs a cool, humus-rich but drained root run, especially during summer bloom.
Front Bed 5.care:
Trim bell heather lightly in spring: Shorten last year's flowering tips without entering bare wood. Keep healthy evergreen leaves and remove dead shoots individually. This is not winter-flowering Erica carnea, despite the shared heather name.

Protect both shallow root balls: Mulch lightly with lime-free material and use rainwater where practical. Retain an open crown and space around the two plants. Deadhead selectively if a tidier extended summer display is wanted.

Check both bell-heather plants: For this Oak Lodge specimen Maintain moisture around the matching Providence root balls on either side of the central planting.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Remove only damaged stems and top-dress with an airy acidic mulch.
Summer: Use rainwater in drought and label each matching plant before neighbouring heathers merge.
Autumn: Trim faded stems lightly after flowering while green leaves remain below every cut.
Winter: Keep fallen leaves from sealing the mounds and protect from drying wind rather than wrapping them wet.
Front Bed 5.description: Two labelled Providence bell heathers carry larger nodding bells than their Calluna neighbours, adding a rose-red summer display above small evergreen leaves. Daboecia cantabrica is associated with western Ireland and Atlantic Europe; it should not be described as native throughout western Britain. Keep both shallow root balls in acidic, humus-rich, freely drained soil and retain the label without inventing a breeder code.

Front Bed 5.name: Ceratostigma
Front Bed 5.position: Low front planting — blue-flowered groundcover added July 2026
Front Bed 5.light: Full sun. Sun strengthens both flowers and autumn colour
Front Bed 5.water: Moderate while establishing. Once rooted, this groundcover tolerates some dryness; keep winter drainage open.
Front Bed 5.care:
Wait for late spring emergence: Mark the dormant patch before working around it. Ceratostigma often starts late. Do not dig out an apparently empty patch simply because earlier perennials are already growing.

Trim old stems and control the spread: Cut dead top growth in spring and remove wandering rooted pieces. Retain room for the blue flowers and red autumn leaves. Divide only to limit or renew the patch, not as an annual requirement.

Mark the late-emerging groundcover: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the Ceratostigma patch labelled through winter so spring work among the heathers does not disturb dormant roots.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Wait for new shoots, cut any frost-damaged old growth to ground level and mark the spreading boundary.
Summer: Water only through sustained drought and prevent vigorous shrubs from shading the low stems.
Autumn: Leave the peak blue-and-red display intact and photograph spread before foliage falls.
Winter: Protect the dormant location from accidental digging and keep wet debris from covering the crown.
Front Bed 5.description: Ceratostigma plumbaginoides spreads through the low front planting with wiry reddish stems and oval leaves that turn scarlet as its clear cobalt-blue flowers peak. That simultaneous blue-and-red display arrives from late summer into autumn, later than most of the boundary planting. The plant is dormant and easy to overlook in winter, so its spreading roots should be marked before spring work begins around the heathers.

Front Bed 5.name: Hypericum ‘Radiance’ — label confirmed
Front Bed 5.position: Mid-bed — compact St John's wort added July 2026
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or partial shade. More light generally improves flowering
Front Bed 5.water: Water during establishment. Once rooted, a drained Hypericum usually needs extra water mainly in drought.
Front Bed 5.care:
Shape Radiance in spring: Remove dead wood and shorten overlong stems to live buds. Retain the label-confirmed garden name. Trade names are reused, so a breeder code should not be attached without matching the original label.

Record foliage as well as flowers: Photograph the young leaves, summer flowers and any fruit. Keep good light around the shrub and do not treat berry production as guaranteed. These details help distinguish conflicting commercial descriptions of Radiance.

Retain Radiance without inventing a breeder code: For this Oak Lodge specimen Compare the original label with future foliage and fruit photographs before choosing among conflicting commercial Radiance descriptions.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Remove dead or weak stems lightly and photograph emerging leaf shape before pruning for size.
Summer: Record flower diameter, stamen length and the calyx; avoid deadheading every bloom so fruit can develop.
Autumn: Photograph ripe berries, calyx colour and mature height, then remove only damaged growth.
Winter: Leave the framework intact until identity and flowering wood are better understood.
Front Bed 5.description: The retained label names this compact Front Bed 5 Hypericum Radiance. The genus gives it yellow flowers with conspicuous stamens, but commercial Radiance descriptions and breeder names are not consistent enough to attach a more precise identity from the name alone. Record its new foliage and any fruit, keep the label-confirmed garden name and avoid promising an unverified berry colour or mature size.

Front Bed 5.name: Bluebell Creeper
Front Bed 5.position: Against the warm brick wall — blue-flowered climber added July 2026
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or partial shade. Warm south- or west-facing shelter
Front Bed 5.water: Moderate in growth. Billardiera needs a drained root run with less water in cold weather.
Front Bed 5.care:
Guide the fine twining shoots: Tie young growth to slender supports against the sheltered wall. Shorten tangled or overlong shoots lightly after flowering. This climber cannot cling directly to smooth masonry.

Protect the H3 framework: Plan shelter before prolonged frost reaches the wall. Take cuttings as insurance if desired. A warm wall reduces exposure but does not guarantee survival of this tender Australian climber in a severe winter.

Keep twining stems on the warm wall: For this Oak Lodge specimen Inspect Bluebell Creeper's fine supports and plan cold protection before the exposed tips are damaged.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Remove only frost-killed growth once new buds show and tie live stems onto fine support.
Summer: Water through drought, feed lightly and guide new twining shoots before they tangle into neighbours.
Autumn: Trim only for access after flowering and prepare dry mulch or fleece for forecast hard frost.
Winter: Protect roots and young stems from severe cold while keeping the crown drained and ventilated.
Front Bed 5.description: Billardiera heterophylla, still widely recognised by its former name Sollya, twines slender evergreen stems against the warm brick wall and carries nodding blue bells from summer into autumn. Pollinated flowers may develop narrow purple berries. Its H3 hardiness makes the wall essential rather than decorative: roots and young stems need shelter from severe Bromsgrove frost, while the support must be fine enough for twining stems to wrap around.

Front Bed 5.name: Hebe 'Rhubarb and Custard'
Front Bed 5.position: Mid-bed — variegated evergreen shrub added July 2026
Front Bed 5.light: Sun or partial shade. Warm shelter preserves foliage and flower quality
Front Bed 5.water: During establishment and drought. Hebe roots require drainage; repeated soaking in cold weather encourages dieback.
Front Bed 5.care:
Trim Hebe lightly after flowering: Shorten spent shoots while leaving green leaves below each cut. Avoid cutting back into old bare wood. Remove winter-damaged shoots only when spring growth reveals living tissue.

Keep wind and wet away from the crown: Maintain shelter and free-draining soil. Watch variegated plants for all-green reversions and remove those at their origin. Do not feed late enough to produce frost-vulnerable autumn growth.

Protect the pink-flushed evergreen: For this Oak Lodge specimen Rhubarb and Custard is rated H3; shelter its foliage and do not use a hardier Hebe's winter expectations.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Wait for new growth before removing winter-damaged tips and apply only a light mulch.
Summer: Deadhead purple spikes and trim green tips lightly to preserve the rounded shape.
Autumn: Stop feeding and let cool weather intensify the pink-red variegation.
Winter: Protect from severe frost and cold wind while ensuring the crown remains drained.
Front Bed 5.description: Rhubarb and Custard (‘Tull 302’) forms a rounded evergreen shrub with dark purple stems and small grey-green leaves edged irregularly in cream-yellow. Cold weather flushes those margins pink and rhubarb-red, while short purple flower spikes appear in mid- to late summer. The cultivar is drought resistant once rooted but only H3, so the boundary wall’s shelter and free winter drainage are central to keeping the variegated crown intact.

Front Bed 5.name: Salvia 'Salgoon Lake Blueberry'
Front Bed 5.position: Against the brick wall — upright blue salvia added July 2026
Front Bed 5.light: Full sun. Warm sheltered wall position
Front Bed 5.water: Moderate in summer; drier in winter. Salvia needs drainage at the crown and moisture for active flowering, without constant saturation.
Front Bed 5.care:
Deadhead above a fresh side shoot: Remove finished spikes to keep new flowers developing. Leave healthy leafy growth and give full sun. Avoid forcing soft stems with excessive nitrogen late in the season.

Protect Lake Blueberry as an H3 Salvia: Retain some old top growth and take cuttings if insurance is wanted. Use frost-free protection where practical; an exposed inland winter is a risk. Delay the main cut until spring growth reveals which stems survived.

Keep a protected Salvia backup: For this Oak Lodge specimen Take Lake Blueberry cuttings if retaining this H3 wall-side plant matters after a severe winter.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Wait until hard frost has passed, then cut old stems back to live buds and remove any dead crown sections.
Summer: Deadhead to branching nodes, water during drought and take healthy non-flowering cuttings.
Autumn: Keep late flowers for pollinators, stop feeding and leave top growth to shelter the crown.
Winter: Mulch lightly with dry material, protect in severe frost and keep insurance cuttings frost-free.
Front Bed 5.description: Salgoon Lake Blueberry (‘Tl1016’) builds an upright 40–60cm framework beside the warm wall, carrying rich blueberry-purple flowers from near-black calyces through summer and autumn. Aromatic leaves and long tubular blooms make it conspicuous to bees. Its H3 rating means the crown should enter winter dry and protected, with old top growth retained until spring and cuttings taken as inexpensive insurance against a severe Bromsgrove freeze.

Front Bed 5.name: Fern 'Jurassic Gold'
Front Bed 5.position: Location 13 — replaced the failed Little Devil in August 2026
Front Bed 5.light: Full shade. Cool sheltered conditions protect the bright fronds
Front Bed 5.water: Cool, evenly moist roots. Check the fern's root pocket despite the shared sprinkler; shade does not guarantee moist soil.
Front Bed 5.care:
Make room for the new croziers: Remove old damaged fronds before the fresh ones expand. Cut individual stems without damaging the tightly curled growth at the crown. Leave healthy fronds contributing to the plant.

Preserve the woodland root conditions: Top-dress with leaf mould and keep the crown clear. Protect the golden new foliage from scorching sun and drying wind. Ferns do not need flower feed, deadheading or a flowering-season calendar.

Check beyond the shared sprinkler: For this Oak Lodge specimen Feel Jurassic Gold's soil at location 13 because its shared irrigation with location 10 does not prove even coverage.
Front Bed 5.seasonal:
Spring: Clear only dead fronds before new croziers rise, then renew a light organic mulch around the crown.
Summer: Check the shared sprinkler reaches the fern’s original root ball and water deeply during prolonged dry shade.
Autumn: Let sound fronds feed the crown and remove only those that collapse or trap heavy debris.
Winter: Expect some frond loss, keep the crown drained and leave a light protective mulch clear of the growing point.
Front Bed 5.description: Jurassic Gold replaces the failed and binned Little Devil at Front Bed 5 location 13. Rose-tinted new croziers unfurl into luminous golden fronds before maturing greener, bringing light to the shaded wall planting without needing flowers. The fern keeps location 13’s existing shared sprinkler with location 10, but the soil should still be checked because its cool moist preference does not mean stagnant roots.

Front Stone Trough.name: Hosta ‘June’ — assumed
Front Stone Trough.light: Partial to full shade. Protect leaves from hot midday sun and wind
Front Stone Trough.water: Keep the root run cool and moist. Hosta's broad leaves lose water rapidly; check below mulch and avoid stagnant water around the crown.
Front Stone Trough.care:
Protect Hosta shoots as they emerge: Check for slugs and snails from the first pointed spring buds. Remove hiding places near the crown and inspect after damp nights. Damaged leaves do not repair; retain sound foliage to feed the roots.

Clear foliage after natural dieback: Let autumn leaves yellow before removing collapsed growth. Divide only when crowded, in spring or autumn, keeping healthy buds on each piece. Avoid burying the crown under dense winter mulch.

Check the stone trough's drainage: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the Hosta root ball moist in heat while ensuring winter rain can leave the heavy stone container.
Front Stone Trough.seasonal:
Spring: Top-dress, protect unfurling leaves from slugs and photograph each mature leaf surface.
Summer: Water deeply whenever the trough begins to dry and remove flower stalks only after recording their colour and height.
Autumn: Clear collapsed foliage and check that drainage holes remain open.
Winter: Move or shelter the trough from relentless rain without allowing the dormant root ball to desiccate.
Front Stone Trough.description: The stone trough contains a broad-leaved Hosta recorded as the assumed cultivar June, with pale centres and blue-green margins supporting that working match. It provides foliage from spring into autumn and may carry lavender summer flowers before dying back in winter. Container moisture and drainage are more useful immediate care priorities than an unverified cultivar-size prediction.

Front Box Hedge.position: Arching screen against the house return wall
Front Box Hedge.light: Sun or partial shade. More sun improves flowers and berries
Front Box Hedge.water: Little once rooted, except in drought. Water the wall-side root area deeply while establishing; avoid persistent wet.
Front Box Hedge.care:
Train the arching Cotoneaster gently: Keep outward-growing stems within the path clearance. Retain flowered shoots if berries are wanted. Do not impose a box-hedge clipping routine just because the old zone name contains Box Hedge.

Keep the working identity qualified: Record winter leaf retention and close views of flowers and fruit. Coral Beauty remains an assumption. Remove unwanted seedlings and contain runners; do not spread cuttings or garden waste into natural areas.

Retain the arching wall screen: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the assumed Coral Beauty off the path while preserving berrying stems and documenting its winter leaves.

Spring: Photograph flowers, leaf arrangement and both leaf surfaces before making any shaping cuts.
Summer: Tie useful shoots into support, remove outward or wall-rubbing growth and record fruit development.
Autumn: Photograph ripe berries and remove any unwanted seedlings within the garden.
Winter: Use the exposed herringbone framework and leaf persistence as identification evidence.

profile.about: Cotoneasters are woody shrubs rather than true climbers, but several species can be pinned to walls. Cotoneaster horizontalis is the most widely used and shows a distinctive herringbone branch pattern, white-pink flowers and red berries. Other wall species differ in evergreen foliage, leaf undersides and fruit clusters, so the Oak Lodge record remains at genus level.

Maintain the mixed display gently: Remove spent flowers, rotten leaves and broken stems individually. Avoid wholesale pruning, division or a heavy feed until the component plants are recorded. Photograph each plant with enough detail to separate the inventory.

Stairs Pots.name: Hedera helix 'Yellow Ripple' · Pot 1
Stairs Pots.position: P1 · white pot on the Steps
Stairs Pots.light: Sun or partial shade. Bright shelter supports variegation without baking the shared root ball.
Stairs Pots.water: Moderate container moisture. Young trailing ivy cannot draw on deep garden roots; allow drainage between watering.
Stairs Pots.care:
Trim ivy before it smothers its companions: Shorten long trails to a leafy joint. Remove solid-green reversions and stems rooting into other pots or masonry. Juvenile trailing ivy is grown for leaves and should not promise mature flowering or berries.

Retain the evergreen edge: Clear dead leaves and inspect stems for scale. Shelter the exposed root ball during severe frost. Refresh tired container compost in spring without burying the stems.

Keep White Pot 1's edge open: For this Oak Lodge specimen Trim Yellow Ripple trails away from the Skimmia stem base and the Fire Red pansy crowns.
Stairs Pots.seasonal:
Spring: Remove all-green reversions and shorten winter-damaged trails to a variegated node, keeping the Skimmia centre visible.
Summer: Guide the ivy around Pot 1's rim, check leaf undersides for scale and trim only strands that shade the pansies.
Autumn: Let the yellow-edged trails frame the autumn planting while lifting fallen leaves out from beneath them.
Winter: Use the evergreen trails as the pot's structure, shielding exposed roots from frost and avoiding wet compost around stem joints.
