Stairs Pots.name: Skimmia 'Double Diamond'
Stairs Pots.position: P1 · white pot on the Steps
Stairs Pots.light: Partial shade. Avoid reflected midday heat on the evergreen leaves.
Stairs Pots.water: Avoid a dry root ball. Shade and reliable drainage matter; yellowing alone does not mean iron deficiency.
Stairs Pots.care:
Shade the Skimmia's roots: Keep moisture steady without standing water. Skimmias do not require ericaceous compost. Check exposure, dryness and drainage before trying to correct yellow leaves with iron or acidifying products.

Preserve flowers and possible berries: Prune only wayward or damaged shoots, usually in spring. Heavy clipping removes flower buds. Female forms generally need a nearby male to set fruit; two female plants do not supply that pollen.

Retain Double Diamond's label: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the white-pot centre clear and record flowers before assuming its sex or berry colour from another Skimmia.
Stairs Pots.seasonal:
Spring: Remove damaged leaves one by one, top-dress around—not over—the stems and record flower buds to confirm how this labelled cultivar performs.
Summer: Shelter from harsh midday sun, water when the upper compost dries and keep Hedera trails from covering the Skimmia's centre.
Autumn: Let new flower buds form undisturbed, stop feeding and clear fallen pansy petals from the evergreen framework.
Winter: Raise Pot 1 on feet, shield the compact root ball from prolonged hard frost and water sparingly on mild mornings only.
Stairs Pots.description: Double Diamond provides the evergreen centre of White Pot 1 among Yellow Ripple ivy and Fire Red pansies. Its retained garden name is useful, but the profile should not borrow another Skimmia's flower sex, berry colour or exact mature size. Give the roots shade, even moisture and drainage, and record the spring flowers as this young pot planting establishes.

Stairs Pots.name: Pansy 'Fire Red' · Pot 1
Stairs Pots.position: P1 · white pot on the Steps
Stairs Pots.light: Sun or partial shade. Open light supports flowers; light shade helps during hot weather.
Stairs Pots.water: Moist, with free drainage. Small Viola and pansy roots dry quickly; cool, saturated compost can rot their crowns.
Stairs Pots.care:
Remove flowers and seed capsules: Pinch each spent stem back to a leaf joint. Clear rain-damaged blooms promptly to limit grey mould. A light feed during growth helps sustain flowers in a container.

Let cool weather set the pace: Expect pauses during hard frost or summer heat. Trim stretched stems to leafy growth if the crown is sound. Give light shade in hot weather and avoid burying small crowns under fallen leaves.

Clear blooms beneath the white-pot Skimmia: For this Oak Lodge specimen Deadhead the Fire Red pansies before damp petals collect around the shared evergreen stem base.
Stairs Pots.seasonal:
Spring: Cut leggy stems to a leafy joint and restart deadheading, taking care not to crowd the central Skimmia with new growth.
Summer: Expect a pause in hot weather; move Pot 1 out of afternoon scorch and retain healthy crowns for a cooler-season return.
Autumn: Deadhead the red display frequently, feed lightly after watering and remove petals that fall into the Skimmia.
Winter: Keep flowers off the wet compost, water early on frost-free days and remove any crown that turns soft rather than trimming only its leaves.

Stairs Pots.name: Pansy 'Fire Red' · Pot 2
Stairs Pots.position: P2 · blue pot on the Steps
Stairs Pots.light: Sun or partial shade. Open light supports flowers; light shade helps during hot weather.
Stairs Pots.water: Moist, with free drainage. Small Viola and pansy roots dry quickly; cool, saturated compost can rot their crowns.
Stairs Pots.care:
Remove flowers and seed capsules: Pinch each spent stem back to a leaf joint. Clear rain-damaged blooms promptly to limit grey mould. A light feed during growth helps sustain flowers in a container.

Let cool weather set the pace: Expect pauses during hard frost or summer heat. Trim stretched stems to leafy growth if the crown is sound. Give light shade in hot weather and avoid burying small crowns under fallen leaves.

Check blue-pot pansy crowns separately: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the Fire Red roots moist without leaving their crowns saturated while watering for Gaultheria.
Stairs Pots.seasonal:
Spring: Trim stretched growth back to healthy leaves and resume deadheading without exposing the Gaultheria roots.
Summer: Give Pot 2 cool morning light during heat and keep seed capsules removed while the plants wait for autumn conditions.
Autumn: Maintain the red flowers by deadheading at the stem base and brushing fallen petals out of the Gaultheria foliage.
Winter: Protect compact crowns from repeated freeze-thaw, keep airflow around them and water only after checking beneath the ivy canopy.

Front Strawberry Tree.name: Arbutus unedo
Front Strawberry Tree.position: By the skinny brick wall, at the purple-circle position in the September plan
Front Strawberry Tree.light: Full sun; sheltered. Protect the young evergreen from cold drying winds.
Front Strawberry Tree.water: Deeply while establishing. Strawberry tree needs drained soil; a young root ball can dry even when surrounding ground looks damp.
Front Strawberry Tree.care:
Give the strawberry tree long-term space: Allow for a broad evergreen crown rather than repeatedly clipping it small. Typical mature height and spread are each 4–8m. Review clearance from the narrow wall and nearby route as the tree grows.

Prune Arbutus as little as possible: Remove only damaged or badly placed growth when needed. Shelter the young plant from cold drying wind. Flowers and last year's ripening fruit can share the autumn canopy; pruning removes both potential displays.

Allow for the evergreen tree's width: For this Oak Lodge specimen Review future clearance beside the narrow brick wall as Arbutus grows beyond its September planting size.
Front Strawberry Tree.seasonal:
Spring: Look for fresh evergreen shoots, renew a modest mulch clear of the trunk and avoid pruning except to remove frost-damaged tips.
Summer: Water deeply through dry spells during establishment and leave the glossy canopy uncut so the tree develops its natural framework.
Autumn: Expect flowers and ripening strawberry-like fruit together; clear fallen fruit from paving and keep checking the young tree's ties.
Winter: Protect the root area during severe cold, shelter the canopy from cutting wind where practical and postpone shaping until active growth returns.
Front Strawberry Tree.description: Arbutus unedo is an evergreen strawberry tree with leathery leaves, reddish peeling bark and small pale urn-shaped autumn flowers. Rounded fruit from the previous year's flowers can ripen on the same canopy. Planted beside the narrow front-garden wall in September, it needs sun, drainage and long-term space: a mature tree can reach 4–8m in both height and spread.

Front Fruit Trees.latin: Malus domestica ‘Bramley’s Seedling’ · rootstock MM106 assumed
Front Fruit Trees.position: Bottom of the drive, by the boundary wall

Front Fruit Trees.water: Deeply in dry spells during fruit swell. Mulch the root area while keeping the trunk clear; shallow frequent splashes do not reach tree roots.
Front Fruit Trees.care:
Prune according to the apple's training: Free-standing trees are normally pruned while dormant; trained forms need their own summer routine. Retain fruiting spurs and remove dead or crossing wood gradually. Do not select a pruning system from the assumed rootstock alone.

Record fruit before relying on a cultivar: Thin crowded fruitlets and pick when fruit releases readily with a gentle lift. Log flavour, skin, picking date and storage. Cox or Bramley and MM106 are working assumptions; pollination and final tree size remain unconfirmed.

Document the drive-side apples: For this Oak Lodge specimen Record the fruit before planning around Bramley's triploid pollination needs; the Bramley and MM106 names are still assumptions.

Front Fruit Trees.name: Damson Tree
Front Fruit Trees.latin: Prunus domestica subsp. insititia (cultivar to confirm)
Front Fruit Trees.position: Beside the apple tree at the bottom of the drive
Front Fruit Trees.light: Full sun. Shelter helps blossom escape frost and fruit ripen
Front Fruit Trees.water: In dry spells while fruit swells. Keep the root area moist without waterlogging; mulch clear of the graft and trunk.
Front Fruit Trees.care:
Prune damson in dry summer weather: Remove dead, damaged and congested wood sparingly. Avoid copying the apple's winter pruning routine. Summer cuts reduce the risk of silver leaf and bacterial canker in Prunus.

Harvest by fruit readiness: Pick when fruits have developed their dark colour and soften slightly. Remove damaged windfalls and inspect branches carrying heavy crops. The cultivar and rootstock remain unknown, so record this tree's own timing.

Separate it from the apple's pruning job: For this Oak Lodge specimen Mark the adjacent damson for dry-summer pruning so a winter apple tidy does not accidentally include it.
Front Fruit Trees.seasonal:
Spring: Protect blossom from avoidable disturbance, mulch moist soil and watch fruit set after frost.
Summer: Water in sustained drought, harvest by colour and softness, and make any necessary pruning only in dry weather.
Autumn: Clear split or mummified fruit and record flavour, stone cling and harvest date.
Winter: Do not routine-prune; inspect for canker, silvered leaves and storm damage.
Front Fruit Trees.description: The second tree in the renamed Fruit Trees strip is a damson, Prunus domestica subsp. insititia. White spring blossom is followed by small oval blue-black fruit with a rich sharp flavour suited to cooking and preserves. The cultivar and rootstock are unknown. Unlike the neighbouring apple, established damsons should be pruned in dry summer weather rather than winter, reducing the risk of silver leaf and bacterial canker.

Front Gate Tree.name: Weeping Crab Apple (cultivar to confirm)
Front Gate Tree.latin: Malus (weeping cultivar; 'Red Jade' is a best-fit possibility)
Front Gate Tree.position: Beside the gateway, at the location marked on the July plan
Front Gate Tree.light: Full sun. Open light supports blossom, fruit colour and airflow
Front Gate Tree.water: During establishment and prolonged drought. Water below the canopy and maintain mulch without covering the graft or trunk.
Front Gate Tree.care:
Preserve the weeping grafted crown: Remove rootstock suckers and upright shoots arising below the graft. Shorten only branches obstructing the gateway. Retain well-placed pendulous growth rather than cutting the tree into an umbrella with a flat lower edge.

Record blossom and ripe fruit: Use spring flower and autumn fruit photographs to test the proposed identity. Red Jade is only a possibility. Retain some sound crab apples for the garden display and birds rather than treating them as a dessert-apple harvest.

Maintain gateway clearance selectively: For this Oak Lodge specimen Shorten only obstructive pendulous branches and retain blossom and ripe-fruit evidence before confirming Red Jade.
Front Gate Tree.seasonal:
Spring: Photograph flower buds, open flowers and leaf emergence; mulch after rain without touching the trunk.
Summer: Water in sustained drought, remove suckers below the graft and preserve the natural pendulous framework.
Autumn: Record ripe fruit colour, size, persistence and bird use; clear badly diseased fallen leaves.
Winter: Remove dead, diseased and crossing wood conservatively, avoiding cuts that flatten the weeping outline.
Front Gate Tree.description: The newly mapped Gate Tree has a compact crown of strongly pendulous branches carrying small developing apples. The additional July fruit and habit photographs put Malus at very high confidence and a weeping crab apple at high confidence. ‘Red Jade’ remains only a possible cultivar because its white spring blossom, ripe red fruit and any surviving label have not yet been recorded. Care therefore follows a small crab apple rather than one cultivar.

House · Hallway · Kentia Palm.name: Kentia Palm — assumed
House · Hallway · Kentia Palm.position: Ground-floor hallway, beside the main staircase
House · Hallway · Kentia Palm.light: Bright indirect. Tolerates lower light but protect the fronds from strong direct sun
House · Hallway · Kentia Palm.water: Free draining. Draining nursery pot inside a cachepot; empty every drop of runoff
House · Hallway · Kentia Palm.care:
Keep the light bright but filtered: The hallway position is suitable while the leaves receive good indirect light. Kentia palms tolerate lower light better than many palms, but growth becomes slower and watering intervals lengthen. Protect the foliage from strong direct sunlight through glass, which can bleach or scorch the broad leaflets.

Check compost before every drink: Water when the upper few centimetres have dried, not because a date has arrived. Water the inner nursery pot thoroughly, let it finish draining, then empty the white cachepot. Never allow the root ball to stand in runoff; permanently wet compost is a greater risk than slight surface dryness.

Protect the fronds from dry-room stress: Keep it away from radiators, cold draughts and repeated brushing at the stair turn. Moderate humidity and stable warmth support clean new growth. Wipe dust gently from both sides of the leaflets and inspect the undersides for spider mites, scale or mealybugs rather than routinely misting a plant that is already wet.

Feed and repot conservatively: Monthly feed in active growth is enough; do not disturb a healthy root ball without evidence. Use a balanced liquid houseplant feed at label strength from spring into early autumn. Repot in spring only when roots are densely congested, moving up by one modest pot size and preserving free drainage.
House · Hallway · Kentia Palm.seasonal:
Spring: Increase moisture checks as daylight and new growth return; begin monthly balanced feed and inspect whether the root ball is genuinely congested.
Summer: Maintain bright filtered light, check compost about weekly and empty the cachepot after every watering; watch for mites during hot, dry spells.
Autumn: Stop routine feeding as growth slows, keep the plant away from colder draughts and lengthen the interval between moisture checks.
Winter: Water sparingly after checking below the surface, maximise indirect daylight and protect the fronds from radiators and sudden cold.
House · Hallway · Kentia Palm.description: This grouped palm makes a dark-green architectural landmark beside the ground-floor staircase. Its broad, leathery leaflets hang in loose arcs from relatively open fronds, strongly favouring Kentia palm over the finer, narrow-leafleted Parlour palm. Several separate Kentia seedlings are commonly planted together for a fuller indoor specimen, which explains the multiple stems in one pot.

profile.about: Howea forsteriana is a solitary-trunked palm native to Lord Howe Island. Indoor nursery pots often contain several seedlings to create a fuller plant, but the palm does not naturally sucker. Mature fronds are pinnate, dark green and arching, with leaflets that bend downward. Parlour palm, Chamaedorea elegans, is a smaller, finer-textured palm with narrow linear leaflets and slender green stems.
profile.provenanceNote: The broad drooping leaflets, open frond structure and grouped nursery planting support Kentia palm at high confidence. No label has been retained, so the public name remains visibly qualified as assumed.

House · Kitchen / Dining · ‘Gioia’ Fern.name: Bird’s Nest Fern ‘Gioia’
House · Kitchen / Dining · ‘Gioia’ Fern.position: Ground-floor kitchen / dining room, at the window marked in September 2026
House · Kitchen / Dining · ‘Gioia’ Fern.light: Bright indirect. Direct sun can scorch the fronds; lower light slows growth
House · Kitchen / Dining · ‘Gioia’ Fern.water: Evenly moist. Allow only the surface to begin drying; never leave the pot saturated
House · Kitchen / Dining · ‘Gioia’ Fern.care:
Hold the light just off direct sun: The window position should stay bright but filtered. Direct sun through glass can burn the glossy fronds. Move it back from the pane or use a sheer barrier if strong sun reaches the leaves.

Water around the edge: Keep compost gently moist, never sodden. Test the upper few centimetres, then water the growing medium around the pot edge. Do not pour water into the nest-like centre, where it can sit and encourage crown rot.

Make humidity more consistent: Dry heated air is more damaging than ordinary still air. Keep it away from radiator flow. A pebble tray or grouping plants nearby can raise local humidity without making the crown wet.

Feed gently in growth: A weak monthly feed from late spring to summer is sufficient. Use a half-strength general liquid feed only while the fern is actively producing healthy fronds, then stop as light levels fall.
House · Kitchen / Dining · ‘Gioia’ Fern.seasonal:
Spring: Increase moisture checks with stronger light; feed lightly only while healthy new fronds are forming.
Summer: Keep light filtered, maintain humidity and check the growing medium regularly without leaving it waterlogged.
Autumn: Stop routine feeding as growth slows and keep the plant clear of cool draughts.
Winter: Use the brightest gentle light available, water less often after checking below the surface and protect foliage from radiator heat.

It moved from the sitting-room window to the kitchen / dining window in September 2026.

House · Hallway · Staghorn Fern.name: Staghorn Fern
House · Hallway · Staghorn Fern.position: Ground-floor hallway, by the porch and radiator
House · Hallway · Staghorn Fern.light: Bright indirect. Strong direct sun can scorch the fronds
House · Hallway · Staghorn Fern.water: Moist, free-draining. Water the growing medium only when it is beginning to dry; drain excess completely
House · Hallway · Staghorn Fern.care:
Give it a bright, sheltered position: Keep the fern in strong indirect light, away from harsh glass sun. The hallway location should also be checked for cold door draughts and radiator heat; either extreme dries and marks the antler fronds.

Water the medium, then let it drain: Moisture should be regular but never stagnant. Check the medium rather than watering by routine. Water thoroughly when it has begun to dry, then ensure there is no standing water beneath the plant.

Respect the brown shield fronds: They are a working part of the plant, not a failure. Do not peel away or cut the dry-looking brown basal shields. They help catch moisture and organic matter around the root area.

Feed only while actively growing: Use a weak houseplant feed in spring and summer. Apply at label dilution to moist growing medium and stop routine feeding as light and growth decline in autumn.
House · Hallway · Staghorn Fern.seasonal:
Spring: Resume dilute feeding as fresh shield or antler fronds appear, keeping all liquid out of the fuzzy growing point.
Summer: Maintain bright filtered hallway light, soak the mounting medium or root ball when nearly dry and let it drain completely.
Autumn: Stop routine feeding, dust antler fronds gently without wiping off their protective fuzz and keep away from cool door draughts.
Winter: Use the brightest indirect light available, lengthen the interval between waterings and never remove a brown papery shield frond merely for appearance.

profile.about: Platycerium bifurcatum is a staghorn fern from tropical and subtropical forests of Australia and Southeast Asia. House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Spid.name: Spider Plant ‘Vittatum’ — assumed
House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Spid.position: Dominant arching plant in Nicola’s shared three-plant pot, beside the sitting-room window

House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Spid.care:
Keep the window light filtered: Bright indirect light maintains clean variegation. The sitting-room window is useful light, but move the planter back or filter the glass if strong direct sun begins bleaching or scorching the leaves.

Water the shared root ball, then drain: Use the compost, not a calendar, to decide. Test below the surface in several places because the large clump can hide dry pockets. Water thoroughly only when the surface is beginning to dry and never leave runoff in the outer container.

Choose which plantlets to keep: The long runners are healthy propagation growth. Root wanted plantlets in small pots while still attached, then cut the connecting stem. Remove spent flowering stems only when no more plantlets are wanted.

Review crowding in spring: Three vigorous species are sharing one root space. If water runs straight through, the centre stays dry or growth weakens, slide out the root ball in spring and decide whether to divide the Spider Plant or separate the three species.

Autumn: Remove spent plantlet stems and stop feeding as growth slows, noting whether its vigorous roots are making separation necessary.

House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Parl.name: Parlour Palm — assumed
House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Parl.position: Upright palm rising through Nicola’s shared three-plant pot, beside the sitting-room window
House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Parl.light: Indirect or light shade. Forest-understorey foliage scorches in strong direct sun
House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Parl.water: Moderate. Moist but free-draining in growth; less water in winter
House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Parl.care:
Shelter the fine fronds from sun: Bright indirect light or light shade suits this understorey palm. Direct summer sun through the sitting-room glass can scorch or bleach the leaflets. Rotate the shared planter periodically for balanced light.

Avoid permanent wetness: The palm likes regular moisture with air around its roots. Check the shared root ball before watering, soak evenly when it has begun to dry and empty all runoff. Reduce the frequency as winter growth slows.

Keep old fronds until fully brown: Remove only finished growth at the base. Do not cut green leaflet tips into a tidy shape. Remove a frond cleanly at its base only after it has become fully brown.

Feed and repot gently: Slow growth needs modest feeding and infrequent disturbance. Apply a balanced liquid feed monthly during spring and summer. Review the whole mixed root ball in spring if crowding or uneven drying becomes a problem.
House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Parl.seasonal:
Spring: Watch for a new palm spear before beginning weak feed, and inspect the shared planter for crowding around the Palm's fine roots.
Summer: Keep the fronds in bright filtered light, rotate the shared pot for even growth and check for spider mite in dry weather.
Autumn: Stop feeding, remove only fully brown fronds at the base and protect the delicate leaflets from cold window draughts.
Winter: Maintain steady room temperature and modest humidity, watering only after the shared compost has partly dried below the surface.

House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Arro.position: Smaller arrow-leaved vine woven through Nicola’s shared three-plant pot, beside the sitting-room window
House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Arro.light: Bright indirect. Green forms tolerate partial shade; strong direct sun can scorch
House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Arro.water: Lightly moist. Water freely in active growth, more sparingly in winter, always with drainage
House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Arro.care:
Keep it bright without harsh sun: Filtered window light maintains compact leafy growth. The larger Spider Plant may shade it heavily, so watch new growth for stretching while also preventing direct sun through the glass.

Balance moisture across the shared pot: This vine prefers slightly steadier moisture than its companions. Test the compost around the vine as well as at the pot edge. Water the whole container when needed, drain fully and reduce watering in winter.

Guide or shorten long stems: Arrowhead Vine naturally becomes a climber. Add a small support or trim leggy stems in spring. Wear gloves, keep sap away from eyes and wash tools and hands after pruning.

Keep away from pets and children: Every part should be treated as harmful if chewed. Place the shared planter and any cuttings out of reach. Seek veterinary or medical advice promptly after suspected ingestion or significant sap exposure.
House · Sitting Room · Shared Pot · Arro.seasonal:
Spring: Pinch the Arrowhead Vine above a node to encourage a compact shoot and begin light feeding only when new arrow-shaped leaves open.
Summer: Guide or trim the fastest vine so it does not climb through the Palm, and check undersides of tender leaves for pests.
Autumn: Stop feeding, remove yellow leaves at their petioles and decide whether the increasingly vining habit still suits the shared planter.
Winter: Give the Arrowhead Vine bright indirect light, protect it from cold glass and allow the upper shared compost to dry slightly between checks.

Skimmia Pot.name: Skimmia 'Cleopatra'
Skimmia Pot.position: Evergreen centrepiece in the renamed Skimmia Pot — added August 2026
Skimmia Pot.light: Partial or full shade. Shelter from strong sun and drying wind
Skimmia Pot.water: Avoid a dry root ball. Shade and reliable drainage matter; yellowing alone does not mean iron deficiency.
Skimmia Pot.care:
Shade the Skimmia's roots: Keep moisture steady without standing water. Skimmias do not require ericaceous compost. Check exposure, dryness and drainage before trying to correct yellow leaves with iron or acidifying products.

Preserve flowers and possible berries: Prune only wayward or damaged shoots, usually in spring. Heavy clipping removes flower buds. Female forms generally need a nearby male to set fruit; two female plants do not supply that pollen.

Check pollination before expecting berries: For this Oak Lodge specimen Cleopatra shares the pot with Antarctica; do not assume the second Skimmia supplies compatible male flowers.
Skimmia Pot.seasonal:
Spring: Use rainwater where practical, feed with an ericaceous product after flowering and leave pollinated flower clusters intact for berries.
Summer: Keep evenly moist in warm weather, checking beneath the ivy before watering.
Autumn: Stop feeding, enjoy any developing berries and clear fallen debris from the crown.
Winter: Keep drainage open and protect the decorative container during prolonged hard frost.

This female selection can carry red berries when compatible pollen is available; sharing a pot with another female does not provide it. Shade, an evenly moist root ball and drainage matter more than acidity: Skimmias do not require ericaceous compost.

Skimmia Pot.name: Skimmia 'Antarctica'
photos: images/September Hanging Baskets & Pots/Skimmia Pot - Update 1.jpeg
Skimmia Pot.position: Second evergreen Skimmia in the pot — added September 2026
Skimmia Pot.light: Partial shade. Sheltered shade reduces yellowing caused by hot dry exposure.
Skimmia Pot.water: Avoid a dry root ball. Shade and reliable drainage matter; yellowing alone does not mean iron deficiency.
Skimmia Pot.care:
Shade the Skimmia's roots: Keep moisture steady without standing water. Skimmias do not require ericaceous compost. Check exposure, dryness and drainage before trying to correct yellow leaves with iron or acidifying products.

Preserve flowers and possible berries: Prune only wayward or damaged shoots, usually in spring. Heavy clipping removes flower buds. Female forms generally need a nearby male to set fruit; two female plants do not supply that pollen.

Record Antarctica's flowers and fruit: For this Oak Lodge specimen Retain its separate label and observe the berry colour rather than copying Cleopatra's red-fruit description.
Skimmia Pot.seasonal:
Spring: Enjoy the fragrant flower clusters, remove frost-burned leaves individually and top-dress with fresh peat-free compost without covering the stem bases.
Summer: Keep this evergreen pot evenly moist in hot weather and sheltered from harsh midday sun; do not shear off the developing berry clusters.
Autumn: Check whether berries are setting, clear fallen leaves from the pot and stop feeding so the new wood ripens.
Winter: Move the pot out of drying wind, raise it on feet and water only on frost-free days when the compost below the surface is genuinely dry.
Skimmia Pot.description: Antarctica is the second labelled Skimmia in the blue pot, sharing its root space with Cleopatra and three Rocky Purple Picotee Violas. Its compact evergreen framework gives year-round structure, while the spring flowers and any later fruit should be recorded separately from Cleopatra. Protect the root ball from drying and avoid assuming that pale foliage needs acidifying treatment.

Skimmia Pot.name: Viola 'Rocky Purple Picotee' (3 plants)
Skimmia Pot.position: Three plants around the Skimmias — added September 2026
Skimmia Pot.light: Sun to partial shade. Keep the low flowers open to light beneath the two Skimmias.
Skimmia Pot.water: Moist, with free drainage. Small Viola and pansy roots dry quickly; cool, saturated compost can rot their crowns.
Skimmia Pot.care:
Remove flowers and seed capsules: Pinch each spent stem back to a leaf joint. Clear rain-damaged blooms promptly to limit grey mould. A light feed during growth helps sustain flowers in a container.

Let cool weather set the pace: Expect pauses during hard frost or summer heat. Trim stretched stems to leafy growth if the crown is sound. Give light shade in hot weather and avoid burying small crowns under fallen leaves.

Check all three low crowns: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the three Rocky Purple Picotee plants clear of fallen Skimmia leaves and inspect each small root plug.
Skimmia Pot.seasonal:
Spring: Deadhead back to a leaf joint, trim winter-scorched edges and give a light feed once fresh buds begin to move.
Summer: Keep spent flowers and seed capsules removed; if heat stops flowering, shade the pot in the afternoon and expect a cooler-weather recovery.
Autumn: This is the main display period: inspect each of the three crowns, remove rain-damaged blooms and water the compost rather than the flowers.
Winter: Pick off collapsed petals before botrytis spreads and protect the small root ball from alternating waterlogging and hard frost.
Skimmia Pot.description: Three Rocky Purple Picotee Violas form a low purple-and-pale-edged flowering layer beneath the two Skimmias. Their cool-season display can pause in hard frost or summer heat. Each little crown needs light, airflow and reliable moisture, with spent flower stems and seed capsules removed before the shared pot becomes crowded with decaying petals.

Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.name: Viburnum ‘Lisarose’ — label confirmed
Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.light: Sun to shade. Shelter from cold drying winds
Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.water: Check the pot all year. Evergreen Viburnum still loses moisture in winter; water only when the root ball needs it and is unfrozen.
Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.care:
Prune after the winter flowers: Shorten only outgrowing branches after the spring display. Viburnum tinus develops the next flowers on its existing framework. Heavy late-summer or autumn trimming sacrifices buds; removing spent heads also reduces subsequent berries.

Allow for a shrub-sized root system: Top-dress in spring and repot when roots fill the container. Use a stable, drained loam-based container mix. Check leaf undersides and new shoots for Viburnum beetle damage rather than assuming every hole is drought stress.

Allow Lisarose room above the Vinca: For this Oak Lodge specimen Keep the wall pot's ivy-like trailer off the Viburnum base and plan greater root room as the shrub grows.
Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.seasonal:
Spring: Let flowering finish before any shaping, top-dress lightly and inspect for viburnum beetle damage.
Summer: Water the shared pot deeply during drought and take semi-ripe cuttings only if propagation is wanted.
Autumn: Allow the red bud colour to develop, stop feeding and clear fallen debris from the pot surface.
Winter: Enjoy the flower clusters and protect the container from prolonged freezing while keeping drainage open.
Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.description: ‘Lisarose’ is the upright evergreen centre of the new pot between Beds 2 and 3. Deep brick-red buds intensify as temperatures fall, then open to pink-and-white flower clusters from midwinter into spring, followed by dark blue ornamental berries. Its eventual shrub size means the current shared pot is an establishment home rather than unlimited permanent root space.

Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.name: Vinca minor ‘Illumination’ — label confirmed
Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.position: Trailing over the dividing wall — additional plant added August 2026
Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.light: Sun to shade. Bright shade retains colour without scorching
Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.water: Moderate; avoid prolonged drying. Vinca tolerates some dry shade once established, but trailing plants in pots still depend on the container's moisture.
Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.care:
Keep Vinca runners within bounds: Shorten trails that root into neighbouring planting. Remove unwanted rooted pieces completely. Trim after the main spring flowers, retaining leafy growth for the next display.

Remove green reversions: Cut all-green shoots back to their point of origin. Variegated forms can be overtaken by vigorous green growth. Give enough light for leaf colour without letting the shallow roots bake.

Keep the additional Vinca on the wall: For this Oak Lodge specimen Trim rooted runners before this second Illumination leaves its shared wall pot or smothers Lisarose.
Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.seasonal:
Spring: Trim winter damage, guide fresh runners and enjoy the violet flowers.
Summer: Shorten stems that reach unwanted soil and keep them clear of the Viburnum crown.
Autumn: Remove any rooted escapes and decide which cascades should remain for winter.
Winter: Keep drainage holes open and water only when the compost is genuinely dry.
Bed 2/3 Wall Pot.description: This is a second, additional Vinca minor ‘Illumination’, planted to trail over the Bed 2/3 dividing wall while the original remains in the Bed 5 big pot. Broad gold leaf centres edged narrowly in green provide year-round colour, with violet-blue flowers from spring into autumn. Rooting runners make it effective but require deliberate containment.

Viburnum Pot.description: Viburnum tinus Spirit (‘Anvi’) fills the new glazed pot at the foot of the steps with glossy evergreen foliage and a long winter display. facts.detail: Long lightly fragrant late-winter display

facts.label: Water
facts.detail: Evergreen Viburnum still loses moisture in winter; water only when the root ball needs it and is unfrozen.

facts.label: Care priority
facts.detail: Check drainage and root crowding in Spirit's own glazed pot rather than assuming it matches the shared Lisarose container.

careGuide.title: Prune after the winter flowers
careGuide.summary: Shorten only outgrowing branches after the spring display.
careGuide.detail: Viburnum tinus develops the next flowers on its existing framework. Heavy late-summer or autumn trimming sacrifices buds; removing spent heads also reduces subsequent berries.

careGuide.title: Allow for a shrub-sized root system
careGuide.summary: Top-dress in spring and repot when roots fill the container.
careGuide.detail: Use a stable, drained loam-based container mix. Check leaf undersides and new shoots for Viburnum beetle damage rather than assuming every hole is drought stress.

careGuide.summary: For this Oak Lodge specimen

waterSigns.under: The first useful warning is dull leaves, dry margins and buds that fail to develop. Check below the surface before soaking the full root area.
waterSigns.over: Watch for yellow foliage or dieback while compost stays cold and wet. If the root zone is still wet, pause watering and restore air to the compost or soil.

seasons.action: Let flowering finish, then prune only if needed and refresh the top layer of compost.
Water deeply through drought, feed lightly and inspect for viburnum beetle or whitefly.
Allow flower buds to form undisturbed and stop feeding so new growth hardens.
Keep the pot drained, protect it from prolonged hard freezes and enjoy the developing flower clusters.

problems.name: Aphids or scale
problems.sign: Distorted shoots, sticky leaves or fixed bumps on stems
problems.response: Inspect before treating, remove small colonies and improve airflow through crowded growth.

problems.name: Poor flowering
problems.sign: Healthy growth but few buds
problems.response: Check light, pruning time and excess nitrogen before adding more feed.

problems.name: Root stress
problems.sign: Yellowing or dieback in soil that remains wet
problems.response: Pause watering, inspect drainage and rule out root disease before pruning hard.

profile.caution: The ornamental berries are not for eating. Wear gloves and keep fruit away from children and pets.
profile.about: Spirit is the trade name for Viburnum tinus ‘Anvi’, a compact evergreen Laurustinus selected for a prolonged display of pink buds and pale winter flowers.
profile.provenanceNote: The photographed nursery label reads Viburnum tinus Spirit; ‘Anvi’ is its accepted cultivar epithet. This supersedes the earlier unresolved garden record.
